papers.full_text: AbstractCattle now occupy two epidemiologically distinct influenza interfaces. This Mini Review comparatively synthesizes epidemiological, pathological, experimental-transmission, genomic, and surveillance evidence for highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) and influenza D virus (IDV), asking how source ecology, tissue tropism, shedding, transmission, persistence, and zoonotic evidence differ between the two viruses. Genetically distinct H5N1 viruses have spilled over repeatedly from wild birds into United States dairy cattle. In lactating cows, infection is prominent in mammary alveolar epithelium and produces high titers of infectious virus in raw milk; inter-herd cattle movements have disseminated genotype B3.13 through dairy production networks. On affected farms, viral RNA has been detected in milk and respiratory specimens; infectious virus is recovered consistently from raw milk and mammary tissues but only sporadically from respiratory or environmental samples such as milking-parlour air and wastewater. These findings identify exposure settings but do not resolve the dominant natural cow-to-cow transmission route or how the virus reaches the mammary gland. Occupational infections have occurred, but sustained cattle adaptation or long-term reservoir status has not been demonstrated. In contrast, IDV is a cattle-adapted respiratory virus maintained through direct contact and short-range airborne transmission, with interlineage reassortment among IDV genome segments and frequent association with bovine respiratory disease complex (BRDC), although an independent causal role in BRDC remains unproven. Human seroreactivity and efficient replication in human airway models indicate exposure and biological compatibility, but not confirmed productive human infection or onward transmission. These contrasts support event-triggered, milk-centered investigation for H5N1 and longitudinal respiratory and genomic surveillance for IDV, built on shared One Health diagnostic, sequencing, epidemiological, and occupational-health infrastructure.Keywords: bovine respiratory disease complex, cattle, cross-species transmission, highly pathogenic avian influenza a(H5N1), influenza D virus, mammary tropism, one health surveillance 6.DiscussionAlthough both viruses infect cattle, their assessment requires different risk frameworks. Epidemiological consequences depend on the principal replication site and its relationship to production. In H5N1-infected dairy cows, mammary infection links viral shedding to milk production and milking practices. High-titer shedding in milk creates a direct exposure pathway; animal movements facilitate dissemination, while occupational contact creates opportunities for human exposure. IDV lacks this production-linked route; instead, it is maintained by respiratory transmission and interacts with other pathogens within the polymicrobial setting of BRDC. The most informative samples, genomic priorities, and response thresholds therefore differ.The principal uncertainties differ between the two viruses. For H5N1, the natural portal of entry, the relative contributions of milking-associated, respiratory, and environmental transmission, and whether cattle constitute a long-term reservoir remain unresolved. For IDV, respiratory replication and cattle-to-cattle transmission are established, but its independent contribution to naturally occurring BRDC remains uncertain, as does the clinical significance of human exposure signals. Resolving these questions will require studies that integrate viral kinetics with tissue lesions, co-pathogen dynamics, animal-movement histories, clinical outcomes, and transmission phenotypes.The supporting evidence is asymmetric in scope and design. H5N1 evidence derives mainly from intensively investigated outbreaks in lactating United States dairy cattle and a few experiments; extrapolation to non-lactating cattle, beef cattle, calves, and other production systems remains uncertain. IDV studies span more regions and years but often use cross-sectional PCR or serology, heterogeneous sampling, and incomplete genomic data. These differences preclude simple comparisons of prevalence, transmission efficiency, pathogenicity, or zoonotic risk. Preparedness should therefore reflect virus-specific replication sites and production systems rather than host species alone. 1.IntroductionInfluenza A virus ecology is commonly framed around wild aquatic birds as the principal natural reservoir, with poultry, swine, and humans occupying different host roles in amplification, reassortment, adaptation, and disease emergence (Krammer et al., 2018). Cattle received little attention because sustained influenza A virus circulation had not been documented in bovine populations. In 2024, clade 2.3.4.4b highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) [HPAI A(H5N1)] was confirmed in United States dairy cattle (Caserta et al., 2024), and genomic analysis traced spread through interconnected dairy production networks (Nguyen et al., 2025). A joint assessment by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), World Health Organization (WHO), and World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH), based on data available through 1 March 2026, documented several independent spillovers from wild birds into cattle, demonstrating that multiple viral genotypes can infect this host (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations et al., 2026).The emergence of H5N1 in dairy cattle established a production-linked influenza interface centered on lactation, milking, and cattle movement. Field and experimental studies documented mammary infection, high virus titers in milk, mastitis, abnormal milk, and production loss (Caserta et al., 2024; Baker et al., 2025; Peña-Mosca et al., 2025). Movement of infected cattle facilitated long-distance dissemination (Nguyen et al., 2025), whereas genetically distinct spillovers from wild birds created new points of entry (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations et al., 2026). Thus, raw milk and milking procedures are central exposure settings, cattle movement links herds, and contaminated equipment, aerosols, wastewater, cross-species contact, and occupational contact define additional exposure pathways whose contributions to natural transmission remain unresolved.Influenza D virus (IDV) follows a different ecological pattern. First isolated from a pig with respiratory disease (Hause et al., 2013), it was later established as a distinct orthomyxovirus with cattle as its principal maintenance host (Hause et al., 2014). Experimental studies in calves demonstrated direct-contact (Ferguson et al., 2016) and short-range airborne transmission (Salem et al., 2019). Case-control (Ng et al., 2015) and cohort (Nissly et al., 2020) studies associate IDV with bovine respiratory disease complex (BRDC) without establishing independent or dominant causation. Whole-genome studies document diversification and geographic structure (Limaye et al., 2024), interlineage reassortment among IDV genome segments (Collin et al., 2015), and regional persistence (Li H. et al., 2026), favoring longitudinal surveillance over outbreak-limited investigation.The two viruses differ most clearly in their principal replication sites. Mammary replication links H5N1 to milk and dairy production networks, whereas respiratory replication links IDV to enzootic circulation and BRDC. We therefore compare shedding, transmission, disease context, evolutionary dynamics, and surveillance across these compartments, while distinguishing occupational exposure signals from evidence of productive human infection or onward transmission. 2.Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) in dairy cattle: emergence, mammary infection, and unresolved transmission routesThe United States cattle epizootic was initially dominated by genotype B3.13. Phylogenetic and epidemiological analysis support a single wild-bird-to-bovine spillover followed by extensive cattle-associated, movement-linked spread (Nguyen et al., 2025). Genotype D1.1 detections in Nevada and Arizona represented two additional independent spillovers from wild birds, each with limited cattle transmission (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations et al., 2026). Repeated entry and sustained circulation are therefore separate processes. Unresolved questions are how often wild-bird-derived H5N1 crosses into cattle, which changes arise after spillover, and which routes sustain transmission. Extensive cattle-associated spread alone does not establish long-term reservoir status.After introduction, the distinctive pathological feature in lactating cows is mammary infection. Field investigations detected abundant viral RNA and infectious virus in milk, epithelial necrosis, and H5N1 antigen by immunohistochemistry in mammary alveolar epithelial cells (Caserta et al., 2024). Intramammary inoculation reproduced severe mastitis, abnormal milk, reduced production, and high-titer milk shedding (Baker et al., 2025). In contrast, oronasal inoculation of calves produced moderate upper-respiratory replication and nasal shedding, without detected transmission to sentinels (Halwe et al., 2025). Because these experiments differed in age, lactation status, target tissue, and inoculation route, they establish mammary tropism but do not identify the natural entry route.Transmission evidence remains less definitive. Low-dose intramammary challenge caused robust infection and high-titer shedding in milk, but transmission to sentinel cows was not detected despite repeated exposure to contaminated milking equipment and close contact. Respiratory and oral exposures were also less efficient than intramammary inoculation at establishing productive infection under the tested conditions (Lee et al., 2026). Across 14 California dairy farms, infectious virus was recovered from milking-parlour air on three farms and from wastewater on one farm; viral RNA was also detected in exhaled breath and milk from cows without overt clinical signs (Campbell et al., 2026). The persistent, spatially heterogeneous distribution of positive udder quarters suggested that shared milking equipment was unlikely to be the sole route. Collectively, these observations identify plausible exposure settings but do not resolve the natural portal of entry or the route by which the virus reaches the mammary gland.Mechanistic studies have examined why mammary tissue is permissive. Plant lectins and haemagglutinin probes identified glycans compatible with contemporary avian H5 binding, but gave discordant signals for putative human-type receptors; lectin staining cannot establish functional receptor use (Kristensen et al., 2024; Rios Carrasco et al., 2024). Glycan binding also cannot explain route-specific infection or farm transmission. A bovine clade 2.3.4.4b isolate replicated in mammary and airway organoids without demonstrating respiratory transmission in vivo (Li C. et al., 2026). Intramammary challenge elicited compartmentalized cytokine responses, systemic myeloid remodeling, lymphocyte activation, and increased H5- and N1-specific antibody titers (Singh et al., 2026). Protease availability, local innate immunity, tissue physiology, dose, and lactation stage may also contribute.The consequences of mammary infection extend from production loss to cross-species exposure. In one affected herd, about one fifth of adult cows developed clinical disease, and average milk production per affected cow was estimated to be 901 kg lower than expected during the 60 days after diagnosis (Peña-Mosca et al., 2025). Because this estimate comes from a single herd, it should not be extrapolated across management systems. Raw milk or colostrum from infected cows can also expose other species: farm cats fed these products developed fatal systemic and neurological disease, and closely related viruses were found in cattle and cats on the same premises (Burrough et al., 2024).For people, the clearest evidence is occupational spillover. The first recognized infection involved a Texas dairy worker who developed conjunctivitis after exposure to affected cattle (Uyeki et al., 2024). Additional infections were later identified among dairy workers, who usually presented with conjunctivitis or mild respiratory illness (Garg et al., 2025). These cases do not demonstrate sustained human-to-human transmission. The May 2026 FAO/WHO/WOAH assessment rated the global risk to the general population as low and the risk to occupationally or frequently exposed people as low to moderate, depending on local epidemiology and protective measures (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations et al., 2026). A WHO update covering reports available through 7 July 2026 likewise found no sustained human-to-human transmission of A(H5) viruses (World Health Organization, 2026). Validated commercial pasteurization conditions effectively inactivate H5N1, whereas raw milk from infected cattle may expose people and animals to infectious virus (United States Food and Drug Administration, 2026).At the viral level, replication in cattle creates a new selective environment for H5N1. Early in the outbreak, polymerase substitutions including PB2 M631L and PA K497R became enriched among cattle-associated viruses and were shown to increase polymerase activity in bovine cells and enhance viral replication in mammary tissue models (Dholakia et al., 2026). However, these substitutions have not been shown to confer efficient bovine respiratory or airborne transmission, and their detection alone is insufficient to infer pandemic potential (Dholakia et al., 2026; Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations et al., 2026). Substitutions that recur or increase in frequency should be evaluated phenotypically in relevant bovine and other mammalian models. 3.Influenza D virus in cattle: enzootic respiratory circulation, BRDC, and evolutionIDV was first isolated in 2011 from a pig with respiratory disease and described as influenza C-like (Hause et al., 2013). Subsequent work established IDV as a distinct orthomyxovirus and identified cattle as its principal maintenance host, based partly on substantially higher seroprevalence in cattle than in swine (Hause et al., 2014). Surveillance has since documented broad but uneven circulation in bovine populations (Collin et al., 2015; Limaye et al., 2024; Li H. et al., 2026).In experimentally infected cattle, IDV replicates in the upper and lower airways, causes mild clinical signs and tracheal lesions, and transmits to direct-contact animals (Ferguson et al., 2016). In another experiment, sentinel calves housed 3 m from aerosol-inoculated animals became infected despite the absence of direct or fomite contact, supporting short-range airborne transmission (Salem et al., 2019). Together, these experiments support direct-contact and short-range airborne transmission. Transport and commingling may amplify transmission under field conditions, although their contributions to the long-term maintenance of IDV in cattle populations have not been quantified.IDV is transmissible among cattle, but its independent role in BRDC remains uncertain. A metagenomic case-control study detected IDV more often in cattle with severe respiratory disease than in matched controls (Ng et al., 2015). A later cohort linked higher IDV loads and a greater burden of viral coinfection with clinical disease (Nissly et al., 2020). BRDC is nevertheless multifactorial and is shaped by transport stress, crowding, host immune status, bacterial colonization, management practices, and multiple viral infections. An IDV-positive RT-qPCR result confirms the presence of viral RNA in the tested respiratory specimen but does not by itself distinguish active infection from transient carriage or establish that IDV caused the clinical syndrome.Coinfection experiments provide evidence of disease enhancement. Calves infected with both IDV and Mycoplasma bovis developed earlier and more severe disease than calves given either agent alone, and IDV promoted M. bovis colonization of the lower respiratory tract (Lion et al., 2021). These findings support a contributory role for IDV within the BRDC pathogen network, although the magnitude of that contribution remains uncertain. Prospective studies should relate viral kinetics to airway lesions, bacterial colonization of the lower respiratory tract, host responses, and clinical outcomes.Enzootic circulation provides repeated opportunities for diversification. Early work identified cocirculating D/OK and D/660 lineages and interlineage reassortment among the seven IDV genome segments (Collin et al., 2015). Subsequent whole-genome analysis revealed further diversification, geographic structure, and additional interlineage reassortment (Limaye et al., 2024). In Northeast China, D/Yamagata/2019-lineage viruses were detected only sporadically, yet phylogenetic continuity indicated ongoing circulation (Li H. et al., 2026). Neutralizing antibodies were more frequent in cattle-exposed adults than controls (White et al., 2016). A cross-shift study detected IDV RNA in dairy-worker nasal washes without association with symptoms and could not distinguish contamination, carriage, and productive infection (Leibler et al., 2023). full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractCattle now occupy two epidemiologically distinct influenza interfaces. This Mini Review comparatively synthesizes epidemiological, pathological, experimental-transmission, genomic, and surveillance evidence for highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) and influenza D virus (IDV), asking how source ecology, tissue tropism, shedding, transmission, persistence, and zoonotic evidence differ between the two viruses. Genetically distinct H5N1 viruses have spilled over repeatedly from wild birds into United States dairy cattle. In lactating cows, infection is prominent in mammary alveolar epithelium and produces high titers of infectious virus in raw milk; inter-herd cattle movements have disseminated genotype B3.13 through dairy production networks. On affected farms, viral RNA has been detected in milk and respiratory specimens; infectious virus is recovered consistently from raw milk and mammary tissues but only sporadically from respiratory or environmental samples such as milking-parlour air and wastewater. These findings identify exposure settings but do not resolve the dominant natural cow-to-cow transmission route or how the virus reaches the mammary gland. Occupational infections have occurred, but sustained cattle adaptation or long-term reservoir status has not been demonstrated. In contrast, IDV is a cattle-adapted respiratory virus maintained through direct contact and short-range airborne transmission, with interlineage reassortment among IDV genome segments and frequent association with bovine respiratory disease complex (BRDC), although an independent causal role in BRDC remains unproven. Human seroreactivity and efficient replication in human airway models indicate exposure and biological compatibility, but not confirmed productive human infection or onward transmission. These contrasts support event-triggered, milk-centered investigation for H5N1 and longitudinal respiratory and genomic surveillance for IDV, built on shared One Health diagnostic, sequencing, epidemiological, and occupational-health infrastructure.Keywords: bovine respiratory disease complex, cattle, cross-species transmission, highly pathogenic avian influenza a(H5N1), influenza D virus, mammary tropism, one health surveillance
full_text_sections.discussion: 6.DiscussionAlthough both viruses infect cattle, their assessment requires different risk frameworks. Epidemiological consequences depend on the principal replication site and its relationship to production. In H5N1-infected dairy cows, mammary infection links viral shedding to milk production and milking practices. High-titer shedding in milk creates a direct exposure pathway; animal movements facilitate dissemination, while occupational contact creates opportunities for human exposure. IDV lacks this production-linked route; instead, it is maintained by respiratory transmission and interacts with other pathogens within the polymicrobial setting of BRDC. The most informative samples, genomic priorities, and response thresholds therefore differ.The principal uncertainties differ between the two viruses. For H5N1, the natural portal of entry, the relative contributions of milking-associated, respiratory, and environmental transmission, and whether cattle constitute a long-term reservoir remain unresolved. For IDV, respiratory replication and cattle-to-cattle transmission are established, but its independent contribution to naturally occurring BRDC remains uncertain, as does the clinical significance of human exposure signals. Resolving these questions will require studies that integrate viral kinetics with tissue lesions, co-pathogen dynamics, animal-movement histories, clinical outcomes, and transmission phenotypes.The supporting evidence is asymmetric in scope and design. H5N1 evidence derives mainly from intensively investigated outbreaks in lactating United States dairy cattle and a few experiments; extrapolation to non-lactating cattle, beef cattle, calves, and other production systems remains uncertain. IDV studies span more regions and years but often use cross-sectional PCR or serology, heterogeneous sampling, and incomplete genomic data. These differences preclude simple comparisons of prevalence, transmission efficiency, pathogenicity, or zoonotic risk. Preparedness should therefore reflect virus-specific replication sites and production systems rather than host species alone.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand how the ecology, tissue tropism, shedding, transmission, persistence, and zoonotic potential of highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) and influenza D virus (IDV) differ, with a focus on their distinct interfaces in cattle.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved case-control and cohort studies in dairy cattle, examining the epidemiological and clinical associations of H5N1 and IDV with bovine respiratory disease complex (BRDC) and milk production. It also included metagenomic analyses and longitudinal surveillance across different regions and time periods.
analysis.methods: The study employed metagenomic sequencing, PCR, serology, and experimental transmission studies in calves to investigate shedding, transmission, and disease context. Whole-genome sequencing was emphasized to trace viral movement and reassortment events.
analysis.main_results: Viral RNA was detected in milk and respiratory specimens of H5N1-infected cows, with infectious virus consistently recovered from raw milk and mammary tissues. For IDV, higher viral loads and coinfections were associated with clinical disease, but no independent causal role in BRDC was confirmed.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight the distinct replication sites and transmission dynamics of H5N1 and IDV, emphasizing the need for virus-specific surveillance strategies and risk frameworks.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results inform targeted surveillance and risk management strategies for H5N1 and IDV, particularly in dairy production systems and respiratory disease contexts, by identifying unique exposure pathways and transmission routes.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited by the reliance on cross-sectional PCR and serology for IDV, and by unresolved uncertainties regarding the natural portal of entry and transmission routes for H5N1. The confidence is moderate.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the distinct interfaces of highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) and influenza D virus (IDV) in cattle, emphasizing their different replication sites and transmission dynamics. H5N1 is associated with mammary alveolar epithelium, leading to high viral shedding in milk and dissemination through animal movements. IDV, on the other hand, is a cattle-adapted respiratory virus maintained by direct contact and short-range airborne transmission, often linked to bovine respiratory disease complex (BRDC). The research highlights the need for virus-specific surveillance strategies, as the principal replication sites and production systems influence epidemiological consequences. However, the study has limitations, including reliance on cross-sectional methods for IDV and unresolved uncertainties about H5N1 transmission routes. The findings suggest that preparedness should reflect these differences rather than focusing solely on host species, with moderate confidence in the conclusions due to the nature of the evidence and unresolved questions.

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在了解 高致病性禽流感 A(H5N1) 和 D 型流感病毒 (IDV) 的生态学、组织嗜性、脱落、传播、持久性和人畜共患潜力有何不同,重点是它们在牛体内的不同界面。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及奶牛病例对照和 队列研究 研究,研究了 H5N1 和 IDV 与牛呼吸道疾病综合征 (BRDC) 和产奶量的流行病学和临床关联。它还包括跨不同地区和时间段的宏基因组分析和纵向 监测。
analysis_zh.methods: 该研究采用宏基因组测序、PCR、血清学 和实验性 传播 研究来研究犊牛的脱落、传播 和疾病背景。强调全 基因组 测序来追踪病毒运动和重配事件。
analysis_zh.main_results: 在感染 H5N1 的奶牛的牛奶和呼吸道样本中检测到病毒 RNA,并且从原料奶和乳腺组织中始终回收到感染性病毒。对于 IDV,较高的病毒载量和合并感染与临床疾病相关,但在 BRDC 中没有独立的因果作用得到证实。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果强调了 H5N1 和 IDV 的不同复制位点和 传播 动态,强调需要针对病毒的 传播 策略和风险框架。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 结果通过确定独特的暴露途径和 传播 途径,为 H5N1 和 IDV 的针对性 监测 和风险管理策略提供信息,特别是在乳制品生产系统和呼吸道疾病背景下。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 由于 IDV 对横断面 PCR 和 血清学 的依赖,以及 H5N1 自然进入门户和 传播 途径尚未解决的不确定性,证据有限。信心是中等的。

papers.title: Recent advances in universal influenza vaccine platforms: paving the way for universal H5N1 vaccines and pandemic readiness
papers.abstract: Abstract The H5N1 influenza threat is a significant issue to the overall health of the population in the world, and it demands new approaches in vaccine development and implementation. The critical path forward is the development of universal vaccine platforms, which provide long-term cross-protection against various H5N1 strains. This type of vaccines, based on conserved regions of viruses, is necessary to provide long term immunity against antigenic variation. The future of vaccines should be based on the ability to generate both cellular and humoral immunity and provide the greatest level of protection against a variety of viral variants. It is also crucial that agile manufacturing capacities are established, which can swiftly expand the production of vaccines to satisfy the demand in the world in the case of an influenza outbreak. The technology of mRNA vaccines, viral vectors, or microneedle patches can be adapted to novel strains rapidly and responds effectively to the situation when rapid and effective responses are required. Also, fair global distribution policies can be crucial to make it possible to make vaccines available to the population of low- and middle-income countries. The international response needs to focus on equity, whereby inequality in access to vaccines is minimized. This has been the ultimate solution of combining universal vaccines, cross-protection, agile production, and equity over the world to reduce the threat of H5N1 pandemic. By developing these measures, the world community can be more ready to the upcoming outbreak of influenza, and access to a vaccine can be timely, extensive, and efficient.

papers.title_zh: 通用流感 疫苗 平台的最新进展:为通用 H5N1 疫苗 和大流行准备铺平道路
papers.source_body_en: Abstract The H5N1 influenza threat is a significant issue to the overall health of the population in the world, and it demands new approaches in vaccine development and implementation. The critical path forward is the development of universal vaccine platforms, which provide long-term cross-protection against various H5N1 strains. This type of vaccines, based on conserved regions of viruses, is necessary to provide long term immunity against antigenic variation. The future of vaccines should be based on the ability to generate both cellular and humoral immunity and provide the greatest level of protection against a variety of viral variants. It is also crucial that agile manufacturing capacities are established, which can swiftly expand the production of vaccines to satisfy the demand in the world in the case of an influenza outbreak. The technology of mRNA vaccines, viral vectors, or microneedle patches can be adapted to novel strains rapidly and responds effectively to the situation when rapid and effective responses are required. Also, fair global distribution policies can be crucial to make it possible to make vaccines available to the population of low- and middle-income countries. The international response needs to focus on equity, whereby inequality in access to vaccines is minimized. This has been the ultimate solution of combining universal vaccines, cross-protection, agile production, and equity over the world to reduce the threat of H5N1 pandemic. By developing these measures, the world community can be more ready to the upcoming outbreak of influenza, and access to a vaccine can be timely, extensive, and efficient.

The study is based on an administrative announcement, which limits the evidence strength to moderate. It contributes to the understanding of how public health threats can influence operational decisions in isolated settings, particularly regarding staff well-being. The findings suggest that psychosocial considerations should be integrated into broader outbreak preparedness strategies. The study does not provide detailed methods or results, relying instead on a policy-based decision. While it raises awareness about the human dimension of zoonotic outbreaks, it lacks empirical data to support broader scientific or public health implications.

papers.title: Nowcasting officially reported highly pathogenic avian influenza outbreak counts under heterogeneous reporting delays
papers.abstract: Official animal disease series are often incomplete due to delays in reporting. This retrospective observational study evaluated whether increased model complexity enhances probabilistic nowcasts of eventual officially reported outbreak-equivalent counts. We reconstructed historical information states from a fixed extraction from the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) World Animal Health Information System (WAHIS), which included 46,860 highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) and 72,690 African swine fever (ASF) outbreaks. Twelve prespecified methods were assessed over 78 locked cutoffs for 2024–2025 using the Weighted Interval Score (WIS), calibration diagnostics, block bootstrap, simulation, and a separately frozen USDA APHIS transfer evaluation. The primary HPAI analysis included 35,880 observations from 115 country–host units. At week closure, only 7.6% of eventual HPAI and 6.7% of ASF outbreak equivalents were visible, with completeness varying by host, region, year, season, and workload. The prespecified primary hypothesis was not supported: the delay-aware temporal network scored 6.9% worse than the hierarchical Bayesian comparator, and the relational graph changed WIS by only 0.4%. Gradient-boosted quantile regression improved WIS by 18.5% (absolute difference −0.0397, 95% interval −0.0553 to −0.0255), but the improvement reached 26.0% among high-volume reporters and reversed to a 6.3% deficit among units with minimal reporting history. Conditioning on the partial count was 24.7% worse than a matched no-delay network at cohort age 0 and performed better thereafter. The slower-reporting ASF system reversed the pooled contrast, whereas the APHIS module improved WIS by 10.1% after system-specific retraining. Adding an explicit mass at zero enhanced the transparent comparator by 18.8% and resulted in no detectable difference from gradient boosting; the neural model remained 17.4% worse under the same recalibration. In exploratory analyses, gradient boosting cleared the prespecified 5% gate under all six cohort definitions and all three maturity horizons. Performance deteriorated markedly for high-volume countries and regions excluded from training. These estimates pertain to eventual officially reported outbreak equivalents under the surveillance conditions studied, not undetected infections.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the impact of reporting delays on the accuracy of nowcasting models for highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) outbreaks. Using data from the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) World Animal Health Information System (WAHIS), the researchers evaluated whether increased model complexity could improve probabilistic nowcasts. They found that the delay-aware temporal network performed worse than the hierarchical Bayesian comparator, and the relational graph had minimal impact on the Weighted Interval Score (WIS). Gradient-boosted quantile regression showed some improvement, but its effectiveness varied by reporting volume. The study highlights the challenges of using incomplete data for outbreak prediction and suggests the need for more robust models that account for reporting delays. However, the results are limited by the retrospective nature of the analysis and potential issues with generalisability.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在解决由于报告延迟而导致官方动物疾病系列不完整的挑战,特别是 高致病性禽流感 (HPAI)。该研究试图评估增加模型复杂性是否可以改善 暴发 等效计数的概率即时预报。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 使用世界动物卫生组织 (WOAH) 世界动物卫生信息系统 (WAHIS) 的数据进行了一项回顾性观察研究,其中包括 46,860 例 HPAI 和 72,690 例非洲猪瘟 (ASF) 暴发。主要 HPAI 分析涉及来自 115 个国家 宿主 单位的 35,880 个观测值。
elements_zh.methods: 使用加权区间评分 (WIS)、校准诊断、块引导、模拟和单独冻结的 USDA APHIS 转移评估,对 2024-2025 年 78 个锁定截止点对 12 种预先指定的方法进行了评估。作为方法的一部分,还测试了梯度增强分位数回归和零时的显式质量。
elements_zh.main_results: 在一周结束时,只有 7.6% 的最终 HPAI 和 6.7% 的 ASF 暴发 等效项可见,其完整性因 宿主、地区、年份、季节和工作量而异。延迟感知时间网络的得分比分层贝叶斯比较器差 6.9%,而关系图仅改变 WIS 0.4%。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 预先指定的主要假设不受支持,这表明模型复杂性的增加并没有显着增强 暴发 等效计数的临近预报。该研究通过评估报告延迟对模型性能的影响引入了一种新颖的方法。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为 HPAI 暴发 开发更准确的临近预报模型提供了信息,这可以改进 监测 和响应策略。他们还强调了公共卫生和兽医科学报告延迟的重要性。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 对于被排除在培训之外的高容量国家和地区,绩效显着恶化,这表明普遍性受到限制。由于该研究是基于历史数据和回顾性分析,因此证据是中等的。

papers.title: Rare-event modelling of highly pathogenic avian influenza presence for poultry biosecurity surveillance in Delaware
papers.abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) remains a major threat to poultry production and animal-health preparedness, but its rarity makes spatially consistent local surveillance prioritization difficult. This study developed a spatial rare-event modelling framework to transform sparse HPAI detections into 3-kilometre surveillance-priority scores in Delaware and evaluated adjacent-region transfer to Maryland. HPAI presence was modelled using poultry-house infrastructure, wetland and hydrographic proximity, agricultural land cover, topography, and wild-bird occurrence predictors. Model performance was assessed using spatial-block validation in Delaware and transfer to a separate Maryland grid. Elastic-net logistic regression achieved the highest Delaware area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) point estimate of 0.935 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.868–0.986), but discrimination was not statistically distinguishable from ridge logistic regression. The highest-ranked 5%, 10%, and 20% of Delaware cells contained 63.6% (95% CI: 30.8–89.1%), 81.8% (48.2–97.7%), and 90.9% (58.7–99.8%) of the 11 HPAI-positive cells, respectively. In Maryland, the Delaware-trained model achieved an AUC of 0.898 (95% CI: 0.719–0.984) and captured 64.3% (95% CI: 35.1–87.2%) and 85.7% (57.2–98.2%) of the 14 HPAI-positive cells in the highest-ranked 5% and 10%, respectively. Poultry infrastructure provided most of the discrimination (AUC = 0.930); adding environmental predictors increased AUC to 0.935, a difference not statistically distinguishable from zero. These findings support surveillance-priority screening for poultry biosecurity, outreach, and preventive action without attributing disease to individual farms.

papers.abstract_zh: 高致病性禽流感 (HPAI) 仍然是家禽生产和动物健康准备的主要威胁,但其稀有性使得空间一致的局部 监测 优先级变得困难。本研究开发了一个空间罕见事件建模框架,将稀疏 HPAI 检测转换为特拉华州 3 公里 监测 优先级分数,并评估了向马里兰州的邻近区域转移。使用禽舍基础设施、湿地和水文邻近性、农业用地覆盖、地形和野鸟发生预测因素对高致病性禽流感的存在进行建模。使用特拉华州的空间块验证来评估模型性能,并转移到单独的马里兰州网格。弹性网逻辑回归在接受者操作特征曲线 (AUC) 点估计下达到了最高的特拉华面积 0.935(95% 置信区间 [CI]:0.868–0.986),但区分度与岭逻辑回归在统计上没有区别。排名最高的 5%、10% 和 20% 特拉华细胞分别包含 11 个 HPAI 阳性细胞的 63.6%(95% CI:30.8-89.1%)、81.8%(48.2-97.7%)和 90.9%(58.7-99.8%)。在马里兰州,特拉华州训练的模型的 AUC 为 0.898 (95% CI: 0.719–0.984),并分别捕获了排名最高的 5% 和 10% 中 14 个 HPAI 阳性细胞的 64.3% (95% CI: 35.1–87.2%) 和 85.7% (57.2–98.2%)。家禽基础设施提供了大部分歧视(AUC = 0.930);添加环境预测因子将 AUC 增加到 0.935,这一差异在统计上与零无法区分。这些发现支持对家禽生物安全、外展和预防行动进行 监测 优先筛查,而不将疾病归因于各个农场。

papers.title: Dynamical Systems Analysis of Avian Influenza Models: A Scoping Review of Mathematical Frameworks
papers.abstract: Mathematical models have been widely used to investigate avian influenza transmission and disease dynamics. However, to our knowledge, no review has specifically and systematically examined avian influenza models from a qualitative dynamical systems perspective. Consequently, the modelling frameworks, analytical techniques, and theoretical findings generated from these studies have not been adequately synthesized. This scoping review will address this gap by identifying and classifying avian influenza models that employ qualitative dynamical systems analyses and synthesizing their key theoretical findings. The review will provide a clearer understanding of disease transmission, persistence, stability, and control, while identifying gaps and priorities for future modelling research

The review highlights the lack of systematic analysis of these models from a qualitative dynamical systems perspective. It aims to classify and synthesize the key theoretical findings from existing models to improve understanding of disease transmission, persistence, stability, and control. The review identifies gaps in current research and outlines priorities for future modeling studies. The analysis is limited to avian influenza-specific evidence and does not include related entities unless explicitly tied to the target.

papers.full_text: Recent outbreaks of emerging infectious diseases, along with advances in neurological and other biomedical research, have increased the use of non-human primates (NHPs) as preclinical models. Their close phylogenetic and physiological similarities to humans make them valuable for translational research, especially during public health emergencies. However, NHPs can harbor a wide range of viral pathogens, some of which pose zoonotic risks and may compromise animal health and experimental reproducibility. Therefore, quarantine procedures, pathogen surveillance, and biosecurity programs are essential for the safe and reliable use of NHPs in research. Despite this need, comprehensive reviews linking national quarantine policies with the biological and epidemiological characteristics of major viral pathogens and their relevance to disease surveillance and control remain limited. This review compares national quarantine frameworks for NHPs, examines pathogen-specific features, and discusses their implications for quarantine and surveillance. We emphasize the need for an integrated, risk-based approach incorporating longitudinal microbiological monitoring, multimodal diagnostic assessment, facility-level response procedures, occupational health preparedness, and internationally harmonized quarantine standards. 4DiscussionRecent WHO pathogen prioritization efforts have emphasized family-level preparedness and response strategies (197). This concept is also relevant to NHP quarantine because many viruses of concern in primate colonies, particularly members of the families Retroviridae and Herpesviridae, are capable of establishing persistent or latent infections (Table 2). In addition, other important pathogens, such as polyomaviruses and mycobacteria, may persist chronically after introduction. These biological features make complete elimination difficult. Moreover, NHP breeding and research facilities often rely on long-term group-housing systems, which may facilitate pathogen maintenance and transmission within colonies. Given that major NHP-associated viruses can be transmitted through horizontal and, in some cases, vertical routes, the introduction of infected animals may increase the likelihood of transmission to other animals within the colony (Table 3). Therefore, family-level diagnostic preparedness, continuous surveillance, and internationally coordinated quarantine practices are important for NHP facilities.Table 2Quarantine-associated viruses in microbiological monitoring because many NHP-associated viruses generally cause asymptomatic or only mild infections, although various clinical manifestations may occasionally occur (Figure 2). Nevertheless, microbiological surveillance standards differ among countries, and enforceable requirements remain limited. Given that NHPs are commonly distributed from a limited number of breeding facilities to research institutions worldwide, effective quarantine should be addressed not only at the level of individual facilities but also harmonized international standards and coordinated surveillance (18). From a One Health perspective, there is a need to define a minimum set of diseases for quarantine screening, particularly latent or persistent viral infections and tuberculosis, to reduce the risks associated with the international movement of NHPs. Their potential for subclinical infection and zoonotic transmission further highlights the importance of integrated surveillance for NHP colony health, occupational safety, research reliability, and public health (Figure 3). However, important knowledge gaps remain regarding transmission dynamics in NHP research and facility settings and the associated risks to humans. The current evidence base is also limited by uneven species coverage, heterogeneity among institutions and surveillance practices, and insufficient data for certain viral pathogens. Given these uncertainties, a precautionary approach based on a minimum level of routine surveillance is warranted to reduce the risk of undetected infection and transmission. Considering the variability in screening practices among institutions and the limitations of direct antigen or pathogen detection for many retroviruses and herpesviruses, we propose that this minimum surveillance framework should include at least annual antibody testing for major persistent or latent viruses, including SIV, SRV, STLV, B virus, SCMV, and SVV.Figure 2Differential diagnostic overview of quarantine-associated major viral diseases in non-human primates by clinical presentation and host group. Among macaque viruses, B virus, SIV, STLV, and SV40 can infect humans; B virus, STLV, and SV40 are associated with subclinical or persistent infection in nonhuman primates, while B virus is highlighted as potentially fatal in humans.In addition to determining seropositivity using established diagnostic cut-off values, longitudinal evaluation of antibody titers, rather than reliance on a single time-point measurement, may be important for assessing infection status and identifying changes associated with exposure, viral reactivation, or potential transmission within a colony. Antibody results should also be evaluated beyond the individual animal level, with comparisons among groups, housing rooms, and facilities to identify temporal changes in exposure and transmission patterns. Nevertheless, antibody testing should not be used in isolation. Serological findings should be interpreted together with clinical observation, necropsy findings, antigen or molecular assays, hematological and serum biochemical data, and expert interpretation. Because infected animals may exhibit only mild or no apparent clinical signs and viral shedding may be intermittent, repeated antigen or molecular testing of animals with suspected infection or positive serological findings may be necessary to confirm active viral shedding.Furthermore, facility-level standard operating procedures (SOPs) should be established in advance for each pathogen to define appropriate response measures according to different combinations of diagnostic results, such as seropositivity alone or concurrent positive serological and antigen or molecular findings. The detection of these pathogens should prompt the implementation of appropriate SOPs to prevent further transmission within the colony, restrict the transfer of infected or exposed animals, and protect personnel from zoonotic exposure. For high-risk zoonotic agents such as B virus, rapid post-exposure evaluation and appropriate antiviral prophylaxis or treatment are particularly important to reduce the risk of severe human disease. Thus, SOPs, routine training, exposure-response plans, and access to appropriate medical countermeasures should be established before incidents occur.In addition to viruses of the families Retroviridae and Herpesviridae, four viral diseases of particular concern were also included because of their high pathogenicity in humans and recent public health importance. Although NHPs are not generally considered natural reservoirs for these viruses, they may become infected as susceptible or incidental hosts and therefore warrant consideration during quarantine. Because these infections can cause recognizable clinical signs in macaques, as in humans, careful clinical surveillance is important during the quarantine period. Unlike persistent or latent viral infections, quarantine surveillance for Marburg virus, Ebola virus, MPXV, and rabies virus should focus on the early recognition of suggestive clinical signs, followed by the implementation of appropriate precautionary biosafety measures before prompt diagnostic testing using antigen or molecular assays and, when necessary, postmortem examination. Rapid identification of suspected or confirmed cases should then trigger appropriate public health and facility-level response measures, including assessment and management of potentially exposed personnel, isolation of affected animals, and measures to prevent further transmission. 1IntroductionZoonotic infectious diseases are increasingly emerging worldwide, driven by multiple factors, including increased global travel and trade, climate change, urbanization, and land-use change (1). In recent years, viruses with pandemic potential, such as severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) and highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses (HPAIVs), have posed significant global public health threats. In response to these emerging infectious diseases, various preclinical animal models have been widely used in infectious disease researches, including mice, hamsters, ferrets, guinea pigs, and non-human primates (NHPs) (2). Because effective therapeutics and vaccines may not be readily available for newly emerging viral diseases, preclinical studies using animal models play an important role in the development and evaluation of novel countermeasures.NHP models are more anatomically, physiologically, immunologically, and genetically similar to humans than other commonly used preclinical animal models. For this reason, NHPs have often been used as important preclinical models to investigate the pathogenesis of infections, caused by Ebola virus, SARS-CoV-2, and H5N1 HPAIVs and to support the development of vaccines and therapeutics against these viruses (3–6). For example, mRNA vaccines targeting SARS-CoV-2 have been evaluated for efficacy and safety using NHP models. In addition, ZMapp, a monoclonal antibody-based therapy against Ebola virus, demonstrated efficacy in treating Ebola virus infection in NHP models (7). These findings from NHP studies provided evidence supporting the clinical translation and emergency use of these interventions during outbreaks under regulatory and ethical frameworks such as the WHO MEURI guidelines (8). Consequently, the use of NHP models has increased significantly in recent years, resulting in a shortage of available NHPs (9, 10).NHPs have been reported globally to harbor various pathogens that can cause latent or subclinical infections, including B virus (Cercopithecine herpesvirus 1), simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), simian T cell lymphotropic/leukemia virus (STLV), simian type D retrovirus (SRV), and Mycobacterium (M) tuberculosis, all of which should be absent from specific pathogen-free (SPF) colonies (11–13) (Figure 1). Also, simian polyomaviruses, including simian virus 40 (SV40), have been detected macaque species (14). Therefore, latent or subclinical infections in clinically healthy NHPs may compromise the reproducibility of experimental outcomes and pose a risk of zoonotic transmission to laboratory personnel. Potentially lethal zoonotic viruses, including rabies virus, Marburg virus, Ebola virus, monkeypox virus, and yellow fever virus, have been reported in NHP species (15).Figure 1Global distribution of documented viral infections and outbreaks in non-human primates. This heterogeneity may lead to individual variation in susceptibility to infectious agents. Outdoor housing and husbandry practices can further hinder the establishment and maintenance of SPF colonies (17). Therefore, appropriate quarantine procedures are essential for NHPs. This review provides an overview of national quarantine protocols and major viral pathogens relevant to NHPs. We focus on pathogen biology and epidemiology, diagnostic approaches, and interventions, and consider their implications for risk-based quarantine, surveillance, and infection-control strategies. Specific sanitary import requirements are defined in the national import health regulations for NHP species (19). full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionZoonotic infectious diseases are increasingly emerging worldwide, driven by multiple factors, including increased global travel and trade, climate change, urbanization, and land-use change (1). In recent years, viruses with pandemic potential, such as severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) and highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses (HPAIVs), have posed significant global public health threats. In response to these emerging infectious diseases, various preclinical animal models have been widely used in infectious disease researches, including mice, hamsters, ferrets, guinea pigs, and non-human primates (NHPs) (2). Because effective therapeutics and vaccines may not be readily available for newly emerging viral diseases, preclinical studies using animal models play an important role in the development and evaluation of novel countermeasures.NHP models are more anatomically, physiologically, immunologically, and genetically similar to humans than other commonly used preclinical animal models. For this reason, NHPs have often been used as important preclinical models to investigate the pathogenesis of infections, caused by Ebola virus, SARS-CoV-2, and H5N1 HPAIVs and to support the development of vaccines and therapeutics against these viruses (3–6). For example, mRNA vaccines targeting SARS-CoV-2 have been evaluated for efficacy and safety using NHP models. In addition, ZMapp, a monoclonal antibody-based therapy against Ebola virus, demonstrated efficacy in treating Ebola virus infection in NHP models (7). These findings from NHP studies provided evidence supporting the clinical translation and emergency use of these interventions during outbreaks under regulatory and ethical frameworks such as the WHO MEURI guidelines (8). Consequently, the use of NHP models has increased significantly in recent years, resulting in a shortage of available NHPs (9, 10).NHPs have been reported globally to harbor various pathogens that can cause latent or subclinical infections, including B virus (Cercopithecine herpesvirus 1), simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), simian T cell lymphotropic/leukemia virus (STLV), simian type D retrovirus (SRV), and Mycobacterium (M) tuberculosis, all of which should be absent from specific pathogen-free (SPF) colonies (11–13) (Figure 1). Also, simian polyomaviruses, including simian virus 40 (SV40), have been detected macaque species (14). Therefore, latent or subclinical infections in clinically healthy NHPs may compromise the reproducibility of experimental outcomes and pose a risk of zoonotic transmission to laboratory personnel. Potentially lethal zoonotic viruses, including rabies virus, Marburg virus, Ebola virus, monkeypox virus, and yellow fever virus, have been reported in NHP species (15).Figure 1Global distribution of documented viral infections and outbreaks in non-human primates. Geographical locations of documented NHP viral infections and outbreaks reported in the literature; circles, documented natural or captive infections; triangles, reported outbreaks; different colors, individual viruses; locations based on published reports, not necessarily representing the complete geographical distribution or prevalence of each virus. Detailed information on documented infections and outbreaks, including corresponding references, Supplementary Table S1 (127, 162, 179, 182, 198–210).World map showing the geographic distribution of documented cases and endemic or natural infections of twelve viruses affecting nonhuman primates, using color-coded circles for outbreaks and triangles for endemic regions, with a legend identifying each virus.Experimental NHPs are typically outbred and exhibit greater genetic diversity than many inbred preclinical animal models (16). This heterogeneity may lead to individual variation in susceptibility to infectious agents. Outdoor housing and husbandry practices can further hinder the establishment and maintenance of SPF colonies (17). Therefore, appropriate quarantine procedures are essential for NHPs. This review provides an overview of national quarantine protocols and major viral pathogens relevant to NHPs. We focus on pathogen biology and epidemiology, diagnostic approaches, and interventions, and consider their implications for risk-based quarantine, surveillance, and infection-control strategies. We also highlight the need for coordinated facility-level responses, occupational health preparedness, and internationally harmonized quarantine standards from a One Health perspective. 2International quarantine policies and virus surveillance in NHPs facilities2.1Republic of KoreaIn the Republic of Korea, the importation of NHPs is regulated under the Act on the Prevention of Contagious Animal Diseases, and these species are classified as designated quarantine animals subject to mandatory veterinary inspection upon importation. Experimental macaques, primarily cynomolgus (Macaca fascicularis) and rhesus (Macaca mulatta) macaques, are predominantly imported from Asian countries, including China, Vietnam, and Cambodia (10, 18). Imported NHPs must undergo at least 30 days of pre-export quarantine under the supervision of a government-designated veterinarian in the exporting country, followed by an additional 30-day quarantine at a designated national animal quarantine facility in Korea prior to release for research use. Specific sanitary import requirements are defined in the national import health regulations for NHP species (19). These regulations require that the exporting country be free from Ebola virus and Marburg virus diseases. The breeding facility of origin must have no evidence of clinical, serological, or pathological occurrence of measles, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, monkeypox, or tuberculosis (M. tuberculosis and M. bovis) for at least 24 months prior to export. During the mandatory pre-export quarantine period, NHPs must be confirmed negative for tuberculosis, internal and external parasites, and enteric bacterial pathogens, including Salmonella spp., Shigella spp., and Yersinia spp. Tuberculosis screening must include at least one tuberculin skin test (TST) conducted within one week after the start of quarantine, while hepatitis B virus testing is additionally required for gibbons and great apes.Beyond these national regulatory mandates, research institutions often conduct additional microbiological screening. However, the pathogens targeted for screening vary according to facility policies, research objectives, and biosafety requirements. Additional screening may include testing for B virus, SIV, STLV, SRV, and other facility-specific pathogens.2.2United statesIn the United States, the importation of NHPs is regulated by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) under the Public Health Service Act (20). All imported NHPs must undergo quarantine for a minimum of 31 days in a CDC-registered facility prior to release. At the federal regulatory level, tuberculosis surveillance via serial TST is the only routine laboratory test universally required during quarantine. Each NHP must receive at least three TSTs administered on the eyelid using mammalian old tuberculin (MOT), at intervals of at least 2 weeks. Reactions must be evaluated at 24, 48, and 72 h after each test. Routine laboratory screening for other diseases is not uniformly required, although additional diagnostic testing may be required under specific clinical circumstances, including filovirus testing in Old World NHPs exhibiting clinical signs suggestive of filovirus disease.Beyond federal requirements, individual research institutions may implement additional quarantine measures based on their own policies. For example, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) requires documentation of a negative TST within 30 days prior to shipment (21). Recent outbreaks of emerging infectious diseases, along with advances in neurological and other biomedical research, have increased the use of non-human primates (NHPs) as preclinical models. Their close phylogenetic and physiological similarities to humans make them valuable for translational research, especially during public health emergencies. However, NHPs can harbor a wide range of viral pathogens, some of which pose zoonotic risks and may compromise animal health and experimental reproducibility. Therefore, quarantine procedures, pathogen surveillance, and biosecurity programs are essential for the safe and reliable use of NHPs in research. Despite this need, comprehensive reviews linking national quarantine policies with the biological and epidemiological characteristics of major viral pathogens and their relevance to disease surveillance and control remain limited. papers.title_original: Quarantine-associated viral pathogens in non-human primates: pathobiology, diagnostic surveillance, control strategies, and one health implications

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the need for improved quarantine and surveillance strategies for non-human primates (NHPs) due to their role in preclinical research and the risks posed by viral pathogens they may harbor.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a review comparing national quarantine frameworks for NHPs, examining pathogen-specific features, and discussing their implications for quarantine and surveillance. It focuses on the Republic of Korea's policies and the global distribution of documented viral infections in NHPs.
analysis.methods: The methods include a review of national quarantine policies, an analysis of pathogen-specific characteristics, and an examination of microbiological surveillance standards across different countries. The study also considers the biological and epidemiological features of specific viral pathogens.
analysis.main_results: The review highlights the presence of various viral pathogens in NHPs, including rabies virus, Marburg virus, Ebola virus, monkeypox virus, and yellow fever virus. It also notes the geographical distribution of these infections and the variability in surveillance practices among countries.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the heterogeneity in surveillance practices and the presence of high-risk zoonotic agents necessitate a more integrated, risk-based approach to quarantine and surveillance. The novelty lies in the emphasis on harmonized international standards and coordinated facility-level responses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the development of more effective quarantine and surveillance strategies for NHPs, which are critical for preclinical research. They also highlight the importance of international collaboration to mitigate zoonotic risks and ensure the reliability of research outcomes.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited by uneven species coverage, heterogeneity among institutions, and insufficient data for certain viral pathogens. These limitations suggest a moderate confidence in the conclusions drawn.

analysis.summary_en: This study reviews the role of non-human primates (NHPs) in preclinical research and the associated risks of viral pathogens they may harbor, particularly those with zoonotic potential. It highlights the importance of quarantine procedures, pathogen surveillance, and biosecurity programs in ensuring the safe use of NHPs. The review compares national quarantine frameworks, emphasizing the need for an integrated, risk-based approach that includes longitudinal microbiological monitoring, multimodal diagnostic assessment, and internationally harmonized standards. The study identifies several high-risk zoonotic agents, such as rabies virus, Marburg virus, and Ebola virus, and discusses their implications for quarantine and surveillance. However, the evidence is limited by uneven species coverage and variability in surveillance practices, which may affect the generalizability of the findings. The study underscores the importance of coordinated facility-level responses and occupational health preparedness to reduce the risk of undetected infections and transmission.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究解决了对非人类灵长类动物 (NHP) 改进检疫和 监测 策略的需求,因为它们在临床前研究中的作用以及它们可能携带的病毒病原体带来的风险。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是一项综述,比较了 NHP 的国家检疫框架,检查了病原体的特定特征,并讨论了它们对检疫和 监测 的影响。它重点关注韩国的政策和 NHP 中记录的病毒感染的全球分布。
elements_zh.methods: 这些方法包括审查国家检疫政策、分析病原体具体特征以及检查不同国家的微生物 监测 标准。该研究还考虑了特定病毒病原体的生物学和流行病学特征。
elements_zh.main_results: 该审查强调了 NHP 中存在多种病毒病原体,包括狂犬病病毒、马尔堡病毒、埃博拉病毒、猴痘病毒和黄热病病毒。它还指出了这些感染的地理分布以及各国之间 监测 做法的差异。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,监测 实践的异质性和高风险人畜共患病原体的存在需要采取更加综合、基于风险的检疫和 监测 方法。新颖之处在于强调统一的国际标准和协调的设施级响应。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为 NHP 制定更有效的检疫和 监测 策略提供了信息,这对于临床前研究至关重要。他们还强调了国际合作对于减轻人畜共患风险和确保研究结果可靠性的重要性。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 由于物种覆盖范围不均匀、机构之间的异质性以及某些病毒病原体的数据不足,证据受到限制。这些局限性表明对得出的结论有一定的信心。

analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,监测 实践的异质性和高风险人畜共患病原体的存在需要采取更加综合、基于风险的检疫和 监测 方法。新颖之处在于强调统一的国际标准和协调的设施级响应。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为 NHP 制定更有效的检疫和 监测 策略提供了信息,这对于临床前研究至关重要。他们还强调了国际合作对于减轻人畜共患风险和确保研究结果可靠性的重要性。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 由于物种覆盖范围不均匀、机构之间的异质性以及某些病毒病原体的数据不足,证据受到限制。这些局限性表明对得出的结论有一定的信心。
