papers.full_text: AbstractHighly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b viruses have undergone an unprecedented expansion of host range since 2021, moving from wild birds and poultry into dairy cattle, domestic cats, and other mammals, with sporadic human infections in Europe and North America (Food and Agriculture Organization et al., 2025a; Rolfes et al., 2025). This expansion is underpinned by well-characterised molecular mechanisms of influenza A virus evolution — antigenic drift, gene segment reassortment, and receptor-binding adaptation — that shape the frequency and direction of cross-species spillover (McDonald et al., 2016; Steel and Lowen, 2017; Man et al., 2026). Norwegian wild-bird and mammalian surveillance data document recurrent incursions of clade 2.3.4.4b viruses, and international risk assessments continue to describe low, but non-zero, human risk concentrated among individuals with close animal contact (World Health Organization, 2025–2026; Ytrehus et al; European Food Safety Authority et al., 2025a). Translating this fast-moving virological and epidemiological evidence into everyday protective behavior for children, adolescents, and families remains an underdeveloped link in pandemic preparedness, compounded by documented gaps in adolescent One Health literacy (Zucca et al., 2021). This mini review synthesizes current literature on the molecular basis of influenza cross-species transmission, the Norwegian epidemiological and One Health governance context, and established child- and family-oriented risk-communication frameworks, to argue that Norway’s community-based public health nurses (helsesykepleiere) — who deliver near-universal, statutorily mandated contact with children and families through the helsestasjon- and skolehelsetjeneste — occupy a distinctive but underused position as One Health communication nodes (Helsedirektoratet, 2021). I outline a practical three-tier framework for translating zoonotic-influenza science into age-appropriate household guidance, critically appraise the feasibility, workload, training, and governance implications of this role, and identify priority gaps for future empirical and implementation research.Keywords: avian influenza, cross-species transmission, H5N1, health literacy, helsesykepleier, nordic public health, one health, pandemic preparedness Supplementary materialThe Supplementary Material for this article can be found online at: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fcimb.2026.1965045/full#supplementary-material Supplementary Materials 9.ConclusionThe molecular mechanisms driving the expanding host range of HPAI A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b are the subject of continuous, increasingly granular scientific characterization, and Norwegian wildlife and veterinary surveillance is generating an increasingly detailed picture of local risk. What remains comparatively underdeveloped is the corresponding public-facing translation infrastructure connecting this evolving evidence base to the households where behavior actually changes. Norway’s helsesykepleiere, by virtue of their statutory mandate and near-universal, longitudinal reach into families with children, constitute an existing but underused resource for this translation task — one consistent with, and potentially strengthening, Norway’s own stated One Health governance ambitions (Norwegian Ministry of Health and Care Services; BeReady4Pandemics, 2025). Realizing this potential will require deliberate interdisciplinary collaboration between infection-prevention and virology research groups and the school health service, together with the evaluation research needed to ensure that any resulting communication genuinely improves family-level understanding and protective behavior, rather than simply adding to an already crowded preventive-health agenda. Realizing this potential is conditional on the workload, training, and governance safeguards above being resourced, not assumed cost-free. 1.IntroductionInfluenza A viruses remain among the most consequential zoonotic pathogens of the past century, with all major human pandemics traced to animal reservoirs, most often through reassortment of segmented viral genomes in avian or swine intermediate hosts (de Silva et al., 2012; Steel and Lowen, 2017). Since 2021, however, the epidemiology of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b has departed markedly from this historical pattern. Rather than remaining largely confined to wild birds and commercial poultry, clade 2.3.4.4b viruses have spread into an unprecedented range of mammalian species, including foxes, seals, mink, domestic cats, and, since March 2024, dairy cattle in the United States (Food and Agriculture Organization et al., 2025a; Kamel et al., 2025). Sporadic human infections have followed this mammalian expansion, and while sustained human-to-human transmission has not been documented, international risk assessments describe a dynamic and evolving situation that warrants continued vigilance (World Health Organization, 2025–2026; Rolfes et al., 2025).This shift has practical consequences that extend well beyond veterinary and occupational medicine. Families that keep backyard poultry, own cats fed raw-food diets, or live near wild-bird habitats are now plausibly exposed populations, not merely bystanders to a distant agricultural problem (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2025a; Vaughan et al., 2026). Yet the substantial and rapidly evolving virological literature on cross-species transmission mechanisms is rarely translated into a form that reaches children, adolescents, and parents at the point where behavior change actually occurs — in the home, the farmyard, or the veterinary clinic waiting room. In Norway, one existing but underused channel for this translation is the corps of community-based public health nurses (helsesykepleiere), who deliver statutorily mandated, near-universal contact with children and families through the child and youth health centers and school health service (Helsedirektoratet, 2021). This mini review synthesizes current literature on (i) the molecular mechanisms underlying influenza A virus cross-species transmission, (ii) the global and Norwegian epidemiological landscape, (iii) Norwegian One Health governance and pandemic-preparedness structures, and (iv) established risk-communication and health-literacy frameworks for children and families, in order to outline a practical framework through which public health nurses can function as One Health communication nodes.Evidence for this mini review was identified through structured searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for English-language literature published between January 2020 and August 2026, using combinations of the terms ‘H5N1’, ‘avian influenza’, ‘clade 2.3.4.4b’, ‘cross-species transmission’, ‘reassortment’, ‘One Health’, ‘risk communication’, ‘health literacy’, ‘helsesykepleier’, and ‘public health nursing’, supplemented by hand-searched reference lists and direct searches of institutional sources (FHI, Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Mattilsynet, WHO, EFSA, and CDC) for current risk assessments and guidance. Given the breadth of the topic and the mini review format, this is a narrative rather than a systematic review, and no formal quality-appraisal tool was applied. The specific search strings and retrieval steps are documented in Supplementary Search Record S1. 2.Molecular evolution and mechanisms of cross-species transmissionInfluenza A viruses possess a genome of eight discrete, single-stranded, negative-sense RNA segments, a structural feature that permits two distinct evolutionary pathways (McDonald et al., 2016). The first, antigenic drift, results from the gradual accumulation of point mutations introduced by the error-prone viral RNA polymerase during replication. The second, and epidemiologically more consequential for cross-species jumps, is reassortment: when two distinct influenza A viruses co-infect the same host cell, progeny virions can package a novel combination of the eight parental segments, generating genetically — and potentially phenotypically — distinct viruses in a single replication cycle (Steel and Lowen, 2017; Selective genome packaging mechanisms of influenza A viruses, 2021). Reassortment between avian, swine, and human lineages produced the reassortant strains responsible for the 1957, 1968, and 2009 pandemics, historically via swine acting as a permissive co-infection host, or ‘mixing vessel’ (de Silva et al., 2012).A second determinant of host range is the receptor-binding specificity of the viral hemagglutinin protein. Avian-adapted viruses preferentially bind α2,3-linked sialic acid receptors predominant in the avian gut and respiratory tract, whereas mammalian-adapted viruses, including human seasonal strains, preferentially bind α2,6-linked receptors characteristic of the upper mammalian respiratory tract. Single amino acid substitutions in the hemagglutinin receptor-binding site, together with adaptive changes in the viral polymerase complex, can shift this binding preference and materially increase a virus’s capacity to infect and transmit within a new mammalian host (Man et al., 2026). Among these changes, PB2 substitutions such as E627K and D701N improve polymerase activity at mammalian upper-respiratory-tract temperatures and are recurrently detected in mammalian-adapted clade 2.3.4.4b genotypes, making them closely watched risk markers. Recent genotypes circulating in North American dairy cattle and companion animals, including B3.13 and D1.1, carry constellations of such adaptive markers, and ongoing genomic surveillance by joint WHO/FAO/WOAH assessment continues to track their evolution for signals of increased mammalian or human transmissibility (Food and Agriculture Organization et al., 2025a; Man et al., 2026). Because most reassortant or drift-variant genotypes carry fitness costs that limit onward spread, only a minority of spillover events establish sustained transmission chains in a new host — but the frequency of coinfection opportunities, and hence the statistical opportunity for a high-fitness variant to emerge, rises directly with the scale of the current panzootic. This technical surveillance information, while central to expert risk assessment, is rarely rendered in a form accessible to non-specialist audiences, a gap addressed later in this review.These molecular determinants of host range and transmissibility are not simply of virological interest. Because receptor-binding adaptation, polymerase mutation, and reassortment are the specific mechanisms that determine whether a spillover event remains a dead-end infection or acquires the capacity for onward transmission, they define the biological rationale for the tiered, exposure-specific communication framework proposed in Section 7: household guidance calibrated to the animal-contact pathways — raw feeding, wild-bird contact, dairy exposure — most likely to provide the coinfection or exposure opportunities described above. Framing the practical framework in these molecular terms is intended to keep the proposed nursing role anchored to virological evidence rather than to a generic exhortation to be alert to ‘bird flu’. 3.Current epidemiological landscape: global panzootic and the Norwegian contextSince its emergence in Europe in 2020–2021, clade 2.3.4.4b has become globally dominant, spreading across Europe, Africa, the Americas, and, more recently, Antarctica, with unprecedented mortality events in wild bird and marine mammal populations (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2025b; Kamel et al., 2025). The detection of the virus in United States dairy cattle in March 2024 marked a further expansion: as of mid-2025, outbreaks had been confirmed in more than 1,000 herds across multiple states, with clinical signs in cattle including decreased milk yield, abnormal milk consistency, and reduced feed intake (Food and Agriculture Organization et al., 2025a; Morel et al., 2026). Between March 2024 and May 2025, a total of approximately 70 human cases of HPAI A(H5) infection were reported in the United States: 41 following exposure to infected dairy cattle, 24 to commercial poultry, two to backyard poultry flocks, and three with undetermined exposure (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2025c). Most infections presented as mild conjunctivitis, occasionally accompanied by fever or respiratory symptoms; a minority required hospitalization, and one death occurred in a person with underlying health conditions exposed to a backyard flock and wild birds (Rolfes et al., 2025). A first pediatric case with an undetermined exposure source was identified in California in late 2024 (Zhu et al., 2025).Companion animals have emerged as an additional and household-relevant transmission pathway. Domestic cats appear highly susceptible to severe, often fatal, disease, typically following consumption of raw milk, raw pet food, or contact with infected wild birds; a global review identified more than 600 documented feline infections across 12 species and 18 countries since the emergence of clade 2.3.4.4b (CIDRAP, 2025; Sykes, 2025). In late 2024, a cluster investigation in Los Angeles County identified serologic evidence consistent with possible virus transmission from an infected domestic cat to a veterinary professional — one of 25 serosurveyed contacts among 139 potentially exposed persons, with no virus isolated from the human case — providing what may be the first, if unconfirmed, instance of cat-to-human zoonotic transmission for this clade (Vaughan et al., 2026). To date, no sustained human-to-human transmission of clade 2.3.4.4b viruses has been documented anywhere, and joint WHO/FAO/WOAH and European risk assessments continue to classify general population risk as low, with elevated risk restricted to those with direct occupational or household exposure to infected animals (World Health Organization, 2025–2026; European Commission / EFSA).Within this global picture, Norway has not been spared. Norwegian Veterinary Institute wild-bird and mammalian surveillance programs document recurrent clade 2.3.4.4b detections, including spillover into Norwegian foxes and seals, consistent with broader European surveillance trends reported by the European Food Safety Authority and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (Ytrehus et al; European Food Safety Authority et al., 2025a). As elsewhere, the general population risk in Norway is assessed as low, with the principal exposure pathway concentrated among individuals with occupational or hobbyist contact with wild birds, backyard poultry, or other domestic animals (Food and Agriculture Organization et al., 2025a) — a demographic that includes a meaningful proportion of Norwegian households with children, particularly in rural and peri-urban districts. 4.One health governance and pandemic preparedness in NorwayNorway has formally embedded One Health principles — the recognition that human, animal, and environmental health are interdependent — into its national approach to zoonotic disease and pandemic preparedness. The Norwegian Institute of Public Health identifies zoonotic influenza explicitly as a priority One Health working area, alongside food safety and antimicrobial resistance, and coordinates closely with the Norwegian Veterinary Institute and Norwegian Food Safety Authority on surveillance and risk communication (Norwegian Institute of Public Health (FHI), 2020). This institutional commitment is further reflected in Norway’s National One Health Strategy against Antimicrobial Resistance 2024–2033, which establishes cross-sectoral governance mechanisms that could, in principle, extend to influenza preparedness (Norwegian Ministry of Health and Care Services), and in an independent country-profile assessment noting that Norway has integrated One Health principles into its broader pandemic preparedness and response framework through interdisciplinary task forces and improved cross-sector data sharing (BeReady4Pandemics, 2025).Notably, however, these governance frameworks are articulated predominantly at the level of surveillance coordination and inter-agency data sharing among human, animal, and environmental health authorities. None of the reviewed strategy or preparedness documents specify a defined role for frontline, community-based health personnel in the direct translation of One Health surveillance findings into household-level guidance. This represents an implementation gap between governance-level One Health ambition and the last-mile communication needed to change everyday behavior — a gap this review argues the helsesykepleier workforce is structurally well placed to help close. 5.The helsesykepleier as a one health communication nodeHelsesykepleiere are specialist public health nurses operating within Norway’s statutorily mandated child health and school health services (helsestasjons- og skolehelsetjenesten), providing near-universal, longitudinal contact with children and families from infancy through upper secondary school, encompassing routine health checks, vaccination programs, and structured health guidance for parents and, later, directly for adolescents (Helsedirektoratet, 2021). This combination of near-total population reach, repeated contact over many years, and an existing mandate for preventive health counselling distinguishes the helsesykepleier role from generic public health messaging: unlike a one-off media campaign, the relationship is relational and cumulative, allowing guidance to be tailored to a given family’s actual animal exposures — for example, backyard poultry keeping, pet ownership, or proximity to wild-bird habitats — rather than delivered as an undifferentiated general warning.This structural advantage is particularly relevant given documented deficits in existing zoonotic-disease literacy…

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to explore the role of community-based public health nurses in translating virological and epidemiological evidence on cross-species influenza transmission into actionable public health communication for children, adolescents, and families in Norway. This is critical given the documented gaps in adolescent One Health literacy and the need for improved risk communication.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a mini review analyzing the molecular basis of influenza cross-species transmission, the Norwegian epidemiological and One Health governance context, and child- and family-oriented risk-communication frameworks. It focuses on the role of community-based public health nurses (helsesykepleiere) in Norway, who provide near-universal contact with children and families through the helsestasjon- and skolehelsetjeneste.
analysis.methods: The methods involved synthesizing current literature on molecular determinants of host range and transmissibility, reviewing the Norwegian One Health governance context, and examining established risk-communication frameworks for children and families. The study also analyzed surveillance data and institutional commitments to zoonotic influenza preparedness.
analysis.main_results: The study reports that clade 2.3.4.4b viruses have become globally dominant, with recurrent detections in Norwegian wild-bird and mammalian surveillance programs, including spillover into foxes and seals. analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that integrating community-based public health nurses into One Health communication frameworks could improve family-level understanding and protective behavior against zoonotic influenza, particularly in the context of the ongoing global panzootic of clade 2.3.4.4b viruses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on a mini review of existing literature and surveillance data, which may limit the depth of analysis. However, the evidence is grounded in documented epidemiological trends and institutional commitments, supporting a moderate confidence assessment.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the role of community-based public health nurses in Norway in translating virological and epidemiological evidence on cross-species influenza transmission into actionable public health communication for children, adolescents, and families. It highlights the global dominance of clade 2.3.4.4b viruses, their spillover into Norwegian wildlife, and the detection of these viruses in U.S. dairy cattle and companion animals, with documented human cases linked to animal exposure. The authors argue that these nurses, with their near-universal contact with families, are uniquely positioned to improve risk communication and understanding of zoonotic influenza. However, the study is limited to a review of existing literature and surveillance data, and it notes that current governance frameworks do not explicitly define a role for these nurses in influenza preparedness. The findings suggest that integrating these nurses into One Health communication could enhance family-level protective behaviors, but further evaluation research is needed to confirm this. The evidence is moderate in strength due to its reliance on secondary sources and the absence of direct experimental data.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在探讨社区公共卫生护士在将跨物种流感 传播 的病毒学和流行病学证据转化为针对挪威儿童、青少年和家庭的可行公共卫生传播方面的作用。鉴于已记录的青少年“One Health”素养方面的差距以及改进风险沟通的需要,这一点至关重要。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是一项小型综述,分析了跨物种流感 传播 的分子基础、挪威流行病学和 One Health 治理背景以及面向儿童和家庭的风险沟通框架。它重点关注挪威社区公共卫生护士 (helsesykepleiere) 的作用,他们通过 helsestasjon- 和 skolehelsetjeneste 为儿童和家庭提供近乎普遍的接触。
elements_zh.methods: 这些方法包括综合有关 宿主 范围和传播性分子决定因素的现有文献,回顾挪威 One Health 治理背景,并检查已建立的儿童和家庭风险沟通框架。该研究还分析了 监测 数据和机构对人畜共患流感防范的承诺。
elements_zh.main_results: 该研究报告称,分支 2.3.4.4b 病毒已成为全球主导病毒,在挪威野鸟和哺乳动物 监测 项目中反复检测到,包括狐狸和海豹中的 跨物种溢出。它还强调了在美国奶牛和伴侣动物中检测到这些病毒,并记录了与动物接触有关的 HPAI A(H5) 感染人类病例。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,helsesykepleiere 由于与儿童和家庭几乎普遍接触,因此具有独特的优势,可以将 One Health 监测 的研究结果转化为家庭层面的指导。这是利用社区卫生人员进行有效风险沟通的新颖视角。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,将社区公共卫生护士纳入 One Health 沟通框架可以改善家庭层面对人畜共患流感的了解和保护行为,特别是在 2.3.4.4b 病毒分支全球流行的背景下。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究基于对现有文献和 监测 数据的小型回顾,这可能会限制分析的深度。然而,证据基于记录的流行病学趋势和机构承诺,支持适度的信心评估。

papers.title: Antibodies targeting a conserved cryptic epitope at the influenza hemagglutinin head-stem interface via distinct binding modes
papers.abstract: Influenza A virus continues to pose pandemic threats, as demonstrated by the recent global spread of highly pathogenic H5N1 strains. Consequently, the development and characterization of vaccines targeting zoonotic influenza subtypes have become a major focus of the field. In this study, we characterize two broadly reactive antibodies previously isolated from H5N1 vaccinees. Although they have distinct immunoglobulin germline gene usage and binding modes, cryo-EM analysis shows that both antibodies share a highly conserved cryptic epitope at the interface of the hemagglutinin (HA) head and stem domains. The antigenicity of this epitope is influenced by natural amino acid variation at residue 293 of HA subunit 1, and its access is facilitated by acid-induced conformational change of HA. Nevertheless, both antibodies are non-neutralizing and possess only marginal protective efficacy against seasonal and H5N1 viruses in vivo, thus representing suboptimal vaccine responses. Overall, our findings expand the interactions of cross-reactive antibodies with an under-characterized HA epitope and provide insights for next-generation influenza vaccine design.

analysis.summary_en: This study characterizes two broadly reactive antibodies against avian influenza A viruses, specifically H5N1, that target a conserved cryptic epitope at the hemagglutinin head-stem interface. The antibodies, despite differing in germline gene usage and binding modes, share this epitope, which is influenced by amino acid variation at residue 293 and is accessible due to acid-induced conformational changes. The findings expand understanding of cross-reactive antibody interactions with this under-characterized epitope, providing insights for improved vaccine design. However, the antibodies are non-neutralizing and show only marginal protective efficacy in vivo, indicating suboptimal vaccine responses. The study's evidence is based on cryo-EM analysis and in vivo testing, which may limit the generalizability of the results. The research contributes to the development of vaccines targeting avian influenza subtypes, particularly those with zoonotic potential, by highlighting a conserved epitope that could be exploited for broader immunity.

papers.source_body_en: Influenza A virus continues to pose pandemic threats, as demonstrated by the recent global spread of highly pathogenic H5N1 strains. Consequently, the development and characterization of vaccines targeting zoonotic influenza subtypes have become a major focus of the field. In this study, we characterize two broadly reactive antibodies previously isolated from H5N1 vaccinees. Although they have distinct immunoglobulin germline gene usage and binding modes, cryo-EM analysis shows that both antibodies share a highly conserved cryptic epitope at the interface of the hemagglutinin (HA) head and stem domains. The antigenicity of this epitope is influenced by natural amino acid variation at residue 293 of HA subunit 1, and its access is facilitated by acid-induced conformational change of HA. Nevertheless, both antibodies are non-neutralizing and possess only marginal protective efficacy against seasonal and H5N1 viruses in vivo, thus representing suboptimal vaccine responses. Overall, our findings expand the interactions of cross-reactive antibodies with an under-characterized HA epitope and provide insights for next-generation influenza vaccine design.
papers.abstract_zh: 甲型流感病毒继续构成大流行威胁,最近高致病性 H5N1 病毒株在全球的传播就证明了这一点。因此,针对人畜共患流感亚型的 疫苗 的开发和表征已成为该领域的主要焦点。在这项研究中,我们表征了之前从 H5N1 疫苗 中分离出的两种具有广泛反应性的抗体。尽管它们具有不同的免疫球蛋白种系基因使用和结合模式,但冷冻电镜分析表明,两种抗体在血凝素 (HA) 头和干结构域的界面上共享高度保守的隐藏表位。该表位的抗原性受到 HA 亚基 1 残基 293 处天然氨基酸变异的影响,酸诱导的 HA 构象变化促进了其进入。然而,这两种抗体都不是中和性的,并且对体内季节性病毒和 H5N1 病毒仅具有有限的保护功效,因此代表了次优的 疫苗 反应。总体而言,我们的研究结果扩大了交叉反应抗体与未充分表征的 HA 表位的相互作用,并为下一代流感 疫苗 设计提供了见解。

papers.full_text: Animal diseases continuously threaten livestock production and public health, yet current surveillance approaches remain largely passive and fragmented. Conventional artificial intelligence models typically function as open-loop predictors, delivering static outputs that fail to accommodate the dynamic operational needs of veterinarians in real-world farm settings. This review explores an emerging paradigm of AI agents for animal disease monitoring, emphasizing how such agents can transition from passive observation to active intervention through a closed-loop perception–decision–feedback architecture. We first classify multi-scale sensing technologies: at the micro-scale, automated molecular diagnostics and biosensors; at the macro-scale, computer-vision-based phenotyping. These technologies collectively provide the data streams required for continuous surveillance. The review then discusses how multi-modal inputs, time-series forecasting, resource-aware decision-making, and reinforcement learning can be integrated into an agent-based workflow. Importantly, most current veterinary research evidence supports only the individual components of this framework, rather than the deployment of fully autonomous, iteratively evolving closed-loop agents in actual field environments. Translating closed-loop AI from a conceptual framework into a reliable veterinary decision-support tool will therefore require further advances in validation, standardization, governance, and human oversight. 2.1From diagnostic results to data streamsMolecular diagnostics have long been recognized for their ability to identify pathogens before the full manifestation of clinical symptoms, thereby opening earlier windows for intervention. This principle has been systematically discussed in foundational reviews of molecular veterinary diagnostics (12, 13). The current diagnostic landscape is characterized by the parallel development of expanded central laboratory capacity and decentralized detection. On one hand, confirmatory capabilities such as sequencing are being further strengthened and expanded. On the other hand, molecular detection is increasingly moving toward field settings. For example, the integration of conventional (RT-) PCR products with portable nanopore sequencing enables rapid identification of ASFV, CSFV, and FMDV under resource-limited conditions while also providing phylogenetic interpretation. This approach demonstrates how confirmatory workflows can be transformed into operational near-real-time molecular monitoring signals (14). Such strategies are particularly important for transboundary animal epidemics because rapid identification directly determines the speed of control responses.At the same time, immunological rapid detection technologies are evolving toward greater speed, portability, and multiplexing capability, enabling actionable antigen or antibody signals to be generated even in environments lacking full laboratory infrastructure. Fluorescent microsphere immunochromatographic assays (FM-ICA) for SADS-CoV have shown high concordance with qPCR while providing shorter detection times and simpler operation, indicating that immunological detection can support early screening and monitoring during epidemic emergence (15). Quantum-dot dual-channel immunochromatographic sensors developed for ASF and pseudorabies can produce results in approximately 20 min and demonstrate good agreement with commercial diagnostic kits, making them suitable for continuous population-level monitoring (16). In addition, LFIA/LFA technologies are increasingly applied in the detection of zoonotic and animal viruses. Although their sensitivity and detection spectrum still require improvement, their speed and deployability have made them an important form of field detection (17). Immunological rapid tests designed for multi-host applications are also emerging. For instance, chimeric protein A/G lateral flow assays exploit cross-species IgG binding properties to enable screening for brucellosis in livestock, providing a practical tool for multi-species monitoring (18).Biosensors represent another frontier for the generation of diagnostic data streams. Reviews of biosensor technologies in livestock and poultry indicate that electrochemical sensors, quantum-dot fluorescence systems, and carbon nanotube field-effect transistor (FET) platforms can use antibodies, nucleic acids, or aptamers as recognition elements to detect pathogen antigens, antibodies, or nucleic acids. These approaches often provide faster detection than traditional methods and exhibit strong analytical performance, although they remain constrained by background interference, sample stability in complex matrices, and scalability of production (19, 20). CRISPR diagnostics further integrate sequence-specific recognition with portable readout technologies. Electrochemical CRISPR sensors have demonstrated potential for rapid detection and have been proposed for field and wildlife monitoring. However, their effective deployment depends on standardized protocols and improved resistance to environmental interference (21, 22). 5Discussion and future perspectives5.1Intelligent-agent-enabled epidemic management in veterinary medicineThe evidence reviewed here supports an emerging technical foundation for intelligent-agent-enabled animal epidemic management, but the maturity of individual components remains uneven. Molecular diagnostics, biosensors, imaging, thermal monitoring, behavior recognition, and time-series forecasting have each been demonstrated in animal-health or livestock settings, whereas fully integrated systems that autonomously connect perception, resource-aware action, outcome evaluation, and online policy adaptation remain largely prospective. We therefore distinguish between technologies already validated for specific sensing or prediction tasks and the closed-loop agent architecture proposed in this review. The latter should be viewed as a research framework whose farm-level utility, safety, robustness, and cost-effectiveness still require prospective validation.Beyond terrestrial livestock systems, recent reviews have also described the growing use of artificial intelligence in aquaculture for fish disease diagnosis, predictive modeling, and management decision support (72–74). This evidence from aquatic animal health broadens the application context of AI-enabled animal health management and suggests that similar data-driven principles may be adapted across diverse animal production systems. At the same time, these aquaculture studies emphasize challenges including fragmented datasets, interpretability, field adoption, and One Health integration, reinforcing the need for careful validation before more autonomous closed-loop systems are considered for routine use.5.2Future research directionsBuilding on these component-level advances, Future research should first focus on the upgrade of the input end. Existing inputs still have problems such as discrete sampling, insufficient image resolution, and inconsistent cross-platform standards. Subsequently, more sensitive pathogen detection, higher-frequency non-invasive sampling, clearer and more interference-resistant visual recognition systems can be developed, and unified data labeling, collection frequency, and quality control standards can be established. For example, high-definition RGB cameras can be used to identify small skin lesions, thermal imaging can be used to capture early inflammation, depth cameras can be used to quantify body condition and posture changes, and multi-omics and pathogen load data can improve the ability of early risk stratification. The key point is to enable the agent to obtain earlier, more accurate, and more continuous state inputs, rather than relying solely on single detection results.Secondly, future research should focus on solving the problems of time, resources, and multi-modal collaboration. Animal disease prevention and control is not a simple prediction task but rather a matter of achieving the shortest response time under limited sampling personnel, reagent kits, laboratory throughput, and logistics. Therefore, the agent needs to incorporate time series prediction and resource constraints into decision-making: when to sample, which animals to sample, which type of detection to prioritize, and whether to initiate isolation or mobile laboratories should all be dynamically generated by the model based on risk and cost. The core of multi-modal collaboration is not simply stacking data but automatically adjusting weights in different scenarios: when images are occluded, increase the weight of behavior and temperature data; when laboratory throughput is insufficient, prioritize high-risk individuals or non-invasive group samples.Finally, future research should improve the decision-making system and negative feedback regulation mechanism. Currently, many studies still remain at the risk scoring stage, and agents that can continuously correct strategies based on intervention results are still in the early stages. Subsequently, reinforcement learning and human-machine collaboration mechanisms can be introduced, with detection positive rate, early detection time, resource consumption, false alarms and missed detections, animal welfare, and economic losses as positive and negative feedback signals. Positive feedback can reward strategies that detect infections earlier and control transmission at lower costs; negative feedback is used to punish ineffective sampling, excessive isolation, resource waste, or missed high-risk individuals. If validated prospectively under field conditions, such feedback regulation could allow future agents to evolve from one-time prediction tools toward more adaptive and resource-aware epidemic management systems. 6ConclusionIn conclusion, current evidence supports many of the sensing, diagnostic, phenotypic, and predictive components required for AI-enabled veterinary disease surveillance, but fully integrated closed-loop AI agents remain largely prospective. Future progress will depend not only on improvements in individual algorithms, but also on reliable multi-scale inputs, multimodal temporal integration, resource-aware decision support, and validated feedback mechanisms. Prospective field studies will be essential to determine the safety, robustness, cost-effectiveness, and practical value of these systems before their routine implementation in veterinary epidemic management. 1IntroductionIn recent years, outbreaks of African swine fever (ASF), highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI), foot-and-mouth disease (FMD), and porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome (PRRS) have shown that animal epidemics remain a major challenge to livestock production, animal welfare, food security, and public health. These diseases spread rapidly, are often associated with high mortality, and frequently cause trade disruption and production losses. Between 2021 and 2023, ASF was reported in 50 countries and resulted in the death of more than 1.5 million pigs worldwide (1). Likewise, from 2005 to 2024, more than 633 million poultry died or were culled globally because of HPAI. In intensive production systems, high stocking density and extended supply chains make early detection increasingly difficult (2, 3). Under these conditions, animal health diagnostics are no longer expected merely to confirm the presence of disease. There is growing demand for surveillance approaches that can detect abnormal patterns at an earlier stage, support near real-time risk assessment, and provide a basis for timely intervention (4, 5).Traditional diagnostic methods for animal epidemics can generally be classified into molecular diagnostics, immunological diagnostics, and pathogen-based diagnostics according to their underlying principles. These methods remain indispensable, but their limitations are also evident. In clinical practice, disease recognition still relies mainly on clinical observation and laboratory diagnosis (4). In many situations, such approaches are reactive rather than proactive, and they are often too slow when infection remains subclinical or when early signs are mild or atypical. full_text_sections.abstract: Animal diseases continuously threaten livestock production and public health, yet current surveillance approaches remain largely passive and fragmented. Conventional artificial intelligence models typically function as open-loop predictors, delivering static outputs that fail to accommodate the dynamic operational needs of veterinarians in real-world farm settings. This review explores an emerging paradigm of AI agents for animal disease monitoring, emphasizing how such agents can transition from passive observation to active intervention through a closed-loop perception–decision–feedback architecture. We first classify multi-scale sensing technologies: at the micro-scale, automated molecular diagnostics and biosensors; at the macro-scale, computer-vision-based phenotyping. These technologies collectively provide the data streams required for continuous surveillance. The review then discusses how multi-modal inputs, time-series forecasting, resource-aware decision-making, and reinforcement learning can be integrated into an agent-based workflow. Importantly, most current veterinary research evidence supports only the individual components of this framework, rather than the deployment of fully autonomous, iteratively evolving closed-loop agents in actual field environments. Translating closed-loop AI from a conceptual framework into a reliable veterinary decision-support tool will therefore require further advances in validation, standardization, governance, and human oversight.
full_text_sections.results: 2.1From diagnostic results to data streamsMolecular diagnostics have long been recognized for their ability to identify pathogens before the full manifestation of clinical symptoms, thereby opening earlier windows for intervention. This principle has been systematically discussed in foundational reviews of molecular veterinary diagnostics (12, 13). The current diagnostic landscape is characterized by the parallel development of expanded central laboratory capacity and decentralized detection. On one hand, confirmatory capabilities such as sequencing are being further strengthened and expanded. On the other hand, molecular detection is increasingly moving toward field settings. For example, the integration of conventional (RT-) PCR products with portable nanopore sequencing enables rapid identification of ASFV, CSFV, and FMDV under resource-limited conditions while also providing phylogenetic interpretation. This approach demonstrates how confirmatory workflows can be transformed into operational near-real-time molecular monitoring signals (14). Such strategies are particularly important for transboundary animal epidemics because rapid identification directly determines the speed of control responses.At the same time, immunological rapid detection technologies are evolving toward greater speed, portability, and multiplexing capability, enabling actionable antigen or antibody signals to be generated even in environments lacking full laboratory infrastructure. Fluorescent microsphere immunochromatographic assays (FM-ICA) for SADS-CoV have shown high concordance with qPCR while providing shorter detection times and simpler operation, indicating that immunological detection can support early screening and monitoring during epidemic emergence (15). Quantum-dot dual-channel immunochromatographic sensors developed for ASF and pseudorabies can produce results in approximately 20 min and demonstrate good agreement with commercial diagnostic kits, making them suitable for continuous population-level monitoring (16). In addition, LFIA/LFA technologies are increasingly applied in the detection of zoonotic and animal viruses. Although their sensitivity and detection spectrum still require improvement, their speed and deployability have made them an important form of field detection (17). Immunological rapid tests designed for multi-host applications are also emerging. For instance, chimeric protein A/G lateral flow assays exploit cross-species IgG binding properties to enable screening for brucellosis in livestock, providing a practical tool for multi-species monitoring (18).Biosensors represent another frontier for the generation of diagnostic data streams. Reviews of biosensor technologies in livestock and poultry indicate that electrochemical sensors, quantum-dot fluorescence systems, and carbon nanotube field-effect transistor (FET) platforms can use antibodies, nucleic acids, or aptamers as recognition elements to detect pathogen antigens, antibodies, or nucleic acids. These approaches often provide faster detection than traditional methods and exhibit strong analytical performance, although they remain constrained by background interference, sample stability in complex matrices, and scalability of production (19, 20). CRISPR diagnostics further integrate sequence-specific recognition with portable readout technologies. Electrochemical CRISPR sensors have demonstrated potential for rapid detection and have been proposed for field and wildlife monitoring. However, their effective deployment depends on standardized protocols and improved resistance to environmental interference (21, 22).
full_text_sections.discussion: 5Discussion and future perspectives5.1Intelligent-agent-enabled epidemic management in veterinary medicineThe evidence reviewed here supports an emerging technical foundation for intelligent-agent-enabled animal epidemic management, but the maturity of individual components remains uneven. Molecular diagnostics, biosensors, imaging, thermal monitoring, behavior recognition, and time-series forecasting have each been demonstrated in animal-health or livestock settings, whereas fully integrated systems that autonomously connect perception, resource-aware action, outcome evaluation, and online policy adaptation remain largely prospective. We therefore distinguish between technologies already validated for specific sensing or prediction tasks and the closed-loop agent architecture proposed in this review. The latter should be viewed as a research framework whose farm-level utility, safety, robustness, and cost-effectiveness still require prospective validation.Beyond terrestrial livestock systems, recent reviews have also described the growing use of artificial intelligence in aquaculture for fish disease diagnosis, predictive modeling, and management decision support (72–74). This evidence from aquatic animal health broadens the application context of AI-enabled animal health management and suggests that similar data-driven principles may be adapted across diverse animal production systems. At the same time, these aquaculture studies emphasize challenges including fragmented datasets, interpretability, field adoption, and One Health integration, reinforcing the need for careful validation before more autonomous closed-loop systems are considered for routine use.5.2Future research directionsBuilding on these component-level advances, Future research should first focus on the upgrade of the input end. Existing inputs still have problems such as discrete sampling, insufficient image resolution, and inconsistent cross-platform standards. Subsequently, more sensitive pathogen detection, higher-frequency non-invasive sampling, clearer and more interference-resistant visual recognition systems can be developed, and unified data labeling, collection frequency, and quality control standards can be established. For example, high-definition RGB cameras can be used to identify small skin lesions, thermal imaging can be used to capture early inflammation, depth cameras can be used to quantify body condition and posture changes, and multi-omics and pathogen load data can improve the ability of early risk stratification. The key point is to enable the agent to obtain earlier, more accurate, and more continuous state inputs, rather than relying solely on single detection results.Secondly, future research should focus on solving the problems of time, resources, and multi-modal collaboration. Animal disease prevention and control is not a simple prediction task but rather a matter of achieving the shortest response time under limited sampling personnel, reagent kits, laboratory throughput, and logistics. Therefore, the agent needs to incorporate time series prediction and resource constraints into decision-making: when to sample, which animals to sample, which type of detection to prioritize, and whether to initiate isolation or mobile laboratories should all be dynamically generated by the model based on risk and cost. The core of multi-modal collaboration is not simply stacking data but automatically adjusting weights in different scenarios: when images are occluded, increase the weight of behavior and temperature data; when laboratory throughput is insufficient, prioritize high-risk individuals or non-invasive group samples.Finally, future research should improve the decision-making system and negative feedback regulation mechanism. Currently, many studies still remain at the risk scoring stage, and agents that can continuously correct strategies based on intervention results are still in the early stages. Subsequently, reinforcement learning and human-machine collaboration mechanisms can be introduced, with detection positive rate, early detection time, resource consumption, false alarms and missed detections, animal welfare, and economic losses as positive and negative feedback signals. Positive feedback can reward strategies that detect infections earlier and control transmission at lower costs; negative feedback is used to punish ineffective sampling, excessive isolation, resource waste, or missed high-risk individuals. If validated prospectively under field conditions, such feedback regulation could allow future agents to evolve from one-time prediction tools toward more adaptive and resource-aware epidemic management systems.
full_text_sections.conclusion: 6ConclusionIn conclusion, current evidence supports many of the sensing, diagnostic, phenotypic, and predictive components required for AI-enabled veterinary disease surveillance, but fully integrated closed-loop AI agents remain largely prospective. Future progress will depend not only on improvements in individual algorithms, but also on reliable multi-scale inputs, multimodal temporal integration, resource-aware decision support, and validated feedback mechanisms. Prospective field studies will be essential to determine the safety, robustness, cost-effectiveness, and practical value of these systems before their routine implementation in veterinary epidemic management.

papers.title_original: Closed-loop artificial intelligence agents for animal epidemic prediction and decision support in livestock farming: a review

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on the application of closed-loop artificial intelligence agents in animal epidemic prediction and decision support, particularly in livestock farming. The central question is to identify which technical components are supported by veterinary or animal-health evidence, how they can be integrated into a closed-loop decision framework, and where empirical field validation is still lacking.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a narrative synthesis of literature published between January 2015 and June 2026 on PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus. The search keywords included artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, AI agents, veterinary, animal diseases, animal husbandry, epidemiological surveillance, diagnosis, and precision livestock farming. The review examines both technical components and their integration into closed-loop systems.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Current evidence supports many of the sensing, diagnostic, phenotypic, and predictive components required for AI-enabled veterinary disease surveillance. These include molecular diagnostics, biosensors, imaging, thermal monitoring, behavior recognition, and time-series forecasting. However, fully integrated autonomous systems that connect perception, resource-aware action, outcome evaluation, and online policy adaptation remain largely prospective.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: There is heterogeneity in the evidence, with many surveillance systems remaining fragmented, weakly integrated, and difficult to evaluate consistently. Additionally, existing inputs have problems such as discrete sampling, insufficient image resolution, and inconsistent cross-platform standards. The review also highlights the need for prospective validation of the farm-level utility, safety, robustness, and cost-effectiveness of these systems.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Future research should focus on upgrading the input end to enable earlier, more accurate, and more continuous state inputs for AI agents. It should also address the challenges of time, resources, and multi-modal collaboration by automatically adjusting weights in different scenarios. analysis.summary_en: This review explores the use of closed-loop artificial intelligence agents in predicting and managing animal epidemics, particularly in livestock farming. It highlights the current support for various sensing, diagnostic, and predictive components, such as molecular diagnostics, biosensors, and time-series forecasting, while noting that fully integrated systems remain prospective. The review identifies key challenges, including fragmented datasets, inconsistent standards, and the need for robust validation. It emphasizes the importance of improving input quality, multi-modal collaboration, and decision-making systems for effective AI implementation in veterinary surveillance. The findings suggest that while AI has potential in disease detection and risk assessment, further research and field testing are necessary to ensure practical utility and safety.

analysis_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该综述是对 2015 年 1 月至 2026 年 6 月期间在 PubMed、Web of Science 和 Scopus 上发表的文献的叙述性综合。搜索关键词包括人工智能、机器学习、深度学习、强化学习、AI代理、兽医、动物疾病、畜牧业、流行病学监测、诊断、精准畜牧业等。该审查检查了技术组件及其与闭环系统的集成。
analysis_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 目前的证据支持人工智能兽医疾病 监测 所需的许多传感、诊断、表型和预测组件。这些包括分子诊断、生物传感器、成像、热监测、行为识别和时间序列预测。然而,连接感知、资源感知行动、结果评估和在线政策适应的完全集成的自主系统在很大程度上仍然具有前景。
analysis_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 证据存在异质性,许多 监测 系统仍然支离破碎、集成度弱且难以一致评估。此外,现有的输入存在离散采样、图像分辨率不足、跨平台标准不一致等问题。该审查还强调需要对这些系统的农场级实用性、安全性、稳健性和成本效益进行前瞻性验证。
analysis_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 未来的研究应该集中在输入端的升级上,为AI智能体实现更早、更准确、更连续的状态输入。它还应该通过在不同场景下自动调整权重来解决时间、资源和多模式协作的挑战。最后,强调完善决策体系和负反馈调节机制。

papers.full_text: SummaryThis Research Topic brings together 22 contributions that showcase the breadth of mathematical and computational tools now used to understand and respond to infectious disease threats. Spanning mechanistic modeling, statistical forecasting, machine learning, stochastic optimization, computational fluid dynamics, and burden analysis, the Research Topic addresses diseases ranging from COVID-19 and influenza to measles, mumps, and dengue. Contributions cluster around three central themes: extracting robust, decision-relevant forecasts from noisy real-time surveillance data; modeling how interventions, mobility, and connectivity shape transmission dynamics; and linking disease burden to environmental, socioeconomic, and health-system determinants. Together, these papers reinforce a unifying message: no single method suffices for every question, and the right analytical approach must be matched to the decision at hand, the data-generating process, and the practical consequences of getting the inference wrong. IntroductionInfectious diseases spread through a complex mix of factors, including pathogens, hosts, behavior, mobility, environment, health systems, and interventions, all of which interact with each other. Mathematical models and data analysis are essential tools for understanding and scientifically simulating these interactions. These approaches enable researchers to draw robust conclusions from incomplete data, formalize competing hypotheses regarding pathogen transmissions and intervention effects, and integrate diverse sources of evidence to generate forecasts and support evidence-based decision-making. The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic accelerated the use of these tools on an unprecedented scale, with mathematical models informing decisions regarding lockdowns, vaccine allocations, and healthcare capacity-based planning in near real time. But the pandemic also made clear that good models need clear and evidence-based assumptions, must be tested against real data, should be checked against new data whenever possible, and must be used with an understanding of their uncertainty, not treated as perfect predictions (1–3). The challenge has only grown since: infectious-disease data are increasingly high-dimensional and multimodal, spanning genomic surveillance, mobility traces, wastewater signals, and electronic health records, while the methodological toolkit available to analyze them has expanded just as quickly, from classical compartmental models to machine learning and stochastic optimization.The Research Topic Mathematical Modeling and data analysis in infectious diseases responds to this landscape by bringing together 22 contributions spanning public health, applied mathematics, infectious-disease epidemiology, and microbial sciences. The Research Topic covers a wide range of approaches, such as mechanistic modeling, statistical forecasting, machine learning, stochastic optimization, computational fluid dynamics, and burden analyses, applied across diseases including COVID-19, influenza, measles, mumps, dengue, and other pathogens of public health concern. Its unifying message is simple: no single method suffices for every question. Instead, the choice of method should follow from the decision at hand, the process generating the data, the observations actually available, and the consequences of incorrect inference or prediction. Robust inference and disease forecastingSeveral contributions in this Research Topic address a central challenge in infectious-disease surveillance: extracting stable, decision-relevant predictions from data that evolve in real time. Rojas-Díaz et al. propose a robust calibration framework for delayed compartmental models, employing controlled parameter initialization and time-varying parameters to fit COVID-19 incidence, intensive-care burden, and effective reproduction numbers across Chilean regions. Their work underscores practical identifiability and numerical stability as prerequisites for translating mechanistic models into tools that can be used operationally in public health decision-making.A complementary forecasting stream combines classical time-series methods with nonlinear learning. Xian et al. demonstrate that a SARIMA–k-nearest-neighbor (SARIMA-KNN) hybrid model improves prediction of acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis in Chongqing, China, relative to its component models and Prophet-based comparators. Cao et al. integrated ARIMA and bidirectional long short-term memory networks through genetic-algorithm weighting, reporting improved COVID-19 forecasts for Japan with external validation in Germany. Alahmadi et al. applied seasonal-trend decomposition together with LightGBM to forecast post-pandemic influenza A in Saudi Arabia, illustrating the value of hybrid approaches when seasonal patterns are disrupted by structural change. Collectively, these studies point to an important direction for surveillance practice: hybrid models can disentangle recurrent linear or seasonal structure from irregular non-linear behavior, but their value depends on prospective evaluation and reporting forecasts alongside calibrated measures of uncertainty (3, 4).The Research Topic also moves beyond single-location time series. One contribution introduces a spatiotemporal graph-learning framework that leverages geographic and origin-destination relationships to capture both contemporaneous neighborhood effects and lagged spatial spillovers in infectious-disease prediction (Liu et al.). Taken together with the forecasting studies above, this work underscores that local incidence is shaped not only by its own history but also by connections to other places, reporting processes, and shifting epidemic regimes. Beyond spatial and temporal structure, several contributions strengthen the statistical foundations needed for infectious-disease data that are non-normal, highly skewed, or operationally heterogeneous. Gharaibeh et al. introduced a two-parameter skewed Loai distribution for positive, right-skewed data and demonstrate its competitive fit to COVID-19 mortality data. At the healthcare-facility scale, Chen and Zhou compared SARIMA, ETS, Prophet, and NNETAR models for forecasting multidrug-resistant organism infection rates, showing that model choice should reflect both forecast accuracy and residual diagnostics rather than point-error measures alone. Disease transmission, interventions, and mobilityMechanistic models offer a principled way to represent intervention timing, human behavior, and disease progression explicitly within the model structure. Babasola et al. formulated a time-delayed model for a potential human outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza, explicitly incorporating incubation, vaccine deployment, vaccine-to-protection delays, vaccine acceptance, residual susceptibility, and compliance with non-pharmaceutical interventions. Their simulations illustrate why early deployment and rapid protection are critical, and why non-pharmaceutical interventions remain especially important before vaccine-induced protection takes effect. Building on this theme, Ntaimo et al. developed an integrated chance-constrained stochastic-programming model for optimal COVID-19 vaccination and intervention strategies across multiple municipalities in Gauteng, South Africa. By incorporating uncertainty in contact patterns, household transmission, age-specific susceptibility and infectivity, and multiple vaccine-effectiveness endpoints, their approach makes risk tolerance an explicit part of allocation decisions. This work exemplifies a valuable bridge between epidemic modeling and operations research: the goal is not merely to simulate an outbreak but also to identify feasible actions under uncertainty.Mobility is another recurring mechanism in this Research Topic. Drawing on cases from 294 Chinese cities, high-speed-rail records, migration data, and socioeconomic covariates, Zhang et al. found that rail connectivity was associated with early intercity dissemination of COVID-19 and that the Wuhan lockdown and transport suspensions disrupted this pathway. The importance of connectivity is echoed in a different setting: an age-structured, stochastic model of measles outbreaks in Northern British Columbia. Irvine et al. showed that inter-community mobility and school-based contact can increase outbreak probability and diminish the effectiveness of interventions, while the combined use of post-exposure prophylaxis and active case finding substantially reduces outbreak risk across scenarios.At a finer spatial scale, Chong et al. combined epidemiological analyses of high-rise residences in Singapore with computational fluid-dynamics simulations, identifying elevated risk within vertical building stacks, and showed how wind direction and cross-ventilation can shape plausible aerosol transport pathways. Together, these contributions demonstrate that interventions must be conditioned on the structure of connectivity itself: rail networks, buildings, households, and social contacts each create distinct transmission pathways that call for correspondingly tailored control measures. Saha et al. extended this perspective across successive COVID-19 waves through a model-based hypothesis-testing framework that compares competing evolutionary explanations while estimating changes in transmission, virulence, vaccination, immunity, and contact patterns. Their analysis reinforces that epidemic trajectories emerge from the coupling of pathogen evolution and human response and that the dominant mechanism driving transmission may shift as population immunity and intervention conditions evolve. Environment, disease burden, and surveillanceA substantial group of papers demonstrates both the value and the interpretive challenges of linking disease surveillance with environmental, socioeconomic, and health-system data. He et al. assessed meteorological influences on influenza incidence in Wuxi, while Yao et al. examined environmental determinants of influenza-like illness across cities in Fujian Province between 2015 and 2023. Tao et al. characterized severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome and its meteorological associations in Jiangsu Province. Extending this line of work, Guo et al. applied generalized additive and distributed lag non-linear models to identify non-linear, interacting, and delayed meteorological associations with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome on China's Jiaodong Peninsula. Hao and Yu take a broader ecological view, using provincial panel models to examine bacillary dysentery in China and link incidence to healthcare capacity, economic development, and forest coverage. Together, these studies show that contextual covariates can strengthen local early warning and risk stratification when lagged, non-linear, and place-specific effects are properly accounted for; they also call for careful interpretation, since ecological and predictive associations do not, on their own, establish causation.The Research Topic also broadens its scope from incidence to population-level burden. Luo et al. used Global Burden of Disease data to quantify trends, geographic inequalities, risk factors, and projected trajectories of childhood infectious encephalitis across Asia. Their results highlight persistent inequities, with lower socio-demographic development associated with higher disease burden, and underscore the continuing need to integrate surveillance, diagnostic capacity, perinatal care, environmental protection, and vaccination.Gong et al. similarly used Global Burden of Disease data, inequality analysis, decomposition, age-period-cohort modeling, and forecasting to characterize the global burden of infectious diseases attributable to drug use. At a more local spatial scale, Hu et al. combined spatial autocorrelation analysis, spatial error models, and Geodetector methods to identify clustered gonorrhea incidence and its interacting sociodemographic, healthcare, and environmental correlates in China. Agrawal et al. synthesized evidence from 47 studies and 61 mumps outbreaks across 21 countries, estimating a pooled attack rate of 14.5% and a pooled complication rate of 10.3%, while documenting substantial heterogeneity by setting, age, and vaccination context. Their meta-analysis underscores the importance of standardized reporting and context-sensitive interpretation in an era of waning immunity and uneven vaccine access. More broadly, burden estimation and evidence synthesis connect model outputs to the equity questions that should guide infectious-disease policy. SummaryThis Research Topic brings together 22 contributions that showcase the breadth of mathematical and computational tools now used to understand and respond to infectious disease threats. Spanning mechanistic modeling, statistical forecasting, machine learning, stochastic optimization, computational fluid dynamics, and burden analysis, the Research Topic addresses diseases ranging from COVID-19 and influenza to measles, mumps, and dengue. Contributions cluster around three central themes: extracting robust, decision-relevant forecasts from noisy real-time surveillance data; modeling how interventions, mobility, and connectivity shape transmission dynamics; and linking disease burden to environmental, socioeconomic, and health-system determinants. Together, these papers reinforce a unifying message: no single method suffices for every question, and the right analytical approach must be matched to the decision at hand, the data-generating process, and the practical consequences of getting the inference wrong. papers.title: Multivalent antiviral conjugates enhance activity against Influenza via cross-linking viruses
papers.abstract: Abstract Long-acting drug–Fc conjugate (CD388) has emerged as a new class of antivirals against influenza A and B, yet the mechanisms governing how Fc conjugation reshapes small-molecule function remain undefined. Here we establish a programmable multivalent antiviral conjugates (AVCs) platform by click chemistry that enables flexible combination of valencies and conjugated drugs, allowing systematic interrogation of valency-dependent antiviral mechanisms. Using zanamivir as a model, mono-, di-, and trivalent zanamivir are conjugated with Fc, with trivalent zanamivir-Fc conjugates (AVC-Z3) exhibiting higher activity than lower-valent AVCs. AVC-Z3 induces inter-virion aggregation, thereby coupling blockade of viral entry with restriction of viral release. This cross-linking–mediated dual-stage inhibition represents a mechanistic shift from neuraminidase suppression to physical viral immobilization. Furthermore, trivalent peramivir-Fc conjugate (AVC-P3) is synthesised and exhibits stronger antiviral activity than AVC-Z3 in vitro, with much longer half-life in vivo than AVC-Z3, and CD388 with YTE mutation. The in vivo antivirus efficacy of AVC-P3 surpasses other AVCs, baloxavir, and CD388 in H1N1-, H3N2-, H5N1-, and influenza B-infection mice models. Together, our findings define ligand valency as a determinant of antiviral mechanism.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the antiviral mechanisms of multivalent drug-Fc conjugates against avian influenza A viruses. The researchers developed a platform using click chemistry to create mono-, di-, and trivalent antiviral conjugates (AVCs) with zanamivir and peramivir. They found that trivalent zanamivir-Fc conjugates (AVC-Z3) and trivalent peramivir-Fc conjugates (AVC-P3) showed enhanced antiviral activity compared to lower-valent versions. papers.title_zh: 多价 抗病毒药物 缀合物通过交联病毒增强抗流感活性
papers.source_body_en: Abstract Long-acting drug–Fc conjugate (CD388) has emerged as a new class of antivirals against influenza A and B, yet the mechanisms governing how Fc conjugation reshapes small-molecule function remain undefined. Here we establish a programmable multivalent antiviral conjugates (AVCs) platform by click chemistry that enables flexible combination of valencies and conjugated drugs, allowing systematic interrogation of valency-dependent antiviral mechanisms. Using zanamivir as a model, mono-, di-, and trivalent zanamivir are conjugated with Fc, with trivalent zanamivir-Fc conjugates (AVC-Z3) exhibiting higher activity than lower-valent AVCs. AVC-Z3 induces inter-virion aggregation, thereby coupling blockade of viral entry with restriction of viral release. This cross-linking–mediated dual-stage inhibition represents a mechanistic shift from neuraminidase suppression to physical viral immobilization. Furthermore, trivalent peramivir-Fc conjugate (AVC-P3) is synthesised and exhibits stronger antiviral activity than AVC-Z3 in vitro, with much longer half-life in vivo than AVC-Z3, and CD388 with YTE mutation. The in vivo antivirus efficacy of AVC-P3 surpasses other AVCs, baloxavir, and CD388 in H1N1-, H3N2-, H5N1-, and influenza B-infection mice models. Together, our findings define ligand valency as a determinant of antiviral mechanism.
papers.abstract_zh: 摘要:长效药物-Fc 结合物​​ (CD388) 已成为抗甲型和乙型流感病毒的新型 抗病毒药物,但 Fc 结合如何重塑小分子功能的机制仍不清楚。在这里,我们通过点击化学建立了一个可编程多价 抗病毒药物 缀合物(AVC)平台,该平台能够灵活组合化合价和缀合药物,从而允许系统地询问化合价依赖性 抗病毒药物 机制。以扎那米韦为模型,单价、二价和三价扎那米韦与 Fc 缀合,其中三价扎那米韦-Fc 缀合物 (AVC-Z3) 表现出比低价 AVC 更高的活性。AVC-Z3 诱导病毒颗粒间聚集,从而将病毒进入的阻断与病毒释放的限制结合起来。这种交联介导的双阶段抑制代表了从神经氨酸酶抑制到物理病毒固定的机制转变。此外,合成了三价帕拉米韦-Fc缀合物(AVC-P3),并在体外表现出比AVC-Z3更强的抗病毒药物活性,体内半衰期比AVC-Z3和YTE 突变的CD388长得多。在 H1N1、H3N2、H5N1 和乙型流感感染小鼠模型中,AVC-P3 的体内抗病毒功效超过其他 AVC、巴洛沙韦和 CD388。总之,我们的研究结果将配体价态定义为 抗病毒药物 机制的决定因素。

papers.full_text: African swine fever (ASF) and classical swine fever (CSF) are economically significant transboundary viral diseases of pigs and are reportable to the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) due to their severe impact on production and international trade. Both diseases present with similar clinical signs; therefore, they cannot be reliably distinguished without laboratory diagnosis. Given that diagnostic assay performance could vary between laboratories, proficiency testing (PT) exercises play a critical role in ensuring the quality and reliability of laboratory results and in helping laboratories to identify and address procedural issues. As one of the WOAH reference laboratories for ASF and CSF, the National Center for Foreign Animal Disease (NCFAD) organized its first PT exercise for ASF and CSF in 2024, targeting the Americas. A total of 16 international laboratories from 11 countries participated in the PT exercise, which focused on front-line molecular and serological diagnostic assays that are essential for laboratory detection of ASF and CSF. The 15-sample molecular panel contained inactivated ASF (6 samples) and CSF (7 samples) viruses, in addition to two negative samples for genome detection. The 20-sample serological panel comprised serum samples containing antibodies to ASF (10 samples) and CSF (5 samples) viruses. The remaining five serum samples contained no antibodies to ASF or CSF viruses. All laboratories correctly identified the ASF virus (ASFV) genome-positive samples; however, only 85.7% of the laboratories correctly identified the CSF virus (CSFV) genome-positive samples. While 80% of participating laboratories accurately identified the ASF-positive serum samples, only 35.7% accurately identified the CSF-positive serum samples. Overall, most laboratories demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy for the molecular detection of ASF and CSF; however, further improvements are needed in the serological detection of ASF and CSF. The PT exercise helped participating laboratories strengthen their testing performance and advance their efforts toward accreditation. full_text_sections.abstract: African swine fever (ASF) and classical swine fever (CSF) are economically significant transboundary viral diseases of pigs and are reportable to the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) due to their severe impact on production and international trade. Both diseases present with similar clinical signs; therefore, they cannot be reliably distinguished without laboratory diagnosis. Given that diagnostic assay performance could vary between laboratories, proficiency testing (PT) exercises play a critical role in ensuring the quality and reliability of laboratory results and in helping laboratories to identify and address procedural issues. As one of the WOAH reference laboratories for ASF and CSF, the National Center for Foreign Animal Disease (NCFAD) organized its first PT exercise for ASF and CSF in 2024, targeting the Americas. A total of 16 international laboratories from 11 countries participated in the PT exercise, which focused on front-line molecular and serological diagnostic assays that are essential for laboratory detection of ASF and CSF. The 15-sample molecular panel contained inactivated ASF (6 samples) and CSF (7 samples) viruses, in addition to two negative samples for genome detection. The 20-sample serological panel comprised serum samples containing antibodies to ASF (10 samples) and CSF (5 samples) viruses. The remaining five serum samples contained no antibodies to ASF or CSF viruses. All laboratories correctly identified the ASF virus (ASFV) genome-positive samples; however, only 85.7% of the laboratories correctly identified the CSF virus (CSFV) genome-positive samples. While 80% of participating laboratories accurately identified the ASF-positive serum samples, only 35.7% accurately identified the CSF-positive serum samples. Overall, most laboratories demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy for the molecular detection of ASF and CSF; however, further improvements are needed in the serological detection of ASF and CSF. The PT exercise helped participating laboratories strengthen their testing performance and advance their efforts toward accreditation.
