full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThe ASF and CSF proficiency testing exercise organized by the NCFAD successfully evaluated diagnostic performance across 16 laboratories from 11 countries, providing valuable insight into laboratory readiness for two economically devastating swine diseases. Overall, most of the participating laboratories demonstrated acceptable proficiency, especially in real-time PCR detection, with notable variability in ELISA performance. Strengthening diagnostic consistency is critical for early outbreak detection, rapid response, and minimizing trade disruptions associated with ASF and CSF.A major finding of the PT exercise was the high level of consistency in real-time PCR detection, particularly for ASF. All laboratories achieved 100% accuracy in the ASFV real-time PCR panel, despite using eight different PCR protocols and a mix of manual and automated extraction methods. This aligns well with the high analytical sensitivity and specificity of ASFV real-time PCR protocols recommended by the WOAH for routine screening and outbreak detection (38). The performance for CSFV real-time PCR was slightly lower, with 14.3% of laboratories misidentifying 1–3 samples, likely due to reduced assay sensitivity, variability in sample handling or nucleic acid extraction systems. In addition, an increase of approximately 3 Ct values was expected for each serially diluted panel sample, and the results submitted by the laboratories were mostly consistent, with only a few showing slight inconsistencies. Nonetheless, overall real-time PCR proficiency was encouraging, showing that real-time PCR capacity is well established in most participating laboratories.Qualitative concordance can mask quantitative interlaboratory bias. Analysis of Ct value distributions showed that several laboratories reported systematic differences in Ct values relative to the NCFAD reference values. These differences may be attributable to variations in analytical methods (e.g., reagents, master mixes, extraction kits, and protocols), instrumentation (e.g., thermocyclers and calibration status), and operator techniques (e.g., pipetting and master mix preparation). Such shifts are analytically important, as they may correspond to a substantial reduction in detectable template levels, potentially resulting in false-negative results.Specific laboratory examples illustrate these general patterns. Lab 3, a regional reference laboratory, reported multiple elevated CSFV Ct values while using the Eberling et al., CSFV assay with the MagMAX 96 Total RNA extraction kit; the combination of elevated Ct values and assay choice implicates assay sensitivity or primer/probe mismatch to the panel strains rather than extraction performance alone. Lab 9, a food analysis laboratory, reported inconsistent CSFV real time PCR results, producing false negatives despite using an undisclosed automated magnetic bead kit; this pattern is consistent with extraction failure, PCR inhibition, or reporting omissions and highlights that automated platforms do not eliminate workflow or reporting errors. The isolated false-positive detection of S12, an ASFV sample, as CSFV by Lab 2 (Table 4), which was not detected by NCFAD or any other participating laboratory, raises additional concern and may indicate contamination, non-specific amplification, or a reporting error. Labs 2 and 6 used the same commercial kit for CSFV detection (Table 4); however, the Ct values they reported across all samples showed a notable difference, suggesting that the results were likely influenced by other factors, including the different extraction kits used by the two laboratories.In contrast, the serological detection revealed greater performance variability, particularly for CSF. While 80% of laboratories achieved complete accuracy for ASF ELISA, only 35.7% did so for CSF ELISA, with 64.3% missing between 1 and 3 samples (Tables 5, 6). The differences in laboratory workflows and possibly the diversity of ELISA kits used in the PT likely contributed to the result variation. During result review at the NCFAD, a contributor to inconsistent ELISA results was the use of short incubation periods (1–2 h), rather than the overnight (~18 h) incubation specified in most kit manuals for better sensitivity. All the laboratories (except lab 20, IDEXX CSF Ab kit) that got accurate results for all CSF ELISA samples used the overnight sample incubation method. Reduced incubation time decreases assay sensitivity and increases the likelihood of borderline or false-negative results, particularly in samples with low antibody titers. The laboratories that utilized short sample incubation were encouraged to adopt overnight incubation, which should significantly improve their diagnostic performance. Samples 4 and 17 are expected to be positive in E2-based ELISA and negative in Erns-based ELISA, reflecting vaccine-induced antibodies against CSFV E2 but absence of antibodies to Erns, which are only produced after natural infection. full_text_sections.other: IntroductionASF and CSF are considered two of the most significant viral diseases affecting the global swine industry, causing devastating economic losses due to high mortality, trade restrictions, and control costs (1–3). ASF, a hemorrhagic fever with near 100% fatality in domestic pigs (4), is caused by ASF virus (ASFV), a large double-stranded DNA virus belonging to the family Asfarviridae. CSF, also a hemorrhagic fever characterized by systemic hemorrhages and severe immunosuppression (5), is caused by CSF virus (CSFV), a positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus within the family Flaviviridae. ASFV has a large, complex genome (~170–190 kb), which encodes more than 150 proteins (4), while CSFV has a smaller genome (~12.3 kb) that encodes both structural and nonstructural proteins essential for viral replication (6). Despite being different in their genetic compositions, ASFV and CSFV induce similar clinical signs in pigs, including high fever, hemorrhagic lesions, and high mortality, complicating clinical differential diagnosis (4, 7). Both viruses exhibit notable global spread, with ASFV expanding from Africa into Europe, Asia, and the Americas, severely impacting global pork production and trade, and CSFV remaining endemic in parts of Asia, Europe, and Latin America, prompting ongoing control efforts (7–12).Laboratory-based molecular and serological assays are critical for accurate and rapid diagnosis of ASF and CSF (13, 14), which in turn supports the prevention of disease spread, facilitates safe trade, and aids in outbreak control. Several molecular and serological assays have been developed and commercialized for ASF and CSF detection, allowing diagnostic laboratories to select tests based on factors such as speed, cost, and available infrastructure.Routine proficiency testing (PT) in diagnostic laboratories is a vital quality assurance tool for evaluating the performance of laboratory assays. It enhances diagnostic reliability by standardizing protocols, identifying gaps in laboratory capacity, and improving outbreak response strategies (13, 15–17). This is particularly important given the economic consequences and international trade implications of ASF and CSF outbreaks, which often lead to movement bans and culling measures. Participation in PT exercises promotes continuous improvement, reduces false-positive and false-negative results, and increases confidence in diagnostic outcomes. It also provides additional benefits, including supporting accreditation, guiding corrective actions, and evaluating new techniques and technologies. Overall, improvements achieved through PT exercises enhance global preparedness and response capabilities against these devastating swine diseases.As a WOAH reference laboratory for ASF and CSF, the NCFAD conducted its first PT exercise in the Americas in 2024, focusing on the frontline diagnostic assays required for the initial detection and surveillance of ASF and CSF. Sixteen laboratories from 11 countries in the Americas (Dominican Republic, Guatemala, Costa Rica, Brazil, El Salvador, Panama, Chile, Nicaragua, Mexico, Peru, and Belize) took part in this inaugural exercise. The serology panel consisted of heat-treated, lyophilized serum samples, while the molecular panel contained heat-treated and gamma-irradiated cell culture-amplified ASFV and CSFV strains in molecular transport medium (MTM). papers.title_original: Multi-laboratory proficiency assessment for molecular and serological diagnosis of classical and African swine fever in the Americas

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of molecular and serological methods for classical swine fever (CSF) and African swine fever (ASF) in the Americas, highlighting the need for standardized testing to ensure reliable results across laboratories.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A multi-laboratory proficiency testing exercise was conducted, involving 15 molecular samples (6 ASF and 7 CSF viruses, plus 2 negative controls) and 20 serological samples (10 ASF and 5 CSF antibodies). The study took place in the Americas between 2024 and 2026, with participation from regional and national reference laboratories as well as local veterinary diagnostic laboratories.
analysis.methods: The molecular panel was prepared using inactivated ASFV and CSFV propagated in porcine primary leukocytes and PK-15 cell lines, respectively. The serological panel included sera from pigs infected with multiple strains of ASFV, CSFV, BDV, or BVDV. Real-time PCR and immunoperoxidase staining were used for molecular detection, while serological testing involved ELISA kits and confirmatory IPT assays. Samples were tested at 3, 7, 14, and 30 days post-treatment with MTM.
analysis.main_results: All laboratories correctly identified the ASF genome-positive samples, but only 85.7% correctly identified the CSF genome-positive samples. For serological detection, most laboratories demonstrated high accuracy, but further improvements were noted in ASF and CSF detection.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings indicate that while molecular detection of ASF and CSF was generally accurate, there is room for improvement in serological methods. The study highlights the importance of proficiency testing in ensuring consistent diagnostic performance across laboratories.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results provide critical insights for improving diagnostic accuracy in ASF and CSF, which can inform better surveillance and control strategies in swine populations, particularly in the Americas.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on proficiency testing exercises and the potential for variability in laboratory practices. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on performance assessments rather than direct clinical or epidemiological outcomes.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of molecular and serological methods for classical swine fever (CSF) and African swine fever (ASF) across multiple laboratories in the Americas. The molecular panel included inactivated ASF and CSF viruses, while the serological panel comprised sera from pigs infected with these viruses. All laboratories correctly identified ASF genome-positive samples, but only 85.7% correctly identified CSF genome-positive samples. Serological detection showed high accuracy but required further refinement. The study underscores the importance of proficiency testing in ensuring reliable diagnostic results. However, the findings are based on laboratory performance assessments and may not fully capture real-world variability. The results have implications for improving diagnostic standards and surveillance in swine populations, contributing to better disease control strategies.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在评估美洲猪瘟 (CSF) 和非洲猪瘟 (ASF) 的分子和血清学方法的诊断准确性,强调需要标准化测试以确保跨实验室获得可靠的结果。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 进行了多实验室能力验证测试,涉及 15 个分子样本(6 个 ASF 和 7 个 CSF 病毒,加上 2 个阴性对照)和 20 个血清学样本(10 个 ASF 和 5 个 CSF 抗体)。该研究于 2024 年至 2026 年间在美洲进行,区域和国家参考实验室以及当地兽医诊断实验室参与其中。
elements_zh.methods: 分子组是使用分别在猪原代白细胞和 PK-15 细胞系中繁殖的灭活 ASFV 和 CSFV 制备的。血清学组包括感染 ASFV、CSFV、BDV 或 BVDV 多种毒株的猪的血清。实时 PCR 和免疫过氧化物酶染色用于分子检测,而血清学检测则涉及 ELISA 试剂盒和验证性 IPT 测定。使用 MTM 在 治疗 后 3、7、14 和 30 天对样品进行测试。
elements_zh.main_results: 所有实验室都正确识别了 ASF 基因组 阳性样本,但只有 85.7% 正确识别了 CSF 基因组 阳性样本。对于血清学检测,大多数实验室表现出较高的准确性,但非洲猪瘟和脑脊液检测的准确性进一步提高。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,虽然 ASF 和 CSF 的分子检测总体上是准确的,但血清学方法仍有改进的空间。该研究强调了能力验证对于确保各实验室诊断性能一致的重要性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果为提高 ASF 和 CSF 的诊断准确性提供了重要的见解,这可以为猪群(尤其是美洲的猪群)提供更好的 监测 和控制策略。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其对能力验证练习的依赖以及实验室实践的潜在可变性而受到限制。证据是中等的,因为它是基于绩效评估而不是直接的临床或流行病学结果。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在评估美洲猪瘟 (CSF) 和非洲猪瘟 (ASF) 的分子和血清学方法的诊断准确性,强调需要标准化测试以确保跨实验室获得可靠的结果。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 进行了多实验室能力验证测试,涉及 15 个分子样本(6 个 ASF 和 7 个 CSF 病毒,加上 2 个阴性对照)和 20 个血清学样本(10 个 ASF 和 5 个 CSF 抗体)。该研究于 2024 年至 2026 年间在美洲进行,区域和国家参考实验室以及当地兽医诊断实验室参与其中。
analysis_zh.methods: 分子组是使用分别在猪原代白细胞和 PK-15 细胞系中繁殖的灭活 ASFV 和 CSFV 制备的。血清学组包括感染 ASFV、CSFV、BDV 或 BVDV 多种毒株的猪的血清。实时 PCR 和免疫过氧化物酶染色用于分子检测,而血清学检测则涉及 ELISA 试剂盒和验证性 IPT 测定。使用 MTM 在 治疗 后 3、7、14 和 30 天对样品进行测试。
analysis_zh.main_results: 所有实验室都正确识别了 ASF 基因组 阳性样本,但只有 85.7% 正确识别了 CSF 基因组 阳性样本。对于血清学检测,大多数实验室表现出较高的准确性,但非洲猪瘟和脑脊液检测的准确性进一步提高。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,虽然 ASF 和 CSF 的分子检测总体上是准确的,但血清学方法仍有改进的空间。该研究强调了能力验证对于确保各实验室诊断性能一致的重要性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果为提高 ASF 和 CSF 的诊断准确性提供了重要的见解,这可以为猪群(尤其是美洲的猪群)提供更好的 监测 和控制策略。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其对能力验证练习的依赖以及实验室实践的潜在可变性而受到限制。证据是中等的,因为它是基于绩效评估而不是直接的临床或流行病学结果。

papers.title: Breaking the channel barrier: same-fluorescence, different-Tm probe strategy enables seven-target respiratory virus detection on a six-channel PCR platform within 20 minutes.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Respiratory pathogens with overlapping symptoms-including SARS-CoV-2, influenza A/B, H5/H7/H10 avian influenza, and RSV-co-circulate and co-infect, demanding rapid multiplex screening at points of care. Conventional multiplex real-time PCR is constrained by hardware channel capacity (≤6), making it difficult to detect seven targets while distinguishing influenza A and B in a single tube. This work addresses the contradiction between high-order multiplexing and limited fluorescence channels without sacrificing speed or sensitivity. RESULTS We developed a six-channel ultra-fast PCR platform detecting seven respiratory viruses in a single tube within 20 min, using a same-fluorescence, different-Tm probe strategy. Influenza A and B share the FAM channel yet generate distinct melting peaks (∼12 °C difference, 84.8 °C vs. 72.3 °C), enabling accurate typing via melting curve analysis. Primers, probes, and enzymes are pre-embedded as lyophilized beads in sealed cartridges for fully automated sample-to-result operation. The assay achieved 100% detection at 5 copies/test for all targets, linearity (R2 > 0.95) across 5-105 copies/test, 90-110% efficiencies, and no cross-reactivity against 39 non-target pathogens. Cartridges remained stable for 12 months at 25 °C. Validation on 271 clinical specimens showed 100% agreement with sequencing-verified single-plex qPCR. SIGNIFICANCE AND NOVELTY This work provides the first integration of melting-curve-based same-channel multiplexing with lyophilized cartridge technology on an ultra-fast PCR platform. By overcoming channel limitations while maintaining speed and sensitivity, the system offers a practical, field-deployable screening tool for decentralized respiratory pathogen detection in resource-limited settings.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces a novel six-channel PCR platform that enables the detection of seven respiratory viruses, including avian influenza A viruses, in a single tube within 20 minutes. The platform uses a same-fluorescence, different-Tm probe strategy to distinguish between influenza A and B, which share the same fluorescent channel. The assay demonstrated 100% detection at 5 copies per test, linearity across a wide range of copy numbers, and no cross-reactivity with non-target pathogens. The system is designed for fully automated operation using lyophilized beads, making it suitable for decentralized use in resource-limited settings. The work represents the first integration of melting-curve-based same-channel multiplexing with lyophilized cartridge technology on an ultra-fast PCR platform. The study's results are based on validation using 271 clinical specimens, showing 100% agreement with sequencing-verified single-plex qPCR. The findings suggest that this platform could improve rapid and accurate respiratory virus detection at points of care, particularly for avian influenza A viruses.

papers.title_original: Spatially resolved infectious disease models for localized outbreak mitigation (and efficient mathematical software)

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to develop spatially resolved infectious disease models for localized outbreak mitigation and efficient mathematical software, addressing the need for improved pandemic preparedness through advanced modeling techniques.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved a simulated spread of SARS-CoV-2 cases for one initial scenario with about 18% red zones and 8 different strategies. Random initial incidence was set at 75-150 weekly cases per 100,000 individuals for 2-20% of the counties, with incidence below 10 otherwise.
analysis.methods: The study employed a hybrid agent-metapopulation model, combining agent-based models in the focus region with ODE-based models for connected regions. It also included a proof-of-concept spatial hybrid model with 8000 agents, 1% initially infected, and different transmission rates based on regions.
analysis.main_results: The median result after 30 days of simulation time showed that the spatial-hybrid model reduced runtime by 98% for 40,000 agents compared to agent-based models, while maintaining similar scaling behavior.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the results as demonstrating the efficiency of the spatial-hybrid model in capturing stochasticity and individual behavior when necessary, while leveraging the computational advantages of ODE-based models for connected regions. This approach represents a novel integration of different modeling techniques for epidemic control.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of more efficient and accurate models for outbreak mitigation, particularly in scenarios with limited computational resources, and support the use of spatially resolved models in pandemic preparedness.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on simulated data and the absence of real-world validation. The evidence is moderate as it presents a proof-of-concept model and discusses implications for future research and applications.

analysis.summary_en: This study presents spatially resolved infectious disease models for localized outbreak mitigation and efficient mathematical software. The research aimed to address the limitations of traditional models by integrating agent-based and ODE-based approaches, allowing for detailed results in the focus region while maintaining computational efficiency. The methods involved a hybrid model that switches between agent-based and ODE-based simulations based on case numbers and resource constraints. The main results showed that the spatial-hybrid model significantly reduced runtime compared to agent-based models, with a 98% reduction for 40,000 agents. The authors interpreted these results as demonstrating the potential of the hybrid model to balance accuracy and efficiency in epidemic control. The study has implications for improving pandemic preparedness and modeling techniques, particularly in resource-limited settings. However, the evidence is moderate due to reliance on simulated data and lack of real-world validation.

October 2026 12:30 – 13:45 CET Virtual meeting Reading time: 2 min (524 words) Wednesday, 14 October 2026, 12:30 –13:45 (CEST) Background Avian influenza A(H9N2) viruses continue to circulate widely in birds and have caused sporadic human infections, highlighting the ongoing risk of influenza viruses emerging at the animal-human interface. Addressing these risks requires timely risk assessment, coordinated One Health action, across human, animal and environmental health sectors, and sustained preparedness for pandemics through GISRS and its partners. Held shortly after the WHO biannual consultation on influenza vaccine composition, including the review of candidate vaccine viruses for pandemic preparedness, this webinar will provide the latest updates on A(H9N2) epidemiology, virus characterization, animal and environmental surveillance, and global risk assessment. By bringing together experts from human, animal, and environmental health sectors, the webinar will promote a shared understanding of current risks and strengthen coordinated preparedness for future zoonotic and pandemic influenza threats. Objectives The webinar will provide a One Health update and support awareness on avian influenza A(H9N2) and provides an opportunity for engagement around the emerging Strategic Framework to accelerate Quadripartite action on avian influenza. Specific objectives are to: Summarize the current epidemiological situation of avian influenza A(H9N2) at the human–animal interface, including recent human infections and the geographical scope and impact of its spread in bird populations. Describe the virological characteristics of circulating A(H9N2) viruses and those detected in sporadic human cases, including antigenic and genetic diversity, markers of mammalian adaptation, and implications for risk assessment, diagnostics and candidate vaccine virus development. Highlight the roles of WHO, FAO, WOAH and UNEP in surveillance, risk assessment, prevention and control of avian influenza, including wildlife, poultry production, ecosystem and public health considerations. Show how data and expertise from GISRS WHO Collaborating Centres and OFFLU contribute to global monitoring, virus characterization, risk assessment and preparedness for zoonotic and pandemic influenza threats. news.title_zh: 世界卫生组织突发卫生事件 EPI-WIN 网络研讨会:了解甲型流感 (H9N2):当前风险、“单一健康”行动和大流行防范 - 世界卫生组织 (WHO)
news.source_body_en: The World Health Organization (WHO) hosted a webinar on 14 October 2026, titled 'Understanding Influenza A(H9N2): current risks, One Health action and pandemic preparedness.' The event aimed to address the ongoing risks posed by avian influenza A(H9N2), which continues to circulate widely in birds and has caused sporadic human infections. The webinar focused on the epidemiological situation, virological characteristics, and global risk assessment of the virus. It emphasized the need for coordinated One Health action across human, animal, and environmental health sectors to strengthen pandemic preparedness. The discussion highlighted the roles of WHO, FAO, WOAH, and UNEP in surveillance, prevention, and control of avian influenza. The event was held shortly after the WHO biannual consultation on influenza vaccine composition, underscoring its relevance to global health strategies.
news.content_zh: 世界卫生组织 (WHO) 于 2026 年 10 月 14 日举办了一次网络研讨会,题为“了解甲型流感 (H9N2):当前风险、统一健康行动和大流行防范”。该活动旨在解决 禽流感 A(H9N2) 带来的持续风险,该病毒继续在鸟类中广泛传播,并已引起零星人类感染。网络研讨会重点讨论了该病毒的流行病学状况、病毒学特征和全球风险评估。它强调需要在人类、动物和环境卫生部门采取协调一致的“同一个健康”行动,以加强大流行病的防范。讨论强调了世卫组织、粮农组织、WOAH 和环境署在 监测、禽流感 预防和控制中的作用。该活动是在世卫组织每年两次就流感 疫苗 成分进行磋商后不久举行的,强调了其与全球卫生战略的相关性。

Saturday, October 03, 2026 Antiviral Research: N70S/Y155H Combined Mutation of Neuraminidase of Avian Influenza H9N2 Virus confers oseltamivir and zanamivir resistance and pathogenicity to Mice Range Of Endemic H9N2 Viruses #19,357 LPAI H9N2 has gained a reputation for spreading uncontrollably in Asian and African poultry, for frequently reassorting with other viruses, and for increasingly spilling over into humans. Nature: Genetic diversity of H9N2 avian influenza viruses in poultry across China and implications for zoonotic transmission J. Inf.: Zoonotic Threat of Novel H6N2 Avian Influenza Virus with Internal Genes Exclusively Derived from H9N2, China, 2025 Emerg. Microbes & Inf.: Novel emerging reassortant H6 avian influenza viruses with internal genes from G57 genotype of H9N2 pose potential zoonotic risk WHO WPRO Reports 2 Recent H9N2 Cases From Chinese Mainland While H9N2 is rarely thought of as being in the same league as H5N1, the CDC lists two lineages (A(H9N2) G1 and A(H9N2) Y280) as having modest pandemic potential, and several candidate vaccines have been developed. As a standalone virus, H9N2 appears to pose a moderate threat, but it has frequently aided and abetted more formidable novel flu viruses (e.g. H5N1, H5N6, H7N9, H10Nx) by providing some or all of their internal genes (see PNAS: Evolution Of H9N2 And It’s Effect On The Genesis Of H7N9). Last month, we looked at report of 6 H6Nx reassortants - all carrying the internal genes from H9N2 - and 5 with its NA from H5N1, and 1 NA from H9N2. Of note, the H6N2 isolate showed dual receptor binding to both avian and human-like receptor cells. This promiscuous nature magnifies any changes that might increase LPAI H9N2's zoonotic threat, since they could potentially be `shared' with other novel influenza A viruses. Which brings us to a paper published this week reporting reduced in vitro susceptibility to oseltamivir and zanamivir among H9N2 viruses carrying dual N70S/Y155H neuraminidase mutations—a combination the authors suggest has become common among recently circulating viruses in China. The authors report as much as a 42-fold reduction in viral inhibition in one isolate tested, and a 23-fold reduction in another. Neither is enough to render oseltamivir or zanamivir useless, but it could reduce their effectiveness, particularly in cases of delayed treatment or severe infections. This is a fairly technical paper, so I've only posted a few excerpts. Those wishing a deeper dive will want to follow the link and read the paper in its entirety. I'll have a brief postscript after the break. N70S/Y155H Combined Mutation of Neuraminidase of Avian Influenza H9N2 Virus confers oseltamivir and zanamivir resistance and pathogenicity to Mice Shenyu Ma a 1, Yuting Chen a 1, Jianwen Zhu a 1, Yuhan Zong b c, Keyu Cai b c, Zhonglong Yang b c, Wenlei Wang a, Yunfei Guo b c, Yan Guo a, Xinyue Duan a, Ziyan Fang a, Nan Zhu a, Sujuan Chen b c, Pinghu Zhang a c 10.1016/j.antiviral.2026.106540 Highlights • H9N2 viruses recently circulating in China harbors novel N70S/Y155H dual mutations in N2; • H9N2 viruses with N70S/Y155H mutations exhibit high pathogenicity to BALB/c mice. • N70S/Y155H linked mutations in N2 confer resistance to oseltamivir and zanamivir, rather than peramivir. • Neuraminidase inhibitors exhibited limited efficacy on H9N2 virus with novel N70S /Y155H dual mutations. Abstract Recently, H9N2 avian influenza virus (AIV) poses a significant threat to both the poultry industry and public health. Therefore, investigating the impact of its neuraminidase mutations on susceptibility to neuraminidase inhibitors (NAIs) is of great importance for clinically preventing potential cross-species transmission of H9N2. In this study, our results revealed that NAI resistance-related mutations of most H9N2 viruses isolated from China during 1998 to 2024 mainly occurred at positions N70S, E119A/D/G/V, Q133K, Q136A, D151E, Y155H, I222V, R224K, E276D, R292K, N294S, and R371K. Among them, the combined N70S and Y155H mutations are common characteristics of H9N2 viruses circulating in recent years. In vivo experiments demonstrated that these H9N2 viruses harboring the combined N70S and Y155H mutations exhibit high pathogenicity to BALB/c mice without prior adaption. In vitro neuraminidase inhibition assays confirmed that these H9N2 viruses bearing the N70S/Y155H mutations exhibited greater reduced inhibition than their counterparts bearing the N70S or Y155H single mutation to oseltamivir and zanamivir, but remained highly sensitive to peramivir. Notably, the in vivo protective effect of NAIs against H9N2 virus with combined N70S and Y155H mutations is limited, possibly due to the restricted ability of these drugs to ameliorate the excessive inflammatory responses. Therefore, there is an urgency to strengthen research on epidemiological surveillance and prevention strategies for avian influenza H9N2 harboring these mutations. (SNIP) Discussion In this study, we performed phylogenetic and comparative sequence analyses of the neuraminidase (NA) genes from 125 H9N2 avian influenza viruses isolated from poultry between 1998 and 2024. Our results showed that early H9N2 viruses circulating in China mainly belonged to the G1-like lineage, whereas more recent strains were predominantly classified within the Y280-like lineage. Sequence analysis further revealed that most of H9N2 viruses harbored multiple mutations associated with reduced susceptibility to neuraminidase inhibitors (NAIs), including substitutions at catalytic or framework residues (E119A/D/G/V, R292K, N294S, and R371K), as well as N70S, D151E, Y155H, R224K, and E276D mutations, which may affect enzyme conformation or the substrate-binding microenvironment[25]. These findings suggest that H9N2 viruses may have gradually accumulated a genetic background associated with altered antiviral susceptibility during long-term evolution. (SNIP) Collectively, our findings provide new experimental evidence for understanding the relationship between the combined N70S and Y155H mutations in N2 and altered susceptibility to NAIs in avian influenza H9N2 viruses. This study expands current understanding of the susceptibility of H9N2 to NAIs and highlights the need for continued surveillance of emerging neuraminidase mutations of H9N2 viruses circulating in poultry. (Continue . . . ) While none of this necessarily elevates the public health threat of LPAI H9N2, this general trend of LPAI H9N2 to accrue resistance mutations bears watching, particularly when you consider the numerous other warnings we've seen of its zoonotic potential. analysis.location_and_population: The research focuses on H9N2 avian influenza viruses circulating in poultry in China, with a mention of the CDC listing two lineages (A(H9N2) G1 and A(H9N2) Y280) as having modest pandemic potential.
analysis.event: A study published in Antiviral Research reports that H9N2 avian influenza viruses with combined N70S/Y155H mutations in their neuraminidase (NA) gene confer resistance to oseltamivir and zanamivir, and show high pathogenicity in BALB/c mice.

analysis.brief_en: A study published on October 3, 2026, in Antiviral Research highlights the emergence of N70S/Y155H dual mutations in the neuraminidase (NA) gene of H9N2 avian influenza viruses circulating in China. These mutations, found in viruses isolated from poultry between 1998 and 2024, confer resistance to oseltamivir and zanamivir, reducing their effectiveness, particularly in severe infections. In vivo experiments showed that these mutated H9N2 viruses exhibit high pathogenicity in BALB/c mice without prior adaptation. The study underscores the growing zoonotic risk associated with H9N2 due to its potential to share these mutations with other novel influenza A viruses. While the public health threat of low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI) H9N2 remains moderate, the findings emphasize the importance of continued surveillance and research into its genetic evolution and antiviral susceptibility. The CDC has noted that two H9N2 lineages (G1 and Y280) have modest pandemic potential, and several candidate vaccines have been developed. The study suggests that these mutations may affect the enzyme's conformation or substrate-binding microenvironment, potentially altering the virus's behavior. The authors call for increased attention to the genetic changes in H9N2 viruses, as they may contribute to future zoonotic transmission risks.

news.source_body_en: A study published on October 3, 2026, in Antiviral Research highlights the emergence of N70S/Y155H dual mutations in the neuraminidase (NA) gene of H9N2 avian influenza viruses circulating in China. These mutations, found in viruses isolated from poultry between 1998 and 2024, confer resistance to oseltamivir and zanamivir, reducing their effectiveness, particularly in severe infections. In vivo experiments showed that these mutated H9N2 viruses exhibit high pathogenicity in BALB/c mice without prior adaptation. The study underscores the growing zoonotic risk associated with H9N2 due to its potential to share these mutations with other novel influenza A viruses. While the public health threat of low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI) H9N2 remains moderate, the findings emphasize the importance of continued surveillance and research into its genetic evolution and antiviral susceptibility. The CDC has noted that two H9N2 lineages (G1 and Y280) have modest pandemic potential, and several candidate vaccines have been developed. The study suggests that these mutations may affect the enzyme's conformation or substrate-binding microenvironment, potentially altering the virus's behavior. The authors call for increased attention to the genetic changes in H9N2 viruses, as they may contribute to future zoonotic transmission risks.

Although human infections have so far produced lower mortality than earlier H5N1 outbreaks, the virus’s expanding host range and its ability to replicate to high titres in bovine mammary glands have sharpened concerns about its pandemic potential. A new computational study published in npj Viruses now offers a detailed structural perspective on one of the key molecular barriers that still separate this bird virus from efficient human-to-human spread: the acid stability of its hemagglutinin, the trimeric spike protein that mediates both receptor binding and membrane fusion. Hemagglutinin, or HA, is the major surface glycoprotein of influenza A virus. Each of its roughly 500-amino-acid monomers is cleaved into two subunits: HA1, which forms the globular head that docks onto sialic acid receptors on host cells, and HA2, which forms the stem anchoring the trimer to the viral envelope. In highly pathogenic avian viruses, a polybasic cleavage site allows activation by the protease furin throughout the body, contributing to systemic infection in birds. After a virus particle is taken up by endocytosis, the acidification of the endosome triggers an irreversible conformational change in HA that exposes the hydrophobic fusion peptide at the N-terminus of HA2, enabling the viral and endosomal membranes to merge and release the segmented viral genome into the cell. The prefusion form of the HA trimer is metastable by design. It must be stable enough to survive the journey between hosts, yet primed to refold when the right pH is reached. If the trimer is too labile, it may fire prematurely in transmission droplets or early endosomes, destroying infectivity; if it is too stable, fusion may fail altogether. This balance differs markedly between host species. In wild aquatic birds, the natural reservoir of avian influenza viruses, greater acid stability helps virions persist in water. The jump to poultry is typically accompanied by acquisition of the polybasic cleavage site and reduced acid stability, while adaptation to mammals generally demands the opposite: a lower fusion-triggering pH, shifting from roughly 5.7 to 6.0 in avian strains to about 5.0 to 5.5 in human-adapted viruses. That extra stability helps the virus survive the mildly acidic environment of the human respiratory tract and of airborne droplets, a prerequisite for efficient airborne transmission. Discover more Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges Donate to Research Find Conferences Clade 2.3.4.4b, which likely emerged around 2020 through reassortment between a highly pathogenic H5N8 strain and a low-pathogenic avian virus in Central Asia or Europe, still binds preferentially to avian-type α2,3-linked sialic acid receptors and shows only weak affinity for the human-type α2,6-linked receptors. Experimental work has shown that a small number of HA mutations, such as Gln226Leu, Asn224Lys and Gly228Ser in the receptor-binding pocket, can shift receptor specificity, and that increased acid stability is essential for airborne transmission in ferrets. Yet these receptor-shifting substitutions remain rare in circulating strains, suggesting that efficient human adaptation will require multiple coordinated changes across at least three viral functions: polymerase activity, receptor-binding specificity and HA stability. The new analysis, led by Daniel Christian Lauster, Christian Sieben, Matthias Ballauff and Andreas Herrmann of Freie Universität Berlin and the Helmholtz Centre for Infection Research, does not generate new experimental data. Instead, it builds on the deep mutational scanning study by Dadonaite and colleagues published in 2024, which used a lentivirus-based pseudovirus platform to measure how nearly every possible amino acid substitution in the HA of A/American Wigeon/South Carolina/2021, a clade 2.3.4.4b strain, affected receptor specificity, acid stability and antibody escape. The Berlin team took the stabilising mutations identified in that screen and asked a structural question: what, mechanically, do these substitutions actually do to the protein? Discover more Find Study Aids cancer Cancer Because no three-dimensional structure exists for the exact strain used in the mutational scan, the researchers used the crystal structure of the HA ectodomain from A/Texas/37/2024, the reference strain of the dairy cattle outbreaks, which shares 99.4 percent sequence identity with the scanned virus, differing at only three positions. Using PyMOL to map polar interactions and the Adaptive Poisson-Boltzmann Solver to compute electrostatic surface potentials at both neutral pH 7.4 and acidic pH 5.3, they dissected each stabilising substitution in molecular detail. The electrostatic calculations, performed at physiological salt concentrations, revealed a recurring theme: many stabilising mutations act by taming a patch of dense positive charge in the lower HA1 head domain that becomes more repulsive as acidic residues become protonated at low pH. In the HA1 subunit, the team found that substitutions such as Lys57Glu, Lys62Glu, Arg81Gly, Arg90Glu, Lys262Ile and Lys269Glu all reduce the strongly positive local surface potential of the lower head domain, diminishing electrostatic repulsion that would otherwise destabilise the prefusion trimer under acidic conditions. Other mutations work through different physics. Glu106Asp preserves the existing contact with Asn71 of HA2 while forging an additional interaction with Arg76 of a neighbouring monomer, thereby reinforcing the HA1-HA2 interface both within and between monomers. Thr318Ile, located near the fusion peptide pocket, enhances hydrophobic packing with surrounding residues, consistent with earlier work by Imai and colleagues showing that this substitution lowers the fusion pH by about 0.3 units. Histidine substitutions at positions 18 and 110 also stabilise the protein, likely because replacing these protonatable pH-sensing residues with non-charged amino acids removes a destabilising positive charge that appears at acidic pH. In the HA2 stem, where most mutations are destabilising because the region is so finely tuned, the researchers identified a distinct set of permissive sites concentrated in the long helix and its connecting loop. Here, hydrophobic substitutions dominate: Ile77Leu, Val91Met, Asp95Met and Leu99Met all introduce methionine or leucine side chains oriented toward the centre of the three-helix bundle, creating new networks of hydrophobic interactions between the long helices of the three HA2 subunits. Asp90Glu, by contrast, strengthens a salt bridge with Lys307 of the adjacent HA1 subunit, shortening it from 3.5 to 2.9 angstroms while preserving the surrounding polar network. Arg106Glu reduces repulsion between positively charged side chains projecting into the stem centre. The short helix, notably, tolerated no stabilising mutations at all, underscoring its critical role in maintaining the metastable prefusion architecture. The authors are careful to frame their conclusions as computationally derived hypotheses. The analysis treats each mutation in isolation and cannot capture epistasis, the phenomenon whereby combinations of mutations produce effects not predictable from their individual contributions. Recent work by Dosey and colleagues has shown that simultaneous mutations in the HA stem of clade 2.3.4.4b can stabilise the protein in ways not observed when the same mutations are studied one at a time. The study also deliberately excludes the wider viral context: neuraminidase activity must remain balanced with HA binding for efficient mucus penetration and viral release, and polymerase mutations in the circulating genotype B3.13 already point toward mammalian adaptation. Effects on acid stability, moreover, do not necessarily correlate with effects on cell entry, meaning the two phenotypes must be evaluated separately. Nevertheless, the structural framework has immediate practical value for pandemic preparedness. By identifying which positions in the circulating H5N1 hemagglutinin can accept acid-stabilising substitutions, and by explaining the mechanisms involved, the study gives genomic surveillance teams a prioritised watch list of mutations whose appearance in sequencing data would signal progressive adaptation toward mammalian hosts. The finding that HA retains substantial structural plasticity, with multiple independent routes to enhanced acid stability spanning electrostatic tuning, hydrogen-bond reinforcement and hydrophobic packing, is a sobering one: it suggests the virus does not need a single improbable mutation to clear this barrier, but could assemble the required stability incrementally. The authors emphasise that direct experimental validation with purified mutant proteins, biophysical stability measurements and mutant HA structures will be essential, and that HA-neuraminidase co-adaptation must be studied in parallel. As clade 2.3.4.4b continues its global expansion, this kind of structure-guided surveillance may prove to be one of the most sensitive early-warning tools available for detecting the molecular steps that could bring a bird virus closer to human pandemic capability. The jump to poultry is typically accompanied by acquisition of the polybasic cleavage site and reduced acid stability, while adaptation to mammals generally demands the opposite: a lower fusion-triggering pH, shifting from roughly 5.7 to 6.0 in avian strains to about 5.0 to 5.5 in human-adapted viruses. That extra stability helps the virus survive the mildly acidic environment of the human respiratory tract and of airborne droplets, a prerequisite for efficient airborne transmission. Discover more Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges Donate to Research Find Conferences Clade 2.3.4.4b, which likely emerged around 2020 through reassortment between a highly pathogenic H5N8 strain and a low-pathogenic avian virus in Central Asia or Europe, still binds preferentially to avian-type α2,3-linked sialic acid receptors and shows only weak affinity for the human-type α2,6-linked receptors. Experimental work has shown that a small number of HA mutations, such as Gln226Leu, Asn224Lys and Gly228Ser in the receptor-binding pocket, can shift receptor specificity, and that increased acid stability is essential for airborne transmission in ferrets. Yet these receptor-shifting substitutions remain rare in circulating strains, suggesting that efficient human adaptation will require multiple coordinated changes across at least three viral functions: polymerase activity, receptor-binding specificity and HA stability. The new analysis, led by Daniel Christian Lauster, Christian Sieben, Matthias Ballauff and Andreas Herrmann of Freie Universität Berlin and the Helmholtz Centre for Infection Research, does not generate new experimental data. Instead, it builds on the deep mutational scanning study by Dadonaite and colleagues published in 2024, which used a lentivirus-based pseudovirus platform to measure how nearly every possible amino acid substitution in the HA of A/American Wigeon/South Carolina/2021, a clade 2.3.4.4b strain, affected receptor specificity, acid stability and antibody escape. The Berlin team took the stabilising mutations identified in that screen and asked a structural question: what, mechanically, do these substitutions actually do to the protein? Discover more Find Study Aids cancer Cancer Because no three-dimensional structure exists for the exact strain used in the mutational scan, the researchers used the crystal structure of the HA ectodomain from A/Texas/37/2024, the reference strain of the dairy cattle outbreaks, which shares 99.4 percent sequence identity with the scanned virus, differing at only three positions. Using PyMOL to map polar interactions and the Adaptive Poisson-Boltzmann Solver to compute electrostatic surface potentials at both neutral pH 7.4 and acidic pH 5.3, they dissected each stabilising substitution in molecular detail. The electrostatic calculations, performed at physiological salt concentrations, revealed a recurring theme: many stabilising mutations act by taming a patch of dense positive charge in the lower HA1 head domain that becomes more repulsive as acidic residues become protonated at low pH. In the HA1 subunit, the team found that substitutions such as Lys57Glu, Lys62Glu, Arg81Gly, Arg90Glu, Lys262Ile and Lys269Glu all reduce the strongly positive local surface potential of the lower head domain, diminishing electrostatic repulsion that would otherwise destabilise the prefusion trimer under acidic conditions. Other mutations work through different physics. Glu106Asp preserves the existing contact with Asn71 of HA2 while forging an additional interaction with Arg76 of a neighbouring monomer, thereby reinforcing the HA1-HA2 interface both within and between monomers. Thr318Ile, located near the fusion peptide pocket, enhances hydrophobic packing with surrounding residues, consistent with earlier work by Imai and colleagues showing that this substitution lowers the fusion pH by about 0.3 units. Histidine substitutions at positions 18 and 110 also stabilise the protein, likely because replacing these protonatable pH-sensing residues with non-charged amino acids removes a destabilising positive charge that appears at acidic pH. In the HA2 stem, where most mutations are destabilising because the region is so finely tuned, the researchers identified a distinct set of permissive sites concentrated in the long helix and its connecting loop. Here, hydrophobic substitutions dominate: Ile77Leu, Val91Met, Asp95Met and Leu99Met all introduce methionine or leucine side chains oriented toward the centre of the three-helix bundle, creating new networks of hydrophobic interactions between the long helices of the three HA2 subunits. Asp90Glu, by contrast, strengthens a salt bridge with Lys307 of the adjacent HA1 subunit, shortening it from 3.5 to 2.9 angstroms while preserving the surrounding polar network. Arg106Glu reduces repulsion between positively charged side chains projecting into the stem centre. The short helix, notably, tolerated no stabilising mutations at all, underscoring its critical role in maintaining the metastable prefusion architecture. The authors are careful to frame their conclusions as computationally derived hypotheses. The analysis treats each mutation in isolation and cannot capture epistasis, the phenomenon whereby combinations of mutations produce effects not predictable from their individual contributions. Recent work by Dosey and colleagues has shown that simultaneous mutations in the HA stem of clade 2.3.4.4b can stabilise the protein in ways not observed when the same mutations are studied one at a time. The study also deliberately excludes the wider viral context: neuraminidase activity must remain balanced with HA binding for efficient mucus penetration and viral release, and polymerase mutations in the circulating genotype B3.13 already point toward mammalian adaptation. Effects on acid stability, moreover, do not necessarily correlate with effects on cell entry, meaning the two phenotypes must be evaluated separately. Nevertheless, the structural framework has immediate practical value for pandemic preparedness. By identifying which positions in the circulating H5N1 hemagglutinin can accept acid-stabilising substitutions, and by explaining the mechanisms involved, the study gives genomic surveillance teams a prioritised watch list of mutations whose appearance in sequencing data would signal progressive adaptation toward mammalian hosts. The finding that HA retains substantial structural plasticity, with multiple independent routes to enhanced acid stability spanning electrostatic tuning, hydrogen-bond reinforcement and hydrophobic packing, is a sobering one: it suggests the virus does not need a single improbable mutation to clear this barrier, but could assemble the required stability incrementally. The authors emphasise that direct experimental validation with purified mutant proteins, biophysical stability measurements and mutant HA structures will be essential, and that HA-neuraminidase co-adaptation must be studied in parallel. As clade 2.3.4.4b continues its global expansion, this kind of structure-guided surveillance may prove to be one of the most sensitive early-warning tools available for detecting the molecular steps that could bring a bird virus closer to human pandemic capability. analysis.time: The study was published on October 8, 2026. The event date is not explicitly stated in the evidence, but the research focuses on the ongoing spread of H5N1 bird flu since 2024.
analysis.location_and_population: The research is centered on the global spread of the H5N1 virus, particularly in the United States where it has established itself in dairy cattle. The virus primarily affects birds, including wild and domestic populations, and has been detected in mammals.
analysis.event: A computational study published in npj Viruses analyzed the structural changes in the hemagglutinin (HA) protein of H5N1 bird flu to understand how it could stabilize for human adaptation. The study did not generate new experimental data but built on prior research from 2024.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The H5N1 virus has been spreading globally, causing significant impact on bird populations and establishing itself in dairy cattle in the United States with sustained mammal-to-mammal transmission. The study highlights the potential for the virus to adapt to human hosts, though this remains a concern rather than a confirmed event.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study provides a structural analysis of HA mutations that could enhance acid stability, which is essential for airborne transmission. However, it does not confirm or report any actual human infections or pandemic potential, only suggesting that such adaptations may be necessary for the virus to become more transmissible among humans.

analysis.brief_en: A new computational study published on October 8, 2026, by researchers at Freie Universität Berlin and the Helmholtz Centre for Infection Research offers insights into how the H5N1 bird flu virus could potentially adapt for human transmission. The research focuses on the hemagglutinin (HA) protein, which is crucial for receptor binding and membrane fusion. The study, based on prior work from 2024, examines mutations that increase HA stability under acidic conditions, a key factor for airborne spread. While the virus has been spreading globally and has established itself in dairy cattle in the United States, it has not yet demonstrated efficient human-to-human transmission. The findings suggest that multiple coordinated changes in HA, polymerase activity, and receptor-binding specificity may be required for the virus to adapt to humans. The study provides a framework for genomic surveillance to detect early signs of such adaptation, which could signal a potential shift toward pandemic capability. However, no confirmed human infections or pandemic risk are reported in the evidence.

news.content_zh: 柏林自由大学和亥姆霍兹感染研究中心的研究人员于 2026 年 10 月 8 日发表的一项新计算研究提供了有关 H5N1 禽流感病毒如何适应人类 传播 的见解。该研究的重点是血凝素(HA)蛋白,它对于受体结合和膜融合至关重要。该研究以 2024 年的先前工作为基础,检验了 突变 在酸性条件下提高 HA 稳定性的能力,酸性条件是空气传播的关键因素。虽然该病毒已在全球传播,并已在美国奶牛中扎根,但尚未表现出有效的人传人 传播。研究结果表明,HA、聚合酶活性和受体结合特异性的多重协调变化可能是病毒适应人类所必需的。该研究为 基因组监测 提供了一个框架来检测这种适应的早期迹象,这可能标志着向大流行能力的潜在转变。然而,证据中没有报告确认的人类感染或大流行风险。

news.content_title: Is Anyone Safe from the H5N1 Bird Flu?
news.content: Is Anyone Safe from the H5N1 Bird Flu? Bird flu is a quickly evolving disease currently spreading like wildfire through the dairy industry, farmed birds, backyard chicken flocks, fur farms, zoos, and wild animal populations, with devastating consequences. The human death toll from avian influenza A(H5N1) sits at 464, with one human succumbing to the bird flu in the United States as of January 2025. The death toll for other animals is considerably more massive, causing global organizations to call H5N1 the “Animal Apocalypse.” A shocking 485 bird species and 48 mammal species have suffered fatalities. Wild animals—including bald eagles, condors, albatross, raccoons, skunks, badgers, minks, foxes, lynx, bobcats, tigers, leopards, otters, seals, sea lions, and dolphins—as well as domestic cats allowed to roam outdoors, have died en masse. Between 2022 and 2023, the death of roughly 30,000 sea lions was reported in South America, about 10,000 albatross carcasses were found in the UK, and over 17,000 southern elephant seal pups (95% of the population) succumbed to the virus in Argentina. Unsurprisingly, 51,986 minks were killed on a single Italian fur factory farm in 2023 after the virus spread through the entire operation in a matter of days. These are only four of countless tragedies. In addition to killing tens of thousands of animals used for their skins, tens of millions of chickens across the U.S. are being executed using slow and painful mass-extermination methods. During past outbreaks, farms have been caught killing animals via ventilation shutdown (VSD). In this cruel practice, ventilation fans are turned off to slowly suffocate the animals. “VSD Plus” incorporates heat, humidity, and/or carbon dioxide in the process—suffocating and baking them to death. As of early 2025, the human and animal death tolls are rising in the United States, with experts worrying that human-to-human transmission is possible. Scientists have already sounded the alarm that a highly pathogenic strain of the influenza H5N1 (clade 2.3.4.4b) virus has been found in cows in the U.S. and may only need to undergo a single mutation for it to be able to attach to human receptors. In other words, the H5N1 bird flu spreading among humans may be a single mutation away. As more outlets publish updates on this devastation, remember that human activities caused this epidemic—specifically, humans breeding, raising, milking, killing, and eating animals, and if we truly want to stop the spread of H5N1, we must live and promote a vegan lifestyle. HELP STOP THE SPREAD – SPREAD THE WORD Thank you for your compassion for animals

news.content_title: What Is Bird Flu, and How Can You Avoid It?
news.content: Experts have warned Congress that avian influenza, or “bird flu,” could kill one in every eight people worldwide—including 40 million Americans—and cause a collapse of the world economy. People who take chicken flesh and eggs into their homes may be putting themselves and their families at risk. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization, the virus can be caught simply by eating undercooked meat or eggs, by eating food prepared on the same cutting board as infected meat or eggs, or even by touching eggshells contaminated with the disease. Former U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Michael Leavitt called the likelihood of an influenza pandemic “very high, some say even certain.” Just walk into any chicken or turkey shed on a factory farm and it’s easy to see why. One shed houses tens of thousands of birds who are never allowed outside. They are surrounded by their own waste and breathe ammonia-laden air that burns their lungs and damages their immune systems. The conditions in these sheds provide ideal breeding grounds for pathogens because birds live amid their own feces from birth to slaughter. Egg-laying hens are kept in stacked cages that become encrusted with waste. When one bird gets sick, the disease can quickly spread to all the birds in the shed. The giant corporations that run factory farms know that they have created ideal breeding grounds for deadly viruses and other diseases, so they dose the animals with massive amounts of drugs. In fact, in the U.S., chickens receive more than three times as many antibiotics (by weight) as humans do. But these drugs are only temporarily effective. Over time, pathogens can mutate and become immune to the medications, leaving humans defenseless against an outbreak. In fact, the widespread use of the antiviral drug amantadine to control viral outbreaks in animals on Chinese farms has made bird flu resistant to that drug, rendering it useless for protecting humans against a bird flu epidemic. The problem is not restricted to birds: Factory-farmed cows and pigs, who also live in crowded and unsanitary conditions, can get and spread influenza and similar viruses. Hans-Gerhard Wagner, a senior officer with the U.N.’s Food and Agriculture Organization, has called the “intensive industrial farming of livestock” an “opportunity for emerging disease.” Giant factory farms are veritable flu-making facilities. The risk posed by bird flu could not be more real or more dire. Senior U.N. System Coordinator for Avian and Human Influenza Dr. David Nabarro describes it as a threat to “the survival of the world as we know it.” Dr. Gregory A. Poland of the Mayo Clinic has called it “what could arguably be the most horrific disaster in modern history.” A contingent of scientists called together by the U.N.’s Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Organization for Animal Health agrees that bird flu is primarily spread by the poultry industry. Experts believe that it’s only a matter of time before a strain of bird flu causes a widespread human outbreak. These viruses are constantly changing, and weaker forms in birds are known to take just months to mutate into highly pathogenic forms for which no effective treatment or vaccine exists. Outbreaks of other strains are regularly detected—Pennsylvania alone detects 15 to 20 outbreaks each year. Factory farming and people who eat chicken flesh and eggs are putting the world at risk for a catastrophe. For more information about bird flu and how factory farming is largely responsible for the disease, read Dr. Michael Greger’s book Bird Flu: A Virus of Our Own Hatching

Poland of the Mayo Clinic has called it “what could arguably be the most horrific disaster in modern history.” A contingent of scientists called together by the U.N.’s Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Organization for Animal Health agrees that bird flu is primarily spread by the poultry industry. Experts believe that it’s only a matter of time before a strain of bird flu causes a widespread human outbreak. These viruses are constantly changing, and weaker forms in birds are known to take just months to mutate into highly pathogenic forms for which no effective treatment or vaccine exists. Outbreaks of other strains are regularly detected—Pennsylvania alone detects 15 to 20 outbreaks each year. Factory farming and people who eat chicken flesh and eggs are putting the world at risk for a catastrophe. For more information about bird flu and how factory farming is largely responsible for the disease, read Dr. Michael Greger’s book Bird Flu: A Virus of Our Own Hatching

news.title: Avian influenza spread beyond a backyard coop on an Illinois farm, analysis finds
news.excerpt: The Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory found spillover from a backyard flock to a cat and a rat on an Illinois farm.

news.content: Strategic Communications and Marketing News Bureau RSS Contact Search Research News Arts Business Education Health and Medicine Humanities Law and Policy Library Information Sciences Science and Technology Agriculture Earth and Environmental Sciences Engineering Life Sciences Physical Sciences Veterinary Medicine Social Sciences Campus News Announcements Campus Life Honors For Faculty and Staff For Journalists About Avian influenza spread beyond a backyard coop on an Illinois farm, analysis finds October 6, 2026 10:21 am by Liz Ahlberg Touchstone Biomedical Sciences Editor Health and Medicine Veterinary Medicine Share on Facebook Share on Bluesky Share on X Share via email Dr. Leyi Wang, the virology section head at the U. of I. Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory, analyzed viruses from animal remains collected on an Illinois farm after avian influenza ravaged the farm’s flock. He found an adaptation allowed the virus to spill over from the flock to a cat and a rat. View Images CHAMPAIGN, Ill. — An outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza virus that nearly wiped out an Illinois farmer’s backyard flock also spread to a domestic cat and wild rats on the farm, an analysis of the animals by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory and the University of Missouri Veterinary Medical Diagnostic Laboratory found. “Bird flu does not stop at birds. On this farm, a cat and a rat were infected too, most likely after contact with dead or dying infected birds, and any wild animal that scavenges or handles carcasses could be exposed the same way,” said Dr. Leyi Wang, the virology section head at the U. of I. Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory and corresponding author of the report. After quickly losing 100 out of 105 of his backyard birds in March 2025, the farmer brought the remains of five birds and a rat to the University of Missouri. Located a mere two miles from a reservoir lake, the farm was ideally situated for avian influenza to travel from wild waterfowl to the flock. The Missouri lab collected a sample from one of the farm chickens, which unsurprisingly tested positive for avian influenza. Four days later, the farm’s primary veterinarian collected the remains of a cat and another rat and sent them to the U. of I. Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory, as there had been a few reports of infections in cats at the time. Wang and his team examined the mammals and tested and sequenced the viruses collected. Both animals tested positive for the same subtype of H5N1 avian influenza as the chicken had. Wang’s team then tested tissue samples from assorted organs to see how extensive the infections were in the mammals; all 12 cat tissues were infected, as were 11 out of 15 rat tissues, and viral RNA was present in the rat’s urine as well. “The cat was expected, but the rat is the surprise,” said Wang, who also is a professor of veterinary clinical medicine at the U. of I. “Since rats live on nearly every farm despite biosecurity, they may be an overlooked link between wild birds, poultry and other mammals. Rodents live close to people, livestock and feed, so infected, shedding rodents could contaminate the farm environment and create new exposure routes.” The labs then sequenced the viral genomes from all three animal sources: chicken, cat and rat. They found that the sequences were nearly identical, indicating a shared source— likely spillover from the poultry to the cat and the rat, Wang said. Crucially, all three had a certain mutation that makes the avian virus more adapted to mammals, which raised a red flag for Wang. “Because the mammalian-adaptation marker was already present in the bird virus, crossing into mammals may not require new mutations,” Wang said. “Shared changes arising in two mammalian species are exactly the kind of adaptation signal worth watching.” The researchers reported their findings in the journal Emerging Infectious Diseases, a publication of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. In light of the findings, particularly the mammalian adaptation and the presence of viral RNA in the rat’s urine, Wang cautions farmers, backyard coop owners and veterinarians to be vigilant. “For flock owners: keep poultry away from wild waterfowl, report sudden die-offs, control rodents and don’t let farm cats scavenge dead birds. For veterinarians: when poultry die of suspected HPAI, treat sick or dead mammals on the same premises as potentially infected and use appropriate precautions.” Read Next Humanities Book counters AI hype by examining how researchers talk about their work A new book by English professor John Gallagher aims to counter the hype surrounding artificial intelligence by focusing on AI researchers and their work. (Animal Wellness Action) 16     Save Story Leer en español Listen:4 Minutes 04:11 KEY TAKEAWAYS Animal welfare groups are criticizing Utah's response to a mink farm bird flu outbreak. Advocates demand transparency on mink-to-mink transmission and worker exposure findings. Officials face challenges due to lack of precedent for mink avian flu. SALT LAKE CITY — After reports of a bird flu outbreak at a mink farm in Utah emerged, animal welfare advocates are describing the state's response to it as "dangerously lax." Details about the outbreak are still publicly unclear. A spokesperson for the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food said that "due to the limited reach and ongoing nature of the outbreak, we are unable to answer some questions that are too specific about the case in order to protect the privacy of the producer." However, records from the Department of Agriculture show seven cases of avian influenza among captive mink in Salt Lake County collected and confirmed in August — though the data may be incomplete, the agency said on its website. Animal Wellness Action and the Center for a Humane Economy, two advocacy groups, criticized the lack of information released to the public, including the mink population of the affected farm, whether there was mink-to-mink transmission of the virus, its source, or any worker exposure findings. Advertise with us Report ad "This isn't an obscure infection in an isolated wild animal," Wayne Pacelle, president of Animal Wellness Action and the Center for a Humane Economy, said in a news release. "It occurred among intensively confined mink, animals with a documented history of amplifying respiratory viruses and providing opportunities for viral evolution. Americans deserve to know what happened and what government found." In 2020, COVID-19 killed about 12,000 mink in Utah, one of the top mink-producing states in the country. The bird flu outbreak is the first of its kind documented in the country, according to the Animal Welfare Institute. The group found through a public records request to the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food that the affected farm was expecting to lose about 80% of its mink to the disease, and that officials were uncertain on the appropriate protocol to contain the virus. Without a standard to quarantine the farm, an official said: "our only options at this point are to watch them die or get emergency vaccine approval." Leon Page, a Utah Department of Agriculture and Food public information officer, said that because this is the first avian influenza outbreak in mink in the country, there isn't an existing precedent for treatment or response. "However, (Utah Department of Agriculture and Food) staff also do everything they can during the process to support producers and make sure that we maximize safety and minimize damage wherever we can," he said. But animal rights groups were not reassured. "It only takes one unlucky mutation of this dangerous virus to trigger a human health crisis, and we can no longer ignore the threat posed by disease proliferation on mink farms," Kate Dylewsky, the assistant director of government affairs at the Animal Welfare Institute, said in a release. "The failure of state and federal officials to prepare for this scenario, or to implement important biosecurity measures in response to the outbreak, demonstrates how mink farming operates with almost no oversight, compounding the threat to the public." Advertise with us Report ad The agency informed the Utah Department of Health and Human Services of the case while it investigated the possibility of transmission to humans, "which has not yet proven to be a high risk," Page said. The department also issued a "verbal hold" to the facility rather than a legal quarantine, before officials continued their investigation. Similar cases in other countries were solved through depopulation instead of quarantines, "so there is also little international precedent for a protocol that doesn't immediately resort to depopulation," he said. The options the department has contemplated for the outbreak are depopulation, quarantine and vaccination, Page said. But the latter can only be approved by the Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins, not by state departments. "Because (avian flu) in mink is new to the U.S., research is limited, and there is little guidance for dosage or efficacy in mink specifically," Page said. "If approved, the vaccine would be released to the state veterinarian and tracked closely by that office to ensure there was no diversion to poultry, dairy cattle, or other farms. The USDA is having internal discussions on when they can or would allow vaccinations." × The Key Takeaways for this article were generated with the assistance of large language models and reviewed by our editorial team. news.source_body_en: In August 2026, the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food confirmed seven cases of avian influenza among captive mink at a Salt Lake County farm. Animal welfare groups have criticized the state's response as "dangerously lax," citing a lack of transparency and biosecurity measures. The affected mink population is expected to lose about 80% of its members to the disease, though details on transmission and worker exposure remain unclear. Officials are uncertain about the appropriate containment protocol, as this is the first documented avian influenza outbreak in mink in the U.S. The state has issued a verbal hold rather than a legal quarantine and is considering depopulation, quarantine, or vaccination as options. However, vaccination requires approval from the Secretary of Agriculture, and research on the virus in mink is limited. The risk to human health is described as "not yet proven to be a high risk," but concerns about viral evolution and mutation persist. The Utah Department of Health was informed about the case while investigations continued, highlighting the lack of established protocols for handling such outbreaks.

Healthy Living Fewer Than 1 in 10 Initial Screenings Asked About Sick Animals When Actors Posed as Bird Flu Patients Published Oct 03, 2026 11:00 AM EDT By Dorothy Brooks CN-STR | AFP via Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pocket When trained actors walked into emergency departments, hospital outpatient clinics, and urgent care centers with pink eye, a reported fever, and a cough, staff doing the initial screening asked about contact with sick or dead birds, livestock, or other mammals in only 7 of 73 drills, or 9.6%. The finding comes from a CDC Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report published October 1, 2026. No real patients were involved. Every "patient" was a professional actor, and every visit was an unannounced drill testing whether facilities could recognize a possible avian influenza A(H5) infection and keep it from spreading in a waiting room. That matters to anyone who has sat in a crowded emergency room during flu season. Bird flu can look like an ordinary respiratory illness, and the question most likely to flag it (have you been around sick animals?) was usually skipped at the front desk. Inside the Unannounced Drills Across Three Jurisdictions The 73 drills took place at 69 facilities from January through June 2026. Of those drills, 52 were in New York City, 15 in the rest of New York State, three in New Jersey, and three in the U.S. Virgin Islands. Forty-two took place in emergency departments, 19 in hospital outpatient clinics, and 12 in urgent care centers. The NYC Health Department ran the drills with the Regional Emerging Special Pathogen Treatment Center at NYC Health + Hospitals/Bellevue, which announced the voluntary mystery patient program for avian flu preparedness in April. Actors from the NYU Standardized Patient Program carried out the visits. Each actor played a 20- to 28-year-old who developed pink eye, then fever, muscle aches, and a cough after trying to rescue a sick duck in Central Park without wearing gloves. Makeup, petroleum jelly, and eye drops mimicked conjunctivitis. When staff asked about sick contacts, the actor replied, "Does a sick bird count?" Each drill lasted no more than two hours and ended after the first clinical evaluation or a decision to notify the health department. Staff debriefings followed. Masks Came Quickly, but Isolation and Protective Gear Lagged Staff screened for symptoms in 93.2% of drills and asked about travel in 79.5%. The actor was given a mask in 82.2% of drills, at a median of two minutes after arrival, but only 43.1% of timed drills met the one-minute target. Isolation was weaker. The actor was placed in an isolation room in 71.2% of drills, at a median of 11 minutes, and fewer than half of those placements met the 10-minute goal. Only 23 of the 52 placements were negative-pressure airborne infection isolation rooms. Overall, 44 drills (60.3%) counted as successful, meaning the patient was both masked and isolated. Protective equipment showed the clearest gap. Among 68 clinician encounters, the clinician wore all required gear (gloves, mask, gown, and eye protection) in only 25% and wore none in 5.9%. Urgent care clinicians wore full gear in one of 12 drills. Staff identified the actor as at risk for avian influenza in 63.4% of drills, and the health department was or would have been notified in 49.3%. Security guards, receptionists, or registrars met the actor first in 69.9% of drills. The authors wrote that both clinical and nonclinical public-facing staff could benefit from "role-specific, competency-based" infection prevention and control training. Exposure Questions Can Change a Diagnosis H5 infection has no unique symptom. CDC guidance for clinicians evaluating possible H5N1 patients lists signs such as eye redness, fever, cough, sore throat, body aches, and shortness of breath, which can resemble other respiratory illnesses. Without asking about contact with birds, dairy cattle, or other animals, a clinician may not order the specialized testing that public health laboratories and CDC perform. The authors wrote that "exposure-specific questions unique to avian influenza were asked considerably less often than were questions about general symptoms or travel history." Clinicians did better in the exam room. Among the 61 drills in which clinicians asked about exposures, they asked about sick or dead birds, livestock, or other mammals in 60.7%, which still left many visits without the question. The report has limits. Not every hospital in the region took part, relatively few clinics and urgent care centers were tested, actors could not show every sign of infection, such as an actual fever, and some staff may have recognized the drill. The findings describe gaps in preparedness, not missed infections. The CDC situation summary counts 71 confirmed and probable human H5 cases in the U.S. since February 2024, as of its March 6, 2026, update, with dairy and poultry workers among those affected. CDC says "the current public health risk is low," though its page on H5N1 bird flu in people notes that people with close or prolonged contact with infected animals face greater risk. If you develop red eyes, fever, or a cough after handling sick birds or working with livestock, mention it at check-in, not only to the doctor. Trouble breathing, chest pain, or rapidly worsening symptoms call for prompt medical care. The report points facilities and health departments to an updated mystery patient drill toolkit for running similar drills. Read more H9N2, H5N1, and H5N2 Are All Being Monitored for Human Risk — Here Is the Honest State of Avian Flu in 2026 Bird Flu Claims First US Victim As Louisiana Man Dies in Hospital Man In Mexico Dies From Bird Flu; First Human Case Of H5N2 Virus: WHO Key Questions Answered Were any real bird flu patients involved? No. All 73 drills used trained actors simulating H5 symptoms. Where did the drills happen? At 69 emergency departments, hospital outpatient clinics, and urgent care centers in New York, New Jersey, and the U.S. Virgin Islands from January to June 2026. Did only 1 in 10 clinicians ask about birds? No. The 9.6% figure reflects initial screening by front-desk and triage staff. Clinicians who asked about exposures asked about sick birds, livestock, or other mammals in 60.7% of those drills. Why does animal exposure history matter? H5 symptoms can resemble common respiratory illnesses, so exposure history can prompt isolation, full protective gear, and specialized testing. How many Americans have had H5 bird flu? CDC reports 71 confirmed and probable cases since February 2024, as of its March 6, 2026, update. What should I do if I get sick after contact with birds or farm animals? Mention the exposure when you arrive, wear a mask, and talk with a clinician. Seek prompt care for severe symptoms.
