Healthy Living Fewer Than 1 in 10 Initial Screenings Asked About Sick Animals When Actors Posed as Bird Flu Patients Published Oct 03, 2026 11:00 AM EDT By Dorothy Brooks CN-STR | AFP via Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pocket When trained actors walked into emergency departments, hospital outpatient clinics, and urgent care centers with pink eye, a reported fever, and a cough, staff doing the initial screening asked about contact with sick or dead birds, livestock, or other mammals in only 7 of 73 drills, or 9.6%. The finding comes from a CDC Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report published October 1, 2026. No real patients were involved. Every "patient" was a professional actor, and every visit was an unannounced drill testing whether facilities could recognize a possible avian influenza A(H5) infection and keep it from spreading in a waiting room. That matters to anyone who has sat in a crowded emergency room during flu season. Bird flu can look like an ordinary respiratory illness, and the question most likely to flag it (have you been around sick animals?) was usually skipped at the front desk. Inside the Unannounced Drills Across Three Jurisdictions The 73 drills took place at 69 facilities from January through June 2026. Of those drills, 52 were in New York City, 15 in the rest of New York State, three in New Jersey, and three in the U.S. Virgin Islands. Forty-two took place in emergency departments, 19 in hospital outpatient clinics, and 12 in urgent care centers. The NYC Health Department ran the drills with the Regional Emerging Special Pathogen Treatment Center at NYC Health + Hospitals/Bellevue, which announced the voluntary mystery patient program for avian flu preparedness in April. Actors from the NYU Standardized Patient Program carried out the visits. Each actor played a 20- to 28-year-old who developed pink eye, then fever, muscle aches, and a cough after trying to rescue a sick duck in Central Park without wearing gloves. Makeup, petroleum jelly, and eye drops mimicked conjunctivitis. When staff asked about sick contacts, the actor replied, "Does a sick bird count?" Each drill lasted no more than two hours and ended after the first clinical evaluation or a decision to notify the health department. Staff debriefings followed. Masks Came Quickly, but Isolation and Protective Gear Lagged Staff screened for symptoms in 93.2% of drills and asked about travel in 79.5%. The actor was given a mask in 82.2% of drills, at a median of two minutes after arrival, but only 43.1% of timed drills met the one-minute target. Isolation was weaker. The actor was placed in an isolation room in 71.2% of drills, at a median of 11 minutes, and fewer than half of those placements met the 10-minute goal. Only 23 of the 52 placements were negative-pressure airborne infection isolation rooms. Overall, 44 drills (60.3%) counted as successful, meaning the patient was both masked and isolated. Protective equipment showed the clearest gap. Among 68 clinician encounters, the clinician wore all required gear (gloves, mask, gown, and eye protection) in only 25% and wore none in 5.9%. Urgent care clinicians wore full gear in one of 12 drills. Staff identified the actor as at risk for avian influenza in 63.4% of drills, and the health department was or would have been notified in 49.3%. Security guards, receptionists, or registrars met the actor first in 69.9% of drills. The authors wrote that both clinical and nonclinical public-facing staff could benefit from "role-specific, competency-based" infection prevention and control training. Exposure Questions Can Change a Diagnosis H5 infection has no unique symptom. CDC guidance for clinicians evaluating possible H5N1 patients lists signs such as eye redness, fever, cough, sore throat, body aches, and shortness of breath, which can resemble other respiratory illnesses. Without asking about contact with birds, dairy cattle, or other animals, a clinician may not order the specialized testing that public health laboratories and CDC perform. The authors wrote that "exposure-specific questions unique to avian influenza were asked considerably less often than were questions about general symptoms or travel history." Clinicians did better in the exam room. Among the 61 drills in which clinicians asked about exposures, they asked about sick or dead birds, livestock, or other mammals in 60.7%, which still left many visits without the question. The report has limits. Not every hospital in the region took part, relatively few clinics and urgent care centers were tested, actors could not show every sign of infection, such as an actual fever, and some staff may have recognized the drill. The findings describe gaps in preparedness, not missed infections. The CDC situation summary counts 71 confirmed and probable human H5 cases in the U.S. since February 2024, as of its March 6, 2026, update, with dairy and poultry workers among those affected. CDC says "the current public health risk is low," though its page on H5N1 bird flu in people notes that people with close or prolonged contact with infected animals face greater risk. If you develop red eyes, fever, or a cough after handling sick birds or working with livestock, mention it at check-in, not only to the doctor. Trouble breathing, chest pain, or rapidly worsening symptoms call for prompt medical care. The report points facilities and health departments to an updated mystery patient drill toolkit for running similar drills. Read more H9N2, H5N1, and H5N2 Are All Being Monitored for Human Risk — Here Is the Honest State of Avian Flu in 2026 Bird Flu Claims First US Victim As Louisiana Man Dies in Hospital Man In Mexico Dies From Bird Flu; First Human Case Of H5N2 Virus: WHO Key Questions Answered Were any real bird flu patients involved? No. All 73 drills used trained actors simulating H5 symptoms. Where did the drills happen? At 69 emergency departments, hospital outpatient clinics, and urgent care centers in New York, New Jersey, and the U.S. Virgin Islands from January to June 2026. Did only 1 in 10 clinicians ask about birds? No. The 9.6% figure reflects initial screening by front-desk and triage staff. Clinicians who asked about exposures asked about sick birds, livestock, or other mammals in 60.7% of those drills. Why does animal exposure history matter? H5 symptoms can resemble common respiratory illnesses, so exposure history can prompt isolation, full protective gear, and specialized testing. How many Americans have had H5 bird flu? CDC reports 71 confirmed and probable cases since February 2024, as of its March 6, 2026, update. What should I do if I get sick after contact with birds or farm animals? Mention the exposure when you arrive, wear a mask, and talk with a clinician. Seek prompt care for severe symptoms. analysis.event: In 7 out of 73 unannounced drills, hospital staff asked about contact with sick animals when actors posed as bird flu patients. The drills were conducted to test facilities' ability to recognize avian influenza A(H5) infections and prevent spread in waiting rooms.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Only 9.6% of initial screenings during the drills included questions about contact with sick animals. The study highlights a potential gap in early detection of avian influenza, which could lead to increased risk of transmission in healthcare settings.

analysis.brief_en: A recent study conducted from January through June 2026 revealed that fewer than 10% of initial screenings in emergency departments, outpatient clinics, and urgent care centers included questions about contact with sick animals when actors posed as bird flu patients. The drills, organized by the NYC Health Department and the Regional Emerging Special Pathogen Treatment Center at Bellevue, involved 73 simulated visits with actors representing 20- to 28-year-olds. The findings, published in the CDC Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report on October 1, 2026, highlight a potential gap in early detection of avian influenza A(H5) infections. The study underscores the need for improved screening protocols to prevent the spread of the virus in healthcare settings. The drills were unannounced and tested whether facilities could identify possible avian flu cases. The results suggest that healthcare staff may not be adequately prepared to recognize and respond to avian influenza symptoms, raising concerns about public health risks.

news.wechat_summary_zh: 时间：该研究于2026年1月至6月进行，CDC报告于2026年10月1日发布。新闻报道于2026年10月3日发布。；地点与对象：演习在三个辖区的 69 个设施中进行：52 个位于纽约市，15 个位于纽约州其他地区，3 个位于新泽西州。演习涉及 73 次模拟访问，演员代表 20 至 28 岁的青少...；事件：在 73 次未经事先通知的演习中，有 7 次当演员冒充禽流感患者时，医院工作人员询问了与患病动物的接触情况。进行演习的目的是测试设施识别 禽流感 A(H5) 感染并防止候诊室传播的能力。；影响与风险：演习期间只有 9.6% 的初步筛查包括有关与患病动物接触的问题。该研究强调了 禽流感 早期检测的潜在差距，这可能导致医疗机构中 传播 的风险增加。；应对与不确定性：这些演习是纽约市卫生局和贝尔维尤地区新兴特殊病原体 治疗 中心准备活动的一部分。研究结果基于模拟场景，没有涉及真实的患者。该研究是初步的，旨在改进筛查方案。

Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search CLOSE Search Support Menu USDA notes more H5N1 avian flu on poultry farms News brief Stephanie Soucheray, MA Topics Avian Influenza (Bird Flu) Share Copied to clipboard USDA, Lance Cheung / Flickr cc According to the latest update from the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS), there were six new detections of H5N1 avian flu this past week, including major outbreaks at two large facilities in Indiana and Minnesota. Minnesota remains the epicenter of H5N1 activity, with 34,400 birds affected at a Stearns County commercial turkey farm. The state has noted eight affected commercial flocks, three affected backyard flocks, and a total of 343,050 birds affected in the past 30 days. In Indiana, a Jay County commercial duck meat facility with 24,300 birds was affected. In the past 30 days, 550,000 birds in 12 commercial flocks and nine backyard flocks have been hit with H5N1. Texas cattle also affected In other news, APHIS also noted a new H5N1 detection in a dairy cattle herd in Texas. In the past 30 days there have been three avian flu detections in cattle, all in Texas. Lawmakers want answers from CDC director on childhood vaccine recommendations, measles response News brief Chris Dall, MA Topics Childhood Vaccines Measles US Coast Guard, Nicole Foguth / Flickr A letter to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) director Erica Schwartz, MD, MPH, JD, from Democratic lawmakers indicates a growing frustration with her leadership amid attempts by President Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to change childhood vaccine recommendations. In a letter sent earlier this week, Sen. Michael Bennet (D-CO), Rep. Kim Schrier (D-Wash.) and 29 Democratic colleagues asked Schwartz whether she or any CDC career scientists were consulted about or played a role in developing President Trump's August 10th executive order (EO), which cut the number of recommended childhood vaccines from 18 to 11 and called for the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine to be broken up into three separate shots. Following the order, the Department of Health and Human Services posted a request for information (RFI) aimed at laying the groundwork for the changes. Citing Schwartz's comments at her confirmation hearing, where she pledged to "never betray the science," the lawmakers challenged the director about the scientific basis behind the EO and asked if and how the CDC plans to implement it. "As CDC Director, you bear a responsibility to uphold scientific integrity, and we write seeking answers on how the CDC will respond to the EO and the RFI, and how you will honor the pledge you made to ensure that the CDC leads with evidence-based public health," the letter states. Questions about measles response Bennet and his colleagues called into question the CDC's handling of measles deaths in Pennsylvania and asked whether the agency has instituted a new policy for handling state-reported health data. While Pennsylvania officials have identified five measles-associated deaths, the CDC currently only acknowledges two deaths. "If the agency under your leadership is altering verified state data to fit political preferences, the pledge you made at your confirmation hearing has already been broken," they wrote. The letter also asks Schwartz to explain why the CDC delayed opening orders for COVID vaccines through the Vaccines for Children program, which provides vaccines for low-income children. The lawmakers asked Schwartz for written responses by October 16th. Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search CLOSE Search Support Menu USDA notes more H5N1 avian flu on poultry farms News brief Stephanie Soucheray, MA Topics Avian Influenza (Bird Flu) Share Copied to clipboard USDA, Lance Cheung / Flickr cc According to the latest update from the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS), there were six new detections of H5N1 avian flu this past week, including major outbreaks at two large facilities in Indiana and Minnesota. Minnesota remains the epicenter of H5N1 activity, with 34,400 birds affected at a Stearns County commercial turkey farm. The state has noted eight affected commercial flocks, three affected backyard flocks, and a total of 343,050 birds affected in the past 30 days. In Indiana, a Jay County commercial duck meat facility with 24,300 birds was affected. In the past 30 days, 550,000 birds in 12 commercial flocks and nine backyard flocks have been hit with H5N1. Texas cattle also affected In other news, APHIS also noted a new H5N1 detection in a dairy cattle herd in Texas. In the past 30 days there have been three avian flu detections in cattle, all in Texas. Lawmakers want answers from CDC director on childhood vaccine recommendations, measles response News brief Chris Dall, MA Topics Childhood Vaccines Measles US Coast Guard, Nicole Foguth / Flickr A letter to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) director Erica Schwartz, MD, MPH, JD, from Democratic lawmakers indicates a growing frustration with her leadership amid attempts by President Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to change childhood vaccine recommendations. In a letter sent earlier this week, Sen. Michael Bennet (D-CO), Rep. Kim Schrier (D-Wash.) and 29 Democratic colleagues asked Schwartz whether she or any CDC career scientists were consulted about or played a role in developing President Trump's August 10th executive order (EO), which cut the number of recommended childhood vaccines from 18 to 11 and called for the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine to be broken up into three separate shots. Following the order, the Department of Health and Human Services posted a request for information (RFI) aimed at laying the groundwork for the changes. Citing Schwartz's comments at her confirmation hearing, where she pledged to "never betray the science," the lawmakers challenged the director about the scientific basis behind the EO and asked if and how the CDC plans to implement it. "As CDC Director, you bear a responsibility to uphold scientific integrity, and we write seeking answers on how the CDC will respond to the EO and the RFI, and how you will honor the pledge you made to ensure that the CDC leads with evidence-based public health," the letter states. Questions about measles response Bennet and his colleagues called into question the CDC's handling of measles deaths in Pennsylvania and asked whether the agency has instituted a new policy for handling state-reported health data. While Pennsylvania officials have identified five measles-associated deaths, the CDC currently only acknowledges two deaths. "If the agency under your leadership is altering verified state data to fit political preferences, the pledge you made at your confirmation hearing has already been broken," they wrote. The letter also asks Schwartz to explain why the CDC delayed opening orders for COVID vaccines through the Vaccines for Children program, which provides vaccines for low-income children. The lawmakers asked Schwartz for written responses by October 16th. Featured Spotlight Avian influenza detected at two Yakima County dairy farms TAMMY AYER Yakima Herald-Republic Tammy Ayer Features/The Vanished Editor Author facebook Author twitter Author email Oct 8, 2026 Oct 8, 2026 Updated 1 hr ago 0 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save The first detection of avian influenza in cattle in Washington state has been confirmed at two dairy farms in Yakima County, the Yakima Health District reported Thursday. The U.S. Department of Agriculture National Veterinary Services Laboratory and the Washington State Department of Agriculture confirmed the H5N1 detection, according to a news release from the health district. The health district is working with the two dairies to monitor and protect the health of people exposed to the infected cattle, it said. The dairies weren't identified. Dairy cattle in 19 states have been infected since the outbreak began in March 2024, the release said. There are currently no confirmed human cases of avian influenza, commonly called bird flu, in Yakima County. Avian influenza is caused by Type A influenza viruses that occur naturally in wild birds. The virus can spread from wild birds to other animals, including poultry and mammals such as dairy cattle. Human infections with avian influenza viruses are rare, the release said. “The risk to the general public remains low," Dr. Dave Atteberry, health officer for the health district, said in the release. Pasteurized milk products remain safe for consumers, according to a news release from the state agriculture department, and milk supply shortages aren't expected. Officials: Avoid raw milk Infected cows can shed the virus in their milk, making raw milk and other raw dairy products unsafe for consumption, county health officials said. Avoid raw dairy product consumption and don't allow pets to consume raw milk or other dairy products, or raw foods such as raw meat. The two Yakima County farms that are impacted are under quarantine and have employed strict biosecurity measures, a news release from the state agriculture department said. Veterinarians are treating sick cows. The county health district "is working closely with dairy producers, workers, and our local, state, and federal partners to provide guidance and resources to protect the health of people who may have been exposed to the infected cattle," Atteberry said. Though there is no evidence of human-to-human transmission at this time, avian influenza can spread to humans following close contact with infected animals or contaminated environments, state agriculture and county health officials said. Those who may be at higher risk include animal agricultural workers, backyard flock owners, hunters and people who work with wildlife, such as wildlife biologists. Taking precautions The health district can help coordinate testing for any exposed person who develops symptoms to ensure prompt identification and appropriate treatment for any human cases. To reduce the risk of avian influenza, don't touch wild birds or animals. Wild birds and other animals can carry avian influenza even if they appear healthy. Avoid contact with sick or dead birds or animals, and with bird droppings or contaminated surfaces. People with job-related exposures to infected birds or other infected animals or their environments should take additional precautions, including wearing recommended PPE. Those who suspect illness in cattle or backyard birds should use extra precautions. Hunters should practice good hygiene when handling game. Wear disposable gloves when cleaning harvested birds or cleaning bird feeders. And though the seasonal flu vaccine doesn't prevent bird flu, it reduces the risk of co-infection with human and avian influenza viruses, county health officials said. Featured Spotlight Avian influenza detected at two Yakima County dairy farms TAMMY AYER Yakima Herald-Republic Tammy Ayer Features/The Vanished Editor Author facebook Author twitter Author email Oct 8, 2026 Oct 8, 2026 Updated 1 hr ago 0 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save The first detection of avian influenza in cattle in Washington state has been confirmed at two dairy farms in Yakima County, the Yakima Health District reported Thursday. The U.S. Department of Agriculture National Veterinary Services Laboratory and the Washington State Department of Agriculture confirmed the H5N1 detection, according to a news release from the health district. The health district is working with the two dairies to monitor and protect the health of people exposed to the infected cattle, it said. The dairies weren't identified. Dairy cattle in 19 states have been infected since the outbreak began in March 2024, the release said. There are currently no confirmed human cases of avian influenza, commonly called bird flu, in Yakima County. Avian influenza is caused by Type A influenza viruses that occur naturally in wild birds. The virus can spread from wild birds to other animals, including poultry and mammals such as dairy cattle. Human infections with avian influenza viruses are rare, the release said. “The risk to the general public remains low," Dr. Dave Atteberry, health officer for the health district, said in the release. Pasteurized milk products remain safe for consumers, according to a news release from the state agriculture department, and milk supply shortages aren't expected. Officials: Avoid raw milk Infected cows can shed the virus in their milk, making raw milk and other raw dairy products unsafe for consumption, county health officials said. Avoid raw dairy product consumption and don't allow pets to consume raw milk or other dairy products, or raw foods such as raw meat. The two Yakima County farms that are impacted are under quarantine and have employed strict biosecurity measures, a news release from the state agriculture department said. Veterinarians are treating sick cows. The county health district "is working closely with dairy producers, workers, and our local, state, and federal partners to provide guidance and resources to protect the health of people who may have been exposed to the infected cattle," Atteberry said. Though there is no evidence of human-to-human transmission at this time, avian influenza can spread to humans following close contact with infected animals or contaminated environments, state agriculture and county health officials said. Those who may be at higher risk include animal agricultural workers, backyard flock owners, hunters and people who work with wildlife, such as wildlife biologists. Taking precautions The health district can help coordinate testing for any exposed person who develops symptoms to ensure prompt identification and appropriate treatment for any human cases. To reduce the risk of avian influenza, don't touch wild birds or animals. Wild birds and other animals can carry avian influenza even if they appear healthy. Avoid contact with sick or dead birds or animals, and with bird droppings or contaminated surfaces. People with job-related exposures to infected birds or other infected animals or their environments should take additional precautions, including wearing recommended PPE. Those who suspect illness in cattle or backyard birds should use extra precautions. Hunters should practice good hygiene when handling game. Wear disposable gloves when cleaning harvested birds or cleaning bird feeders. And though the seasonal flu vaccine doesn't prevent bird flu, it reduces the risk of co-infection with human and avian influenza viruses, county health officials said. Surprising findings from B.C.’s human case of H5N1 avian flu Sunday, October 04, 2026 Avian flu (bird flu) is a contagious viral disease caused by Avian Influenza Type A viruses that primarily affects wild aquatic birds and domestic poultry. Photo credit: File By The Conversation What you need to know: Canada's first human H5N1 infection was a medical mystery: the virus shouldn't have bound well to human cells, yet it caused severe respiratory failure. New research suggests there is more to learn about what makes a virus dangerous. How do we know when an animal virus might pose a risk to humans? Canada confirmed a human case of H5N1 avian influenza (often called “bird flu”) in 2024, the first ever known to have been acquired in Canada. The patient, a thirteen-year-old British Columbian, suffered severe symptoms including respiratory failure but recovered with intensive care in hospital. Uncovering insights into how pathogens can switch from animals to humans — as in this human case of bird flu — can help researchers and public health agencies prepare for future outbreaks. In a recent study, our lab examined viral mutations in this case and uncovered an unexpected result: the effects of these mutations were inconsistent with the usual warning signs we expect to see in a virus adapted to infect humans. How we usually monitor influenza Public health agencies and collaborating groups use complementary approaches to monitor infectious disease outbreaks and risk. Human outbreak data comes from many places, including care settings and associated surveillance labs, volunteers reporting disease status, and wastewater monitoring. Current routine virological tests in public health labs include sequencing viral genes, testing for antiviral resistance and assessing immunity against strains of interest. The other two mutations caught our attention since they are less understood. Both were in hemagglutinin, the viral surface protein that binds to cells and initiates infection by fusing the virus and cell membranes. These mutations, E190D and Q226H (representing 28 per cent and 35 per cent, respectively, of hemagglutinin genetic material sequenced), were at the part of hemagglutinin known to interact with receptors on host cells. Bird and human cells tend to display different types of receptors, which is why scientists use receptor binding as a common test for species adaptation. These hemagglutinin mutations had not previously been observed to switch binding to human-type receptors in H5N1 influenza. What this case revealed Our lab investigated the role of these two mutations in what types of receptors these viruses bind to more favourably. Receptor binding can influence which cells, and which species, a virus is more likely to infect. Therefore, we made versions of the hemagglutinin protein with and without each mutation and measured how they bound to different receptors. The results were unexpected. When we produced hemagglutinin protein with either of these mutations, not only did we not observe the expected binding to human-type receptors that would support human infection, but the binding to avian receptors was severely diminished. Using standard approaches, binding to any receptor was essentially undetectable. Yet the virus in the B.C. patient clearly replicated in human tissue. So, our team tested the ability of the hemagglutinin variant carrying both mutations to fuse cells derived from human lung cells. After binding to host cells, fusion is the second major step mediated by hemagglutinin. The result of fusion is that viral genetic material and proteins required for replication are released from inside the viral particle into the host cell where they can function. Just as we saw when we looked at the receptor binding, we saw a substantial reduction in the virus’s hemagglutinin protein’s ability to fuse membranes of the lung-derived cells, likely a consequence of the reduced binding. However, we did detect a low level of fusion, which suggests that we might see both receptor binding and membrane fusion activity under conditions that better mimic actual human lungs. In a human case of infection with a virus that usually affects birds, we would normally expect to see the surface protein (hemagglutinin) binding with human receptors. That would be typical in a virus that was adapting from birds to humans. But what we saw in the B.C. case of human infection with H5N1 was a reduced ability not only to bind to human receptors, but also to bird cell receptors, resulting in a low ability to fuse with cell membranes. However, the combination of lots of hemagglutinin proteins on the virus’s surface, and many receptors on the cell’s surface, may have compensated for the poor ability to bind to individual receptors. What we can learn from this case This case demonstrates that there is much to learn about the complex factors that may result in a virus developing the ability to infect humans. From decades of investigation, we had reason to believe these hemagglutinin mutations were interesting, so it’s a success for our existing knowledge base. Our lab depended on successes in the public health system leading up to the B.C. Centre for Disease Control Public Health Laboratory being able to sequence viruses in the patient, and releasing its data to the influenza research community, as well as generous support of our research from the federal and provincial sources. The unexpected findings suggest that we need greater functional understanding of human disease risk. Our existing set of mutational warning signs does not capture all threats as we monitor animal outbreaks. Functional laboratory studies are slower and more expensive, but they can tell us more directly how viruses behave. Public health agencies already run certain on-the-fly functional tests such as assessing vaccine match to seasonal influenza. This data continues to inform our response to outbreaks. Greater monitoring of other influenza functions would further enhance public health efforts. The stronger our basic knowledge of how these viruses work, the better we can interpret surveillance data, prepare for outbreaks and design interventions. -John Ni, PhD Candidate in Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, University of British Columbia,and Sriram Subramaniam, Professor, Faculty of Medicine, University of British Columbia Login to join the discussion Please enable JavaScript to view the comments powered by Disqus. analysis.location_and_population: The case occurred in British Columbia, Canada, involving a thirteen-year-old patient. The affected population includes humans exposed to H5N1 avian influenza.
analysis.event: A human case of H5N1 avian flu was confirmed in British Columbia, Canada, in 2024. The patient, a thirteen-year-old, suffered severe respiratory failure but recovered with intensive care. The study analyzed viral mutations in this case and found unexpected results regarding receptor binding and cell fusion.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: This case represents a single human infection with H5N1 avian flu. The study found that the mutations in hemagglutinin did not support binding to human-type receptors, and binding to avian receptors was severely diminished. analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The case was confirmed by public health agencies. The study was conducted by a lab, and the findings are based on virological tests, including sequencing and receptor binding analysis. The results suggest the need for further research to understand the mechanisms of zoonotic transmission and the implications for future outbreaks.

news.title_zh: 鸟类病毒如何感染人? BC省人类感染H5N1禽流感病例的惊人发现 - Daily Nation
news.source_body_en: A recent article from Daily Nation discusses a human case of H5N1 avian flu confirmed in British Columbia, Canada, in 2024. The patient, a thirteen-year-old, experienced severe respiratory failure but recovered with intensive care. Researchers analyzed the viral mutations in this case and found unexpected results. The mutations in hemagglutinin, a key surface protein, did not support binding to human-type receptors, and binding to avian receptors was severely reduced. However, the virus still replicated in human tissue, suggesting potential for zoonotic transmission. The study highlights the need for further research to understand how such mutations might influence the virus's ability to infect humans and the broader implications for public health preparedness. The findings are based on virological tests, including sequencing and receptor binding analysis, conducted by a lab. The article emphasizes the importance of monitoring influenza outbreaks and understanding the mechanisms of species adaptation.

Number 8860726. keyboard_arrow_up QuotesWeatherDigital EditionsPodcasts menuMenusearchSearchsearchSearch menu Subscribe Subscribe Registeraccount_circleLog In search close menu Agribusiness Newskeyboard_arrow_down Related Topics Policy Commentary See Allchevron_right Market Newskeyboard_arrow_down Related Topics Grain Market News Livestock & Poultry Market News Market Reports See Allchevron_right Ingredient Market Priceskeyboard_arrow_down Related Topics Corn Price Updates Soybean Meal Price Updates See Allchevron_right Nutrition & Healthkeyboard_arrow_down Related Topics Poultry Health & Nutrition Beef Health & Nutrition Dairy Health & Nutrition Swine Health & Nutrition See Allchevron_right Feedstuffs 365 search close Poultry Health and Nutrition Nutrition & Health Research Host-adapted bird flu follows ‘clear seasonal pattern’ Understanding migration timing can help poultry growers plan ahead to protect their flocks from exposure. University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture October 6, 2026 schedule2 Min Read University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture/Fred Miller By Mary Hightower Understanding the timing of outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) can help poultry farms prepare and protect their flocks, according to economists. Between February 2022 and April 2026, HPAI has affected 212 million birds, with more than 1,000 commercial flocks affected, according to the Animal & Plant Health Inspection Service, part of the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Jada Thompson, associate professor of agricultural economics for the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture (UADA) who specializes in poultry, has done extensive research on the effects of HPAI. “When the United States poultry industry encountered the H5N2 strain of HPAI in 2014, it was mostly spread house-to-house through contaminated materials, trucks and laborers,” she said. “This prompted sweeping changes in biosecurity culture that still exist today,” Thompson said. “These changes, along with a hot summer, helped to end the outbreak by June 2015. Related:How nest cover and light affect egg laying in cage-free systems “However, since the 2022 introduction of a host-adapted H5N1 virus, poultry growers in the Mississippi Flyway have faced increased disease risk, despite the wide adoption of these enhanced biosecurity measures. This most recent outbreak has spread instead by external introduction rather than house to house as in 2014,” she said. “‘Host-adapted’ refers to the virus’s ability to persist in wild bird populations. Where previous HPAI events ravaged both poultry and wild birds, the current H5N1 2.3.4.4b classification is less likely to kill some wild bird species,” Thompson said. “This means that waterfowl can become infected and still survive migration, spreading the disease across the flyway.” “Examining the geographic distribution of HPAI detections over time reveals a clear seasonal pattern that mirrors waterfowl migration,” said Matthew Marchant, whose findings are contained in the paper “Bird Flu on the Move,” published in Southern Ag Today earlier this year. Marchant is a Ph.D. student in environmental dynamics at the University of Arkansas, working with Thompson in the department of agricultural economics and agribusiness. Thompson is a faculty member with UADA’s research arm, the Arkansas Agricultural Experiment Station, and the Dale Bumpers College of Agricultural, Food and Life Sciences at the University of Arkansas. “During the summer months, detections are sparse and concentrated in the northern reaches of the flyway, where birds spend the breeding season. As fall migration begins, HPAI’s geographic footprint expands southward, spanning nearly the entire flyway from October through May,” he said. Related:Chore-Time introduces CATALYST OVO for layer operations “Understanding seasonality affords producers a predictable window each year to prepare before peak exposure periods arrive. A host-adapted virus in a migratory population means recurring seasonal risk for the foreseeable future. However, that seasonality also gives producers, researchers and communities time to plan ahead,” Marchant said. “Understanding when and where the disease is likely to appear turns an unpredictable force into a manageable calendar of preparation and vigilance,” Marchant said. “Community preparedness, which begins at the farm level, remains the most effective tool available against this disease.” According to APHIS, current cases are concentrated in the northern Plains states. analysis.time: The article was published on October 6, 2026. The event date is not explicitly stated, but the seasonal pattern of HPAI is described as occurring from October through May, with sparse detections during the summer months.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak is concentrated in the northern Plains states, and the Mississippi Flyway is mentioned as a region where poultry growers have faced increased disease risk. The affected population includes poultry farms and wild bird populations.
analysis.event: The article reports that host-adapted bird flu (H5N1) follows a clear seasonal pattern, spreading through migration rather than house-to-house transmission. This is a reported observation based on research by Jada Thompson and Matthew Marchant.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Between February 2022 and April 2026, HPAI affected 212 million birds, with over 1,000 commercial flocks impacted. The current host-adapted H5N1 virus is described as posing recurring seasonal risk for the foreseeable future.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The article discusses the need for community preparedness and planning ahead to manage the seasonal risk. It also notes that biosecurity measures have been adopted, but the outbreak continues to spread through external introduction.

analysis.brief_en: The article published on October 6, 2026, by Feedstuffs highlights that host-adapted bird flu, specifically the H5N1 strain, follows a clear seasonal pattern linked to waterfowl migration. This pattern, observed in the Mississippi Flyway, has led to increased disease risk for poultry growers despite enhanced biosecurity measures. The outbreak, which began in 2022, has affected over 212 million birds and more than 1,000 commercial flocks since February 2022. Current cases are concentrated in the northern Plains states, and the virus is described as persisting in wild bird populations, allowing for seasonal spread. Researchers emphasize that understanding this pattern enables producers to prepare for peak exposure periods, but the recurring nature of the outbreak means the risk remains for the foreseeable future. The article does not provide specific confirmed cases or deaths but underscores the importance of community-level preparedness to mitigate the impact of the disease.

This pattern, observed in the Mississippi Flyway, has led to increased disease risk for poultry growers despite enhanced biosecurity measures. The outbreak, which began in 2022, has affected over 212 million birds and more than 1,000 commercial flocks since February 2022. Current cases are concentrated in the northern Plains states, and the virus is described as persisting in wild bird populations, allowing for seasonal spread. Researchers emphasize that understanding this pattern enables producers to prepare for peak exposure periods, but the recurring nature of the outbreak means the risk remains for the foreseeable future. The article does not provide specific confirmed cases or deaths but underscores the importance of community-level preparedness to mitigate the impact of the disease.

news.content: ___ × Market Information Top Poultry Companies Expert Insights Blogs Regions Magazines Sign In Poultry Meat Egg Poultry Health Sustainability Poultry Future Chicken Marketing Summit Poultry Tech Summit Broilers & Turkeys Diseases & Health Avian Influenza Avian influenza detected again in Manitoba During the past month, the province has had eight flocks struck by the virus. Roy Graber October 5, 2026 Tatiana53 | Bigstock Article Summary Highly pathogenic avian influenza has been detected again in Manitoba's commercial poultry, with the latest confirmed case in Pembina on October 2, 2026. Eight of the ten Canadian poultry flocks infected by HPAI in the past month were in Manitoba, with the remaining two in Alberta. Latest case confirmed October 2, 2026 in Pembina municipality, Manitoba Eight of ten commercial poultry flocks affected by HPAI in Canada were in Manitoba First Pembina case in 2026; Manitoba had no HPAI cases from December 2025 through September 2026 Earlier September cases included meat turkeys in Rhineland and mixed flocks of broilers, laying hens, and turkeys in Cartier and Rockwood CFIA continues monitoring; interactive map available for tracking HPAI cases across North America Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) continues to be found in commercial poultry in Manitoba. The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) reported that the latest case in Manitoba was confirmed Oct. 2 in the municipality of Pembina. Further information about that flock infection has not yet been disclosed by CFIA. During the past month, 10 commercial poultry flocks in Canada have been struck by HPAI. Of those, eight have been in Manitoba, while the remaining two were in Alberta. This is the first case in Pembina during 2026. Until September, Manitoba had not had any instances of HPAI in poultry since December 2025. Updates on previously reported cases CFIA has traditionally not released information concerning flock sizes or the type of poultry in operations that have been affected by HPAI. However, a recent report from the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) offered additional details on earlier reported cases that were all confirmed on Sept. 21 in Manitoba. An affected flock in Rhineland included meat turkeys, while a flock struck in Cartier was a mixed flock of broilers and laying hens. A third flock, in Rockwood, was also a mixed flock, but in this situation, the flock included broilers, laying hens and turkeys. To learn more about HPAI cases in commercial poultry flocks in the United States, Mexico and Canada, see an interactive map on WATTPoultry.com. analysis.event: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) has been detected again in Manitoba's commercial poultry. The latest confirmed case occurred in Pembina on October 2, 2026. analysis.brief_en: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) has been detected again in Manitoba, Canada, with the latest confirmed case in Pembina on October 2, 2026. This marks the first HPAI case in Pembina during 2026, following a period of no reported cases from December 2025 through September 2026. During the past month, eight out of ten Canadian poultry flocks infected by HPAI were in Manitoba, with the remaining two in Alberta. The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) continues to monitor the outbreak and has provided an interactive map for tracking HPAI cases across North America. However, the CFIA has not disclosed specific details about the affected flock, including its size or the type of poultry involved. The outbreak highlights the ongoing threat of HPAI in commercial poultry, with the CFIA emphasizing the need for continued surveillance and monitoring.

elements_zh.event: 马尼托巴省的商业家禽中再次检测到 高致病性禽流感 (HPAI)。最新确诊病例于 2026 年 10 月 2 日发生在彭比纳。这是彭比纳 2026 年首例病例,曼尼托巴省在 2025 年 12 月至 2026 年 9 月期间没有出现 HPAI 病例。
elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 过去一个月,感染高致病性禽流感的加拿大 10 只家禽中有 8 只在马尼托巴省,其余 2 只在艾伯塔省。CFIA 继续监测局势,并提供了交互式地图来跟踪北美各地的高致病性禽流感病例。该风险被明确表述为持续存在的威胁。
elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 加拿大食品检验局(CFIA)正在监测事态发展,尚未透露有关受影响鸡群的更多细节。CFIA 传统上不会发布有关受影响经营场所的鸡群规模或家禽类型的信息。可以获取先前报告案件的最新情况,但有关彭比纳案件的具体细节尚未披露。

analysis_en.time: The latest case was confirmed on October 2, 2026. Earlier cases in September 2026 included meat turkeys in Rhineland and mixed flocks in Cartier and Rockwood. The outbreak has been ongoing in Manitoba for the past month.
analysis_en.location_and_population: Manitoba, specifically the Pembina municipality, and other regions in Canada such as Rhineland, Cartier, and Rockwood. The affected population includes commercial poultry flocks, primarily turkeys and mixed flocks of broilers, laying hens, and turkeys.
analysis_en.event: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) has been detected again in Manitoba's commercial poultry. The latest confirmed case occurred in Pembina on October 2, 2026. This is the first case in Pembina during 2026, and Manitoba had no HPAI cases from December 2025 through September 2026.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: During the past month, eight of the ten Canadian poultry flocks infected by HPAI were in Manitoba, with the remaining two in Alberta. The CFIA continues monitoring the situation and has provided an interactive map for tracking HPAI cases across North America. The risk is explicitly stated as ongoing and a continued threat.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) is monitoring the situation and has not disclosed further details about the affected flock. The CFIA traditionally does not release information on flock sizes or poultry types in affected operations. Updates on previously reported cases are available, but specific details about the Pembina case have not been disclosed.

news.source_body_en: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) has been detected again in Manitoba, Canada, with the latest confirmed case in Pembina on October 2, 2026. This marks the first HPAI case in Pembina during 2026, following a period of no reported cases from December 2025 through September 2026. During the past month, eight out of ten Canadian poultry flocks infected by HPAI were in Manitoba, with the remaining two in Alberta. The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) continues to monitor the outbreak and has provided an interactive map for tracking HPAI cases across North America. However, the CFIA has not disclosed specific details about the affected flock, including its size or the type of poultry involved. The outbreak highlights the ongoing threat of HPAI in commercial poultry, with the CFIA emphasizing the need for continued surveillance and monitoring.

news.content: My Markets Watchlist Markets News Search Business Strategy Economy Finance Retail Advertising Careers Law Media Real Estate Small Business The Better Work Project Personal Finance Tech Science AI Enterprise Transportation Startups Innovation Markets News Stocks Indices Commodities Crypto Currencies ETFs Lifestyle Entertainment Culture Travel Food Health Education Parenting Military & Defense Politics Reviews Home Kitchen Style Streaming Pets Tech Deals Gifts Tickets Video Big Business So Expensive View From Above Small Business Authorized Account Risky Business Boot Camp Still Standing How Crime Works Life Lessons Level Up Community Games Boxed Pipeline Knighthop Tally Vaxart Announces Publication of Preclinical Study Demonstrating 100% Protection Against a Lethal Dose of H5N1 Avian Flu in a Ferret Challenge Model PRESS RELEASE GlobeNewswire Oct. 8, 2026, 08:40 AM Second-generation oral mucosal vaccine candidate (VXA-H5-02) induced robust cross-neutralizing antibodies, significantly reduced viral load, and completely protected against lethal clade 2.3.4.4b viral challenge SOUTH SAN FRANCISCO, Calif., Oct. 08, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Vaxart, Inc. (OTCQX: VXRT), a clinical-stage biotechnology company developing oral recombinant vaccines administered via tablet, today announced the publication of positive preclinical study results evaluating its adenovirus-based oral mucosal vaccine platform against Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) H5N1, a pathogenic virus that poses a significant threat to public health. The complete, peer-reviewed study results, which were published in Frontiers in Immunology, demonstrate that Vaxart’s second-generation vaccine candidate, VXA-H5-02, elicits both mucosal and systemic neutralizing antibody responses, offering comprehensive protection against lethal challenge with H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b. The company previously reported topline study results in 2025. "The potential spread of H5N1 avian influenza across livestock and mammals underlines the critical need for scalable, rapidly deployable vaccines," said Dr. Sean Tucker, CSO of Vaxart. "These data further support our oral mucosal vaccination technology and highlight the improved immune-stimulating activity of our second-generation H5 construct. The 100% survival rate following challenge with a lethal dose of virus underscores the robust immune protection our oral influenza vaccine candidates may be able to provide. This protection, combined with ease of self-administration and the elimination of complex cold-chain requirements required for injected vaccines, supports the potential of our platform in enabling a novel approach to influenza prevention and pandemic preparedness.” Key Study Highlights 100% Survival Rate: All ferrets immunized with VXA-H5-02 survived a lethal challenge with H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, whereas 100% of unvaccinated control animals rapidly succumbed to infection by Day 6 post-challenge (p< 0.001). Significant Viral Load & Shedding Reduction: VXA-H5-02 vaccination produced a ~2.3-log reduction in infectious viral shedding by Day 3 post-challenge compared to controls. By Day 6–7, viable virus was below the limit of detection in nasal wash samples, and 7 out of 8 animals completely cleared viral RNA by Day 8/9. Mucosal & Cross-Neutralizing Immunity: Immunization with VXA-H5-02 elicited strong serum neutralizing titers and mucosal IgA/IgG responses in nasal wash fluid. Higher pre-challenge nasal IgA levels showed the strongest negative correlation with post-challenge viral shedding (r = -0.6059). Cross-Clade Protection: Serum from VXA-H5-02 immunized animals demonstrated cross-neutralizing activity against divergent H5 strains, including the recently emerged H5N1 clade 2.3.2.1e. Additionally, the clade-mismatched first-generation vaccine (ND1.1, encoding clade 2.1.3.2) conferred 37% survival against the clade 2.3.4.4b challenge. About the Study In the study, non-replicating recombinant adenovirus type 5 (rAd5) vectors expressing viral hemagglutinin (HA) were administered directly to the small intestine of ferrets via endoscopic delivery on Day 0 and Day 28. Ferrets cannot use human tablets, so a liquid formulation delivery method was used to simulate enteric-coated tablet release. On Day 56, animals were challenged intranasally with 1 x 105 TCID50 H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b virus. Protective efficacy, clinical symptoms, mucosal/systemic antibody titers, and viral shedding (measured by RT-qPCR and TCID50) were systematically monitored. About Vaxart Vaxart is a clinical-stage biotechnology company developing a range of oral recombinant vaccines based on its proprietary delivery platform. Vaxart vaccines are designed to be administered using pills that can be stored and shipped without refrigeration and eliminate the risk of needle-stick injury. Vaxart believes that its proprietary pill vaccine delivery platform is suitable to deliver recombinant vaccines, positioning the Company to develop oral versions of currently marketed vaccines and to design recombinant vaccines for new indications. Vaxart’s development programs currently include pill vaccines designed to protect against coronavirus, norovirus, and influenza, as well as a therapeutic vaccine for human papillomavirus (HPV), Vaxart’s first immune-oncology indication. Vaxart has filed broad domestic and international patent applications covering its proprietary technology and creations for oral vaccination using adenovirus and TLR3 agonists. Cautionary Note Regarding Forward-Looking Statements This press release contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of Section 27A of the Securities Act of 1933, as amended, and Section 21E of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended, that involve substantial risks and uncertainties. All statements, other than statements of historical facts, included in this press release regarding Vaxart’s strategy, prospects, plans and objectives, results from preclinical and clinical trials, commercialization agreements and licenses, and beliefs and expectations of management are forward-looking statements, including statements contained in the quotations of Vaxart’s management in this press release. These forward-looking statements may be accompanied by such words as “should,” “believe,” “could,” “potential,” “will,” “expected,” “anticipate,” “plan,” "target," "seek," "intend," "may," "predict," "project," "would," and other words and terms of similar meaning. Examples of such statements include, but are not limited to, statements regarding the potential of VXA-H5-02 and Vaxart’s oral mucosal vaccine platform to induce protective immune responses against H5N1 or other influenza strains in humans; the potential for the preclinical ferret results described in this press release to be predictive of, or replicated in, human clinical trials; the potential for the in vitro cross-neutralizing antibody responses observed in this study to confer cross-clade protection; the anticipated advantages of oral tablet administration, including self-administration and the absence of cold-chain requirements; Vaxart’s plans, objectives and expected timing for further preclinical studies, regulatory submissions and clinical development of VXA-H5-02; Vaxart’s ability to develop and commercialize its product candidates; and Vaxart’s expectations regarding the role of its platform in influenza prevention and pandemic preparedness. About the Study In the study, non-replicating recombinant adenovirus type 5 (rAd5) vectors expressing viral hemagglutinin (HA) were administered directly to the small intestine of ferrets via endoscopic delivery on Day 0 and Day 28. Ferrets cannot use human tablets, so a liquid formulation delivery method was used to simulate enteric-coated tablet release. On Day 56, animals were challenged intranasally with 1 x 105 TCID50 H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b virus. Protective efficacy, clinical symptoms, mucosal/systemic antibody titers, and viral shedding (measured by RT-qPCR and TCID50) were systematically monitored. About Vaxart Vaxart is a clinical-stage biotechnology company developing a range of oral recombinant vaccines based on its proprietary delivery platform. Vaxart vaccines are designed to be administered using pills that can be stored and shipped without refrigeration and eliminate the risk of needle-stick injury. Vaxart believes that its proprietary pill vaccine delivery platform is suitable to deliver recombinant vaccines, positioning the Company to develop oral versions of currently marketed vaccines and to design recombinant vaccines for new indications. Vaxart’s development programs currently include pill vaccines designed to protect against coronavirus, norovirus, and influenza, as well as a therapeutic vaccine for human papillomavirus (HPV), Vaxart’s first immune-oncology indication. Vaxart has filed broad domestic and international patent applications covering its proprietary technology and creations for oral vaccination using adenovirus and TLR3 agonists. analysis.time: The study was published on October 8, 2026, and the preclinical results were previously reported in 2025.

analysis.event: published preclinical study results demonstrating 100% protection against a lethal dose of H5N1 avian flu in a ferret challenge model. The study was conducted by Vaxart and reported by GlobeNewswire.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study showed 100% survival rate in vaccinated ferrets challenged with H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b virus, while unvaccinated controls had 100% mortality by Day 6. The results indicate robust immune protection and reduced viral shedding, but no human cases, deaths, or exposures are reported.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study is preclinical and has been published in Frontiers in Immunology. It demonstrates protective efficacy in ferrets, but no human trials or real-world outcomes are reported. The findings are based on a peer-reviewed study and are considered preliminary.

analysis.brief_en: Vaxart Inc. announced on October 8, 2026, the publication of preclinical study results showing that its second-generation oral mucosal vaccine candidate, VXA-H5-02, provides 100% protection against a lethal dose of H5N1 avian flu in a ferret challenge model. The study, published in Frontiers in Immunology, demonstrated that vaccinated ferrets survived a challenge with H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, while unvaccinated controls had 100% mortality by Day 6. The vaccine significantly reduced viral shedding and cleared viral RNA by Day 8–9. These findings highlight the potential of Vaxart’s oral vaccine platform for influenza prevention, particularly for H5N1, but no human cases, deaths, or exposures are reported. The results are based on a peer-reviewed preclinical study and are considered preliminary, with no mention of real-world application or outcomes.

The source, the UK government's avian influenza in Europe publication, shows a running series of preliminary and updated assessments covering high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) in Great Britain and Europe. The most recent addition came on 5 October 2026, when an updated outbreak assessment for HPAI in Great Britain and Europe for September 2026 was added. Before that, on 18 August 2026, an updated assessment for August 2026 was added. Risk assessments focused on the likelihood of spread of highly pathogenic avian influenza H5Nx associated with bird fairs, shows, markets, sales and other gatherings have also been issued periodically. A June 2026 risk assessment on that topic was added on 23 June 2026, following an April 2026 version added on 22 April 2026 and a March 2026 version added on 25 March 2026. A February 2026 version was added on 6 March 2026. Outbreak assessments for Great Britain and Europe were also added on 1 June 2026, covering 26 May 2026, and on 15 April 2026, covering 10 April 2026. Further assessments were added on 20 March 2026, covering 10 March 2026, and on 10 March 2026, covering 27 February 2026. On 3 March 2026, a preliminary outbreak assessment dated 13 February 2026 was added concerning HPAI antibodies in dairy cattle in the Netherlands. On 4 February 2026, a qualitative risk assessment on HPAI H5 and the control of wild birds under general licences GL40 to GL42 for the period from January 2024 to December 2025 was added; that report was written in December 2024. Earlier additions include an updated outbreak assessment for 19 December 2025, added on 24 December 2025, and a risk assessment on the likelihood of spread of HPAI H5Nx associated with bird fairs, shows, markets, sales and other gatherings, added on 8 December 2025. An updated assessment for 11 November 2025 was added on 17 November 2025, and one for 28 October 2025 was added on 3 November 2025. An updated assessment for 8 October 2025 was added on 21 October 2025. On 16 September 2025, a risk assessment on the likelihood of spread of HPAI H5Nx associated with bird fairs, shows, markets, sales and other gatherings was attached following a change in national risk levels for HPAI. An updated assessment for 11 August 2025 was added on 15 August 2025, and a risk assessment on the same gatherings topic was added on 7 August 2025. Risk levels in the updated outbreak assessment for 21 July 2025 were corrected on 30 July 2025, and that assessment was added on 29 July 2025. A risk assessment on the likelihood of spread of HPAI H5Nx associated with bird fairs, shows, markets, sales and other gatherings for May 2025 was added on 20 June 2025. The 12 May 2025 outbreak assessment was added on 13 May 2025, and the 18 March 2025 assessment was added on 24 March 2025. A risk assessment on the same gatherings topic for January 2025 was added on 20 February 2025. The record also lists assessments and reports from earlier years, including outbreak assessments for Great Britain and Europe, risk assessments on gatherings and on the incursion of HPAI into housed or not housed poultry flocks and captive birds, and scientific opinions. The publication notes that major, notifiable or new and emerging animal disease outbreaks worldwide are monitored, and that a preliminary outbreak assessment may be carried out when a new animal disease outbreak becomes known in the UK or another country. The source, the UK government's avian influenza in Europe publication, shows a running series of preliminary and updated assessments covering high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) in Great Britain and Europe. The most recent addition came on 5 October 2026, when an updated outbreak assessment for HPAI in Great Britain and Europe for September 2026 was added. Before that, on 18 August 2026, an updated assessment for August 2026 was added. Risk assessments focused on the likelihood of spread of highly pathogenic avian influenza H5Nx associated with bird fairs, shows, markets, sales and other gatherings have also been issued periodically. A June 2026 risk assessment on that topic was added on 23 June 2026, following an April 2026 version added on 22 April 2026 and a March 2026 version added on 25 March 2026. A February 2026 version was added on 6 March 2026. Outbreak assessments for Great Britain and Europe were also added on 1 June 2026, covering 26 May 2026, and on 15 April 2026, covering 10 April 2026. Further assessments were added on 20 March 2026, covering 10 March 2026, and on 10 March 2026, covering 27 February 2026. On 3 March 2026, a preliminary outbreak assessment dated 13 February 2026 was added concerning HPAI antibodies in dairy cattle in the Netherlands. On 4 February 2026, a qualitative risk assessment on HPAI H5 and the control of wild birds under general licences GL40 to GL42 for the period from January 2024 to December 2025 was added; that report was written in December 2024. Earlier additions include an updated outbreak assessment for 19 December 2025, added on 24 December 2025, and a risk assessment on the likelihood of spread of HPAI H5Nx associated with bird fairs, shows, markets, sales and other gatherings, added on 8 December 2025. An updated assessment for 11 November 2025 was added on 17 November 2025, and one for 28 October 2025 was added on 3 November 2025. An updated assessment for 8 October 2025 was added on 21 October 2025. On 16 September 2025, a risk assessment on the likelihood of spread of HPAI H5Nx associated with bird fairs, shows, markets, sales and other gatherings was attached following a change in national risk levels for HPAI. An updated assessment for 11 August 2025 was added on 15 August 2025, and a risk assessment on the same gatherings topic was added on 7 August 2025. Risk levels in the updated outbreak assessment for 21 July 2025 were corrected on 30 July 2025, and that assessment was added on 29 July 2025. A risk assessment on the likelihood of spread of HPAI H5Nx associated with bird fairs, shows, markets, sales and other gatherings for May 2025 was added on 20 June 2025. The 12 May 2025 outbreak assessment was added on 13 May 2025, and the 18 March 2025 assessment was added on 24 March 2025. A risk assessment on the same gatherings topic for January 2025 was added on 20 February 2025. The record also lists assessments and reports from earlier years, including outbreak assessments for Great Britain and Europe, risk assessments on gatherings and on the incursion of HPAI into housed or not housed poultry flocks and captive birds, and scientific opinions. The publication notes that major, notifiable or new and emerging animal disease outbreaks worldwide are monitored, and that a preliminary outbreak assessment may be carried out when a new animal disease outbreak becomes known in the UK or another country. It also states that earlier reports are available on the National Archives website and points to detailed guidance on spotting the disease, what to do if it is suspected, and measures to prevent it. news.content: 韩国野生鸟类中新型重配高致病性禽流感A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b病毒的多重引入、基因型多样性及贝叶斯系统发育动力学(2024–2025) 《Veterinary Research》:Multiple introductions and spread of novel reassortant highly pathogenic avian influenza A (H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b viruses via wild birds, South Korea, 2024–2025 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年10月09日 来源:Veterinary Research 3.8 编辑推荐: 2024年10月14日至2025年3月24日期间,通过国家高致病性禽流感(highly pathogenic avian influenza,HPAI)监测项目,在野生鸟类中检测到43例clade 2.3.4.4b HPAI A型(H5N1)感染,并在1只豹猫 欢迎领域“高通量小分子筛选解决方案”>> 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 Research Open access 2024年10月14日至2025年3月24日期间,通过国家高致病性禽流感(highly pathogenic avian influenza,HPAI)监测项目,在野生鸟类中检测到43例clade 2.3.4.4b HPAI A型(H5N1)感染,并在1只豹猫中检测到1例。研究人员对51株分离株进行了全基因组测序,并调查了其系统发育关系。系统发育分析鉴定出9种不同基因型,命名为Kor24–25A至Kor24–25I。最常检出的基因型Kor24–25A(n = 24)在鹈形目(Pelecaniformes)中频繁检出,并在2024年12月至2025年1月间最为流行。使用HA(hemagglutinin,血凝素)基因序列进行的贝叶斯连续和离散性状系统发育动力学分析(Bayesian continuous and discrete trait phylodynamic analyses)确定了经由京畿道、济州岛和朝鲜半岛南部沿海地区的3条最可能病毒引入途径,并提示野鸭是促进病毒在野生鸟类种群中传播的主要储存宿主。2024–2025季节期间,大白鹭(Ardea alba)似乎比其他野生鸟种更频繁受累,提示野生鸟类中物种特异性疾病结局可能存在季节性差异。该研究为HPAI H5N1病毒的系统发育动力学、宿主关联和传播模式提供了重要见解。它强调针对关键禽类宿主和高风险地理区域的强化监测项目的重要性。 论文解读:韩国野生鸟类中新型重配HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b病毒的多重引入与传播(2024–2025) 欢迎领取《放射性同位素检测一站式解决方案》 领 取 研究背景:A/Goose/Guangdong/1/1996(Gs/Gd)谱系H5高致病性禽流感(HPAI)病毒1996年在中国家鹅中首次发现,之后在家禽和野鸟中反复暴发。其血凝素(HA)基因已分化为0–9 clades及多个亚支。clade 2.3.4于2008年在中国出现,演化为2.3.4.4a–h。clade 2.3.4.4b自2014年起与当地禽流感病毒广泛重配,产生H5N2、H5N5、H5N6、H5N8等。至2021年末,clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1成为全球优势HPAI亚型,在亚洲、欧洲、非洲和北美野鸟和家禽中广泛暴发,并因宿主范围扩大和反复溢出至哺乳动物(包括人)引发公共卫生关注。韩国自2003年首次HPAI H5N1侵入后,反复发生H5Nx(H5N1、H5N8、H5N6)暴发,野鸟在引入和传播中持续起关键作用。2020–2021冬季报告234例野鸟clade 2.3.4.4b HPAI病例,2021–2022为47起,2022–2023为174例,2023–2024为19例,季节间规模和病毒活动差异明显,并出现不同基因型,提示反复引入和野鸟种群内重配。2024–2025季节clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1经野鸟传入韩国,且2025年3月在野生豹猫(Prionailurus bengalensis)中检测到HPAI H5N1,为韩国该野生哺乳动物首次记录的溢出事件,显示宿主范围扩大和对动物及公共卫生的持续威胁。因此,研究人员对2024–2025冬季韩国野鸟和豹猫H5N1病毒进行全基因组测序和比较系统发育分析,以阐明时空扩散路径、进化动态和宿主转换。 研究人员开展:2024年10月14日至2025年3月24日,通过国家HPAI监测项目在野生鸟类中报告43例clade 2.3.4.4b HPAI H5N1感染,1例豹猫。研究人员对51株H5N1分离株进行全基因组测序,并开展系统发育和贝叶斯系统发育动力学分析。结论:鉴定出9种基因型Kor24–25A至Kor24–25I;Kor24–25A(n=24)最常见,在鹈形目频繁检出,2024年12月至2025年1月最流行;贝叶斯分析基于HA识别三条最可能引入路线,经京畿、济州和朝鲜半岛南部沿海;野鸭为主要储存宿主;大白鹭更频繁受累,提示季节性物种差异。意义:提供HPAI H5N1系统发育动力学、宿主关联和传播模式见解,强调针对关键禽类宿主和高风险地区加强监测。 关键技术方法(不超过250字):样本来源为2024年10月至2025年3月由韩国国家野生动物疾病控制与预防研究所(NIWDC)开展的全国野动物监测,覆盖92个监测点,收集57,067份粪便和1,007份个体鸟拭子,并被动检查419具尸体;从43起暴发中获得51株病毒,包括2025年3月16日豹猫分离株。关键技术包括:实时逆转录聚合酶链反应(rRT-PCR)筛查M和H5基因;Illumina MiSeq全基因组测序并提交GISAID;MAFFT比对,RAxML最大似然(ML)系统发育,iTOL可视化,PopArt最小生成网络,ggFLU基因型分类,FluMut分子标记筛查;TempEst评估分子钟信号;BEAST/BEAUti贝叶斯连续和离散性状系统发育动力学分析,CIPRES运行,Tracer、LogCombiner、TreeAnnotator、FigTree、EvoLaps、SpreaD3和PACT分析传播路线、宿主转换和状态比例。 研究结果: **Multiple genotypes of 2024–2025 HPAI viruses**:研究人员成功对2024年10月14日至2025年3月24日韩国野生动物中51株H5N1 HPAI病毒测序。ML系统发育显示所有基因片段存在多个遗传簇,bootstrap支持>90:PB2三个、PB1四个、PA三个、HA两个、NP五个、NA两个、M一个、NS一个。多数簇内序列>98%成对核苷酸同一性,但A/Mandarin duck/Korea/24WF743–8P/2025的PB1、A/Wild goose/Korea/24WF894–1P/2025和A/Mandarin duck/Korea/24WF266–5P/2024的NS例外。鉴定九种基因型:Kor24–25A(AAAAAAAA;n=24)、Kor24–25B(BBBBBBAB;n=11)、Kor24–25C(AAABAAAA;n=8)、Kor24–25D(AAAADAAA;n=1)、Kor24–25E(ACAACAAA;n=2)、Kor24–25F(CCCACAAA;n=2)、Kor24–25G(AAAAEAAA;n=1)、Kor24–25H(ADAAAAAA;n=1)、Kor24–25I(DAAAAAAA;n=1)。最小生成网络显示病毒大体按基因型聚类,但核苷酸替换数不总严格对应基因型边界。Kor24–25A、B、C为主要基因型;C的HA与B近,其余七片段与A近;其他六种为短暂次要变异,各1–2株,多数片段与A共享但内部基因不同。Kor24–25D、G、H的PB1或NP来自东亚既往HPAI谱系;Kor24–25E、F、I的PB2或NP与中亚和东亚低致病性禽流感(LPAI)病毒近;E和F的PB1形成独立簇,bootstrap 100,与欧洲–俄罗斯HPAI病毒同一性97.5–98.0%。ggFLU等分类显示Kor24–25B对应B23.2–1,GenoFLU A3/A5,GenIn2 EA–2020–C;其余40样本ggFLU为B.18,GenIn2和GenoFLU未分配。FluMut发现十种突变组合A–J;Kor24–25A含F、E、C型,B含G、J型,C含H、I型,其他各单一型,F由四种基因型共享。 **Temporal and host distributions of HPAI viruses**:2024年10月至2025年3月,51株病毒周分布显示,2024年10月第三周首次检测时Kor24–25A和B同时出现,2024年11月D、E、C出现。野鸟HPAI病例2024年12月达峰。2024年12月第三周优势基因型从B转为A。A全季持续,B在2024年12月后未记录;次要基因型2024年12月后零星检出。宿主分布中,鹈形目占最高比例,其次雁形目、猛禽(Falconiformes和Accipitriformes)、鸻形目和食肉目。鹈形目中大白鹭最多(n=22),主要关联Kor24–25A。雁形目基因型多样性最高,检出7种。猛禽检出A、B、C、I四种。三种主要基因型跨多种宿主:A和B除食肉目外所有宿主组,C见于雁形目、食肉目和猛禽。 **Spatiotemporal transmission patterns of HPAI viruses**:基于HA的贝叶斯系统发育动力学揭示2024–2025冬季H5N1时空传播。cluster 1首例为2024年10月14日京畿地区捕获鸳鸯,HA来自Kor24–25A,tMRCA为2024年5月6日(95% HPD:2023年12月20日至2024年8月29日)。连续系统地理学提示京畿道为cluster 1在韩国最可能祖先地点,随后向南部扩散,部分再向北,另一些可能传播至日本南部。cluster 2含Kor24–25B和C的HA,分2a(主要B)和2b(主要C),提示独立引入。2a tMRCA为2024年7月7日(95% HPD:2024年3月27日至9月20日);2b为2024年7月27日(95% HPD:2024年3月23日至11月9日);cluster 2整体tMRCA为2024年2月23日(95% HPD:2023年11月11日至2024年7月26日)。2a最可能祖先地点为济州,随后向北并向东西扩散;2b最可能为朝鲜半岛南部沿海,分两路,一路向北至忠清,一路向南至济州,北上病毒后来沿西部沿海向南移动。 **Transmission of HPAI viruses between host species**:基于HA的宿主离散性状分析中,BF>3且PP>0.5为显著,BF>20且PP>0.9为强支持。cluster 1最可能经野鸭引入(BF=5.448,PP=0.708);随后野鸭至鹭(BF=30.831,PP=0.932)和其他野鸟(BF=5.467,PP=0.708);鹭至其他野鸟(BF=23.587,PP=0.913);野鸭至韩国外谱系(BF=43.286,PP=0.951)强支持。cluster 2同样可能经野鸭从韩国外引入(BF=75.497,PP=0.971);野鸭至其他野鸟(BF=89.554,PP=0.997)和鹭(BF=39.928,PP=0.947)强支持;未推断鹭起源传播。祖先离散状态主干比例随时间依次为韩国外、韩国野鸭、韩国鹭、韩国其他。源–汇动态显示两簇转换事件均发生在2024年Q3,从野鸭到鹭和其他物种;cluster 1另有2024年Q4和2025年Q1鹭到其他物种。Markov rewards显示cluster 1野鸭最高,其次鹭和其他;cluster 2野鸭最高,其他次之,鹭最低。 讨论部分总结:研究人员报告2024–2025冬季野鸟中九种新HPAI基因型,提示clade 2.3.4.4b HPAI与共循环HPAI或LPAI频繁重配。内部基因中M和NS遗传多样性最低,NP形成最多单系枝。Kor24–25A、B、C为主要基因型,时间分布不同;A持续整个监测期,B仅早期至2024年12月第五周,约占采样期一半。早期基因型短暂优势此前已有,但与2021–2022和2022–2023冬季随暴发进展基因型多样性下降不同,本季持续遗传多样性。A、B、C在多种野鸟检出,宿主范围广。雁形目基因型多样性最高,符合其主要水鸟储存库角色;鹭至其他野鸟传播提示鹭可作易感宿主和潜在中间宿主参与本地传播。猛禽基因型多样性第二,与既往低或无禽流感病毒流行报道不同,可能因捕食感染水禽。豹猫Kor24–25C零星感染可能因食入感染野鸟。HA贝叶斯分析识别三个病毒簇,表明至少三次独立引入。cluster 1引入地区既往为HPAI侵入高风险区,来自俄罗斯、蒙古、中国风险高于日本;cluster 2引入地区济州和南部与日本引入风险较高,且2024–2025日本H5 HPAI HA分析显示来自cluster 2a的24WC025与同期日本分离株同枝。2a和2b可能经野鸟独立引入不同地区,所有基因序列与既往野鸟病毒近,重配更可能发生在亚洲迁徙野鸟而非家禽。离散性状分析提示季节特异性宿主分布和传播。既往研究认为野鸭在早期引入和国内传播重要,鹅在后续传播贡献较大;但2024–2025鹅源病毒仅5.9%(3/51),可能反映鹅死亡或尸体检测减少;鹭源病毒43.13%(22/51),明显高于既往HPAI暴发。2022–2023有鹤类(hooded cranes和white-naped cranes)大规模暴发,2024–2025未检出HPAI阳性鹤,显示受影响宿主季节差异。研究人员强调需继续多物种监测和野鸟病理生物学研究。野生鸟源病毒分析需谨慎,因监测可能不完全代表野鸟多样性,并偏向体型较大、数量较多或致病性较高物种。 研究结论翻译:总体而言,基于HA基因的贝叶斯系统发育动力学分析刻画了HPAI H5N1病毒进入韩国的多条引入途径、国内基因型特异性传播模式,以及野鸭和大白鹭在病毒传播中的关键作用。韩国多条引入途径和频繁重配事件的观察强调了该地区HPAI流行病学的复杂性。这些发现为HPAI H5N1病毒传播动力学提供了有价值的见解,并强调针对关键禽类宿主和高风险地理区域加强监测项目的重要性。然而,野生鸟源病毒分析应谨慎解释,因为监测可能不能完全代表野生鸟类种群多样性,并可能偏向体型较大、数量较多或表现出较高致病性的物种。未来整合病理生物学、野生鸟类生态学和候鸟迁徙数据的综合方法将进一步促进对野生鸟类中clade 2.3.4.4b HPAI生态学和流行病学的理解,并提高对未来暴发的准备。 论文解读:韩国野生鸟类中新型重配HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b病毒的多重引入与传播(2024–2025)研究背景:A/Goose/Guangdong/1/1996(Gs/Gd)谱系H5高致病性禽流感(HPAI)病毒1996年在中国家鹅中首次发现,之后在家禽和野鸟中反复暴发。其血凝素(HA)基因已分化为0–9 clades及多个亚支。clade 2.3.4于2008年在中国出现,演化为2.3.4.4a–h。clade 2.3.4.4b自2014年起与当地禽流感病毒广泛重配,产生H5N2、H5N5、H5N6、H5N8等。至2021年末,clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1成为全球优势HPAI亚型,在亚洲、欧洲、非洲和北美野鸟和家禽中广泛暴发,并因宿主范围扩大和反复溢出至哺乳动物(包括人)引发公共卫生关注。韩国自2003年首次HPAI H5N1侵入后,反复发生H5Nx(H5N1、H5N8、H5N6)暴发,野鸟在引入和传播中持续起关键作用。2020–2021冬季报告234例野鸟clade 2.3.4.4b HPAI病例,2021–2022为47起,2022–2023为174例,2023–2024为19例,季节间规模和病毒活动差异明显,并出现不同基因型,提示反复引入和野鸟种群内重配。2024–2025季节clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1经野鸟传入韩国,且2025年3月在野生豹猫(Prionailurus bengalensis)中检测到HPAI H5N1,为韩国该野生哺乳动物首次记录的溢出事件,显示宿主范围扩大和对动物及公共卫生的持续威胁。因此,研究人员对2024–2025冬季韩国野鸟和豹猫H5N1病毒进行全基因组测序和比较系统发育分析,以阐明时空扩散路径、进化动态和宿主转换。研究人员开展:2024年10月14日至2025年3月24日,通过国家HPAI监测项目在野生鸟类中报告43例clade 2.3.4.4b HPAI H5N1感染,1例豹猫。研究人员对51株H5N1分离株进行全基因组测序,并开展系统发育和贝叶斯系统发育动力学分析。结论:鉴定出9种基因型Kor24–25A至Kor24–25I;Kor24–25A(n=24)最常见,在鹈形目频繁检出,2024年12月至2025年1月最流行;贝叶斯分析基于HA识别三条最可能引入路线,经京畿、济州和朝鲜半岛南部沿海;野鸭为主要储存宿主;大白鹭更频繁受累,提示季节性物种差异。意义:提供HPAI H5N1系统发育动力学、宿主关联和传播模式见解,强调针对关键禽类宿主和高风险地区加强监测。关键技术方法(不超过250字):样本来源为2024年10月至2025年3月由韩国国家野生动物疾病控制与预防研究所(NIWDC)开展的全国野动物监测,覆盖92个监测点,收集57,067份粪便和1,007份个体鸟拭子,并被动检查419具尸体;从43起暴发中获得51株病毒,包括2025年3月16日豹猫分离株。关键技术包括:实时逆转录聚合酶链反应(rRT-PCR)筛查M和H5基因;Illumina MiSeq全基因组测序并提交GISAID;MAFFT比对,RAxML最大似然(ML)系统发育,iTOL可视化,PopArt最小生成网络,ggFLU基因型分类,FluMut分子标记筛查;TempEst评估分子钟信号;BEAST/BEAUti贝叶斯连续和离散性状系统发育动力学分析,CIPRES运行,Tracer、LogCombiner、TreeAnnotator、FigTree、EvoLaps、SpreaD3和PACT分析传播路线、宿主转换和状态比例。研究结果:**Multiple genotypes of 2024–2025 HPAI viruses**:研究人员成功对2024年10月14日至2025年3月24日韩国野生动物中51株H5N1 HPAI病毒测序。ML系统发育显示所有基因片段存在多个遗传簇,bootstrap支持>90:PB2三个、PB1四个、PA三个、HA两个、NP五个、NA两个、M一个、NS一个。多数簇内序列>98%成对核苷酸同一性,但A/Mandarin duck/Korea/24WF743–8P/2025的PB1、A/Wild goose/Korea/24WF894–1P/2025和A/Mandarin duck/Korea/24WF266–5P/2024的NS例外。鉴定九种基因型:Kor24–25A(AAAAAAAA;n=24)、Kor24–25B(BBBBBBAB;n=11)、Kor24–25C(AAABAAAA;n=8)、Kor24–25D(AAAADAAA;n=1)、Kor24–25E(ACAACAAA;n=2)、Kor24–25F(CCCACAAA;n=2)、Kor24–25G(AAAAEAAA;n=1)、Kor24–25H(ADAAAAAA;n=1)、Kor24–25I(DAAAAAAA;n=1)。最小生成网络显示病毒大体按基因型聚类,但核苷酸替换数不总严格对应基因型边界。Kor24–25A、B、C为主要基因型;C的HA与B近,其余七片段与A近;其他六种为短暂次要变异,各1–2株,多数片段与A共享但内部基因不同。Kor24–25D、G、H的PB1或NP来自东亚既往HPAI谱系;Kor24–25E、F、I的PB2或NP与中亚和东亚低致病性禽流感(LPAI)病毒近;E和F的PB1形成独立簇,bootstrap 100,与欧洲–俄罗斯HPAI病毒同一性97.5–98.0%。ggFLU等分类显示Kor24–25B对应B23.2–1,GenoFLU A3/A5,GenIn2 EA–2020–C;其余40样本ggFLU为B.18,GenIn2和GenoFLU未分配。FluMut发现十种突变组合A–J;Kor24–25A含F、E、C型,B含G、J型,C含H、I型,其他各单一型,F由四种基因型共享。**Temporal and host distributions of HPAI viruses**:2024年10月至2025年3月,51株病毒周分布显示,2024年10月第三周首次检测时Kor24–25A和B同时出现,2024年11月D、E、C出现。野鸟HPAI病例2024年12月达峰。2024年12月第三周优势基因型从B转为A。A全季持续,B在2024年12月后未记录;次要基因型2024年12月后零星检出。宿主分布中,鹈形目占最高比例,其次雁形目、猛禽(Falconiformes和Accipitriformes)、鸻形目和食肉目。鹈形目中大白鹭最多(n=22),主要关联Kor24–25A。雁形目基因型多样性最高,检出7种。猛禽检出A、B、C、I四种。三种主要基因型跨多种宿主:A和B除食肉目外所有宿主组,C见于雁形目、食肉目和猛禽。**Spatiotemporal transmission patterns of HPAI viruses**:基于HA的贝叶斯系统发育动力学揭示2024–2025冬季H5N1时空传播。cluster 1首例为2024年10月14日京畿地区捕获鸳鸯,HA来自Kor24–25A,tMRCA为2024年5月6日(95% HPD:2023年12月20日至2024年8月29日)。连续系统地理学提示京畿道为cluster 1在韩国最可能祖先地点,随后向南部扩散,部分再向北,另一些可能传播至日本南部。cluster 2含Kor24–25B和C的HA,分2a(主要B)和2b(主要C),提示独立引入。2a tMRCA为2024年7月7日(95% HPD:2024年3月27日至9月20日);2b为2024年7月27日(95% HPD:2024年3月23日至11月9日);cluster 2整体tMRCA为2024年2月23日(95% HPD:2023年11月11日至2024年7月26日)。2a最可能祖先地点为济州,随后向北并向东西扩散;2b最可能为朝鲜半岛南部沿海,分两路,一路向北至忠清,一路向南至济州,北上病毒后来沿西部沿海向南移动。**Transmission of HPAI viruses between host species**:基于HA的宿主离散性状分析中,BF>3且PP>0.5为显著,BF>20且PP>0.9为强支持。cluster 1最可能经野鸭引入(BF=5.448,PP=0.708);随后野鸭至鹭(BF=30.831,PP=0.932)和其他野鸟(BF=5.467,PP=0.708);鹭至其他野鸟(BF=23.587,PP=0.913);野鸭至韩国外谱系(BF=43.286,PP=0.951)强支持。cluster 2同样可能经野鸭从韩国外引入(BF=75.497,PP=0.971);野鸭至其他野鸟(BF=89.554,PP=0.997)和鹭(BF=39.928,PP=0.947)强支持;未推断鹭起源传播。祖先离散状态主干比例随时间依次为韩国外、韩国野鸭、韩国鹭、韩国其他。源–汇动态显示两簇转换事件均发生在2024年Q3,从野鸭到鹭和其他物种;cluster 1另有2024年Q4和2025年Q1鹭到其他物种。Markov rewards显示cluster 1野鸭最高,其次鹭和其他;cluster 2野鸭最高,其他次之,鹭最低。讨论部分总结:研究人员报告2024–2025冬季野鸟中九种新HPAI基因型,提示clade 2.3.4.4b HPAI与共循环HPAI或LPAI频繁重配。内部基因中M和NS遗传多样性最低,NP形成最多单系枝。Kor24–25A、B、C为主要基因型,时间分布不同;A持续整个监测期,B仅早期至2024年12月第五周,约占采样期一半。早期基因型短暂优势此前已有,但与2021–2022和2022–2023冬季随暴发进展基因型多样性下降不同,本季持续遗传多样性。A、B、C在多种野鸟检出,宿主范围广。雁形目基因型多样性最高,符合其主要水鸟储存库角色;鹭至其他野鸟传播提示鹭可作易感宿主和潜在中间宿主参与本地传播。猛禽基因型多样性第二,与既往低或无禽流感病毒流行报道不同,可能因捕食感染水禽。豹猫Kor24–25C零星感染可能因食入感染野鸟。HA贝叶斯分析识别三个病毒簇,表明至少三次独立引入。cluster 1引入地区既往为HPAI侵入高风险区,来自俄罗斯、蒙古、中国风险高于日本;cluster 2引入地区济州和南部与日本引入风险较高,且2024–2025日本H5 HPAI HA分析显示来自cluster 2a的24WC025与同期日本分离株同枝。2a和2b可能经野鸟独立引入不同地区,所有基因序列与既往野鸟病毒近,重配更可能发生在亚洲迁徙野鸟而非家禽。离散性状分析提示季节特异性宿主分布和传播。既往研究认为野鸭在早期引入和国内传播重要,鹅在后续传播贡献较大;但2024–2025鹅源病毒仅5.9%(3/51),可能反映鹅死亡或尸体检测减少;鹭源病毒43.13%(22/51),明显高于既往HPAI暴发。2022–2023有鹤类(hooded cranes和white-naped cranes)大规模暴发,2024–2025未检出HPAI阳性鹤,显示受影响宿主季节差异。研究人员强调需继续多物种监测和野鸟病理生物学研究。野生鸟源病毒分析需谨慎,因监测可能不完全代表野鸟多样性,并偏向体型较大、数量较多或致病性较高物种。研究结论翻译:总体而言,基于HA基因的贝叶斯系统发育动力学分析刻画了HPAI
